News.title: Morrisons huge change in aisles in 497 stores in ‘end of era’ update
News.content:
Morrisons huge change in aisles in 497 stores in ‘end of era’ update

Chain has been introducing scheme which is aiming to change shopping for customers across the UK

View Image Morrisons is getting rid of paper shelf labels at its stores across the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Morrisons makes huge change in 497 stores in ‘end of era’Morrisons has given an update on a massive scheme which means the ‘end of an era’ for shoppers in all the aisles in its 497 stores. This week the chain explained how the rollout of e-labels which will mean the end of printed price information.

‌



Across the supermarket chain’s 497 stores, 10.8 million smart electronic shelf labels are being installed. This week the chain said the rollout was proceeding ‘well’ as it becomes the first large British grocer to fully digitise its pricing.The smart labels update pricing, promotions, and Morrisons More Card loyalty discounts in real time, while integrating with shelf-edge cameras to boost online picking accuracy and guide staff to product gaps. Morrisons said the electronic shelf labels will eliminate traditional paper labels throughout the store, ‘providing clear and accurate price and product information’ and meaning staff are freed up to help customers more.

‌



The new technology will also use digital shelf-edge cameras, meaning staff spot when lines have sold out. The roll-out of the new digital labelling system across Morrisons supermarket estate started earlier 2026 and today the chain confirmed it is aiming to have it in all stores.

‌



The project will also include an upgrade of Morrisons in-store wi-fi infrastructure, delivering an better in-store connections for customers.

VusionGroupi is installing the changes and other improvements include the roll-out of shelf-edge cameras, the introduction of a digital task management platform and trials of AI-powered shopping trolleys.

Gordon Macpherson, Group Productivity Director of Morrisons, said: “As digital innovation reshapes the retail landscape, we’re constantly evaluating new technology that can help us serve customers better. We’re excited to be the first large supermarket group in the UK to introduce digital shelf edge labelling across our entire supermarket estate. This latest investment further underlines our commitment to modernising and digitising our business to deliver an enhanced shopping experience for Morrisons customers.”

‌



“This agreement with Morrisons is a powerful example of how VusionGroup is executing on its 2027 strategic plan,” said Roy Horgan, CEO UK & Ireland at VusionGroup. “We are building a platform for transformation - one that not only delivers immediate value but also evolves with our clients’ needs. Morrisons is a trusted and innovative retailer, and we are proud to support their transformation journey.”

“This partnership with Morrisons is a cornerstone in our strategic roadmap towards 2027 and exemplifies our commitment to driving transformation at scale,” said Sébastien Fourcy, SEVP EMEA at VusionGroup. “By equipping all their supermarkets with our solutions, we’re not only delivering immediate operational benefits, but also laying the foundation for future innovation in omnichannel retail across the UK which is a key market for us in the EMEA region.”

Last year, Asda rolled out ESLs to its largest and busiest Express stores, with 250 locations now featuring the new technology. Meanwhile, Co-op upgraded its ESLs in August, enabling shoppers to “tap to join” its membership scheme.

‌



It comes as Morrisons announced it is introducing money-saving offers to seasonal favourites both in store and online.

The deals are said to bring together fresh fruit, lunchbox favourites, quick meal ingredients, snacks and drinks ready for days out and picnics. Examples include a three-for-£5 deal on berries, grapes, cherries, nectarines, apples, oranges and pears throughout July and August.

There’s also savings on picnic staples such as a six-pack of Dairylea Dunkers Jumbo Tubes, which have been reduced from £3.29 to £1.50. Original and Light Philadelphia Soft Cheese (165g) has also been reduced from £2.25 to £1.35 until July 28.

‌



There’s also a two-for-£3 offer on 500ml bottles of Fever Tree Refreshingly Light Tonic Water, Light Elderflower Tonic Water, Mexican Lime Soda and Refreshingly Light Ginger Ale.

A seven-pack of Penguin biscuits are now £1.25 and four-packs of Cadbury Dairy Milk Freddos, Little Bars and Cadbury Fudge Bars now all £1.25 throughout July too. They claim the savings will be made clear in stores and online so they’re easier for customers to spot.

The news comes after the reports that the supermarket it would be shutting 100 of its convenience stores. Alex Paver, Morrisons’s customer value and loyalty director, said: “With school holidays meaning more meals at home and more days out, we know value matters more than ever.

Article continues below

“That’s why we have focused these savings on our Market Street fresh fruit alongside popular snacks and drinks, helping customers enjoy fresh, quality food and make the most of summer for less.”

The news comes after Primark slashed prices on hundreds of best-selling womenswear, menswear and kidswear styles in store. They claimed it is part of the firm’s new era of ‘Iconic Value’ which will continue across Autumn and Winter 2026 collections.

News.title: Ryanair CEO says airports shouldn't serve booze until 12pm to stop 'misbehaviour'
News.content:
Ryanair CEO says airports shouldn't serve booze until 12pm to stop 'misbehaviour'

Michael O'Leary says Ryanair flights are being diverted due to 'aggressive' passengers who have had 'copious amounts' of booze while waiting for takeoff in the airport

View 3 Images File photo of friends enjoying a beer (Image: Getty Images )

Airports should stop serving alcohol to passengers before ‘11am or 12pm’ to prevent ‘misbehaviour’ on flights, according to Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary.

‌



The CEO of the budget airline has called for restrictions on the amount of booze passengers can buy before boarding a plane, saying bars and airports are ‘passing the problem on to poor old dumb airlines’.

‌



Speaking on The Travel Expert with Simon Calder podcast on Friday (July 24), Mr O’Leary also suggested policing the amount of alcohol holidaymakers can purchase in bars with similar rules used in duty free.

‌



The 65-year-old Irishman said he would be happy to implement a two-drink limit on Ryanair flights as part of a ‘quid pro quo’ arrangement with airports to stop ‘aggressive, argumentative’ drunk passengers disrupting flights.

View 3 Images Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary (Image: PA)

When asked if airlines should introduce a two drink limit, he replied: “No problem with it. I mean very few passengers on board our aircraft would buy more than two drinks anyway, but if the quid pro quo was the airline’s limited to two drinks? Done. In a heartbeat.

‌



“The real issue we have to recognise is an industry problem of misbehaviour, and the misbehaviour is getting worse. Particularly due periods of flight delays, you have people sitting in airports consuming copious amounts of alcohol.”

Mr O’Leary said stopping drunks boarding is difficult for Ryanair staff. He continued: “It is very hard to identify unless they are staggeringly drunk, unless they can't stand up straight.

“Most people, even drunks, can pass through, show your passport and get onboard. And you have a combination, some cases, of alcohol and drugs, and they get aggressive and argumentative. In the old days, if you drank too much, you just fell asleep on board a plane.”

‌



He then took aim at airport policies for serving customer booze from early in the morning. Mr O’Leary added: “It continues to be a mystery to me why pubs at airports are allowed to open at 6am in the morning, serving alcohol. Why do you not serve tea and coffees until 11 o'clock or 12 o'clock in the afternoon? “

He also suggested to The Telegraph podcast that another measure could work: “But the critical thing here is we limit the amount of people, duty-free, can buy — [we] say, show your boarding pass.

“Why don't we do the same but with alcoholic drinks at bars? [Bars] pass the problem on to the airline. The airports don't care. They just passed the problem on to the airlines, and the poor old dumb airlines are diverting planes.

‌



View 3 Images File photo of a Ryanair flight (Image: Peter Byrne/PA Wire)

“Like it causes real upset to fellow passengers onboard. When you've aggressive people, they're shouting and screaming and drunk and disrupting our crews.

“Our crews shouldn't have to work in that environment. And our fellow passengers deserve the respect that airports will not be shovelling alcohol into these people, particularly during flight delays, copious amounts of alcohol, so that they can misbehave.”

Article continues below

Mr O’Leary’s appearance on the podcast comes days after his company announced pre-tax profits fell by nearly a third as oil prices surged thanks to the Iran War. When pressed on the news, he remained upbeat about the airline’s future, pointing out passenger numbers were rising.

News.title: X Factor man says going to B&M was like 'being transported to hell'
News.content:
X Factor man says going to B&M was like 'being transported to hell'

He filmed the 'ridiculous' situation in a video which hit a nerve

X Factor man says going to B&M was like 'being transported to hell'

A former X-Factor contestant has slammed B&M for being ‘too hot’ as their entire chocolate stock melted on the shelves in the summer heat. Marlon McKenzie, who appeared on the talent show multiple times, had been craving chocolate.

‌



The 43-year-old, along with his friend and daughter, made the 10-minute drive to the store in Burnage, Manchester. But, as they arrived, they were hit with a ‘sweltering’ heat and when reaching the chocolate aisle, were met with devastation.

‌



All the chocolate bars had completely melted. “Instantly, it was like being transported straight to hell,” said the model. “It was scorching hot and I couldn’t bear to be in there for more than 10 minutes. I was beading with sweat and wiping my brow constantly as it was so unbearable.

‌



View 3 Images The chocolate was melting

“Once I saw the chocolate, which was flopping down on the shelf, I was shocked. The bars were practically folding in half.”

‌



Marlon, who was on X Factor in 2005, 2008 and 2010 - when he got through to Judge's Houses - visited the store on July 10. Temperatures, in the middle of the UK’s heatwave, registered at 30C for the area.

While there was air con blasting, Marlon said: “ I didn’t see any shop workers on the floor [thankfully]. All the customers were flustered and shocked by the heat. I got my chocolate bars, picking the ones that weren’t so bad, and got out of there.”

View 3 Images Marlon McKenzie inside the store

‌



In the clip, Marlon shows himself in B&M as he wipes his soaked forehead. He said: “I’ve just stepped foot in here and I’m f*****g melting. “I’ve actually come all the way to B&M purposefully to get chocolate bars – but this is ridiculous.”

Marlon picks up a bar of KitKats and squashes the pack with ease. He then does the same with a bar of Cadbury’s Marvellous Creations. One bar, of Cadbury and More Biscoff, folds over the curve of his hand.

‌



He said: “Everything is just ruined” and asks the question of whether all the stock would be thrown away. U sers have flocked to the comments to share their reactions.

“Didn’t you know? B&M stands for Burn & Melt,” Ollie said. Lucie added: “My B&M I work at is fine we have air con all our chocolate isn’t melted it’s fine freezing inside.”

View 3 Images Marlon was on X Factor and is now a model

‌



“Surely ac is cheaper than a whole shops worth of melted chocolate,” someone else commented. Even Morrisons got in on the banter, saying: “Average B&M experience,” with a snap of SpongeBob engulfed in flames.

“The way you’re squeezing all of them is hilarious,” another user added. Marlon claims he returned to the store a few days later to check on the chocolate and found the section had been cleared out.

Article continues below

He added: “It has to be pretty hot in store for chocolate to melt to that point. It’s so bad.”

A spokesperson for B&M said: "During periods of exceptionally warm weather, we closely monitor conditions across our stores, regularly check temperatures, and continue to invest in air conditioning and additional cooling measures to help maintain product quality.

“As always, any product that does not meet our strict quality standards is removed from sale. We are also taking practical steps to support our colleagues, including more frequent breaks and additional cooling measures, to help keep store teams as comfortable as possible."

News.title: UK airport drop off fees up by a third - full list of most expensive
News.content:
UK airport drop off fees up by a third - full list of most expensive

The cost to drop friends and family off at the airport this summer has increased by a third at most airports across the UK - with some short stays costing a whopping £10

View 2 Images Drop off fees at airports are higher than ever (Image: Chris Radburn/PA Wire)

Dropping off family and friends at the airport this summer will cost you even more as new research has found that fees have increased by a third over the last year.

‌



It was found that 16 out of 20 airports analysed had increased or introduced so-called "kiss and fly" fees since last summer, according to the RAC.

‌



Some airports are now charging as much as £10 just to stop outside the terminal for a few minutes.

‌



The most costly airports are still Gatwick and Stansted, with terminal drop-offs costing £10 at both.

View 2 Images Edinburgh Airport pick up and drop off point where charges have risen to £8.50 for up to 10 minutes.

The bigger shock comes as the only major airport that offered free terminal drop-offs, London City, now has one of the costliest fees charged on a per-minute basis.

‌



Drivers dropping off relatives at London City are now charged £8 for five minutes, making it the highest charge per minute among airports included in the research.

The next most expensive drop off zones are outside of England's capital.

One is in Scotland, as Edinburgh charges £8.50 for up to 10 minutes. Bristol also charges the same fees.

‌



The RAC noted the average cost of airport drop-off fees has increased by around a third over the past year, despite many of the world's busiest airports continuing to offer free terminal drop-offs.

The organisation highlighted that none of the busiest airports in the European Union charge drivers for dropping passengers off outside terminals.

In some of the world's busiest hubs, including Dubai, these fees also do not exist.

‌



Most UK airports do have alternative options that are free, however these are usually located in mid or long-stay car parks, with passengers needing to catch a shuttle bus to the terminal.

RAC senior policy officer Rod Dennis said: "It's disappointing to see so many airports charging so much for what many regard as a simple act of kindness in dropping off family and friends.

"Having a captive audience should be no excuse for these farewell fees, especially when they're completely at odds with how major airports around the world operate.

‌



"Of course, airports need to manage the limited space they have carefully, but if free, convenient drop-off zones work at many other international airports, then why not here?"

Mr Dennis also warned drivers to take extra care when using airports with "park now, pay later" systems without barriers.

He said: "Those that drop off but miss the signage or forget to pay soon afterwards can face a parking charge notice as high as £100 - a fee that feels distinctly disproportionate to the contravention."

Article continues below

There were only four airports in the study that had not increased their costs. Liverpool John Lennon, East Midlands, Belfast City and Southampton.

News.title: Which is actually better for your gut Greek yoghurt or natural yoghurt?
News.content:
Which is actually better for your gut Greek yoghurt or natural yoghurt?

Both yoghurts are packed with nutrients and good bacteria, but the benefits of natural yoghurt and Greek yoghurt differ more than most people realise

View 3 Images Both yoghurts are packed with nutrients and good bacteria, but the benefits of natural yoghurt and Greek yoghurt differ more than most people realise (Image: Arx0nt via Getty Images)

With more people paying closer attention to what they eat, yoghurt has become a staple of the health-conscious kitchen — but not all yoghurts are created equal. Natural yoghurt and Greek yoghurt may look similar on the supermarket shelf, yet the differences between them can have a real impact on your diet, your digestion, and even the way your food turns out when cooking.

‌



Whether you are trying to eat more protein, support your gut health, or simply find the best yoghurt for your favourite recipes, knowing which variety to reach for can make a genuine difference. Both have their own health benefits, but they are not interchangeable — and understanding why could change the way you shop.

‌



View 3 Images Natural yoghurt is a good source of calcium and B vitamins (Image: OlgaLepeshkina via Getty Images)

‌



Natural yoghurt - what is it?

Fermenting milk with beneficial bacteria, typically Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus cultures, creates natural yoghurt. These live cultures are added to heated milk and left to ferment at a warm temperature.

During this time, the bacteria convert the natural sugars in the milk — primarily lactose — into lactic acid, which is what gives yoghurt its distinctively tangy flavour and helps preserve it.

Some varieties may also contain added cream to create a richer texture, while low-fat and skimmed milk versions offer a lighter alternative.

‌



Unlike flavoured yoghurts, natural yoghurt contains no added sugars, artificial sweeteners, or flavourings.

Natural yoghurt tends to have a smooth, creamy consistency and contains a balance of protein, carbohydrates, and fat depending on the type of milk used.

It is also a good source of calcium, B vitamins, and beneficial probiotics, which can support gut health and aid digestion.

‌



View 3 Images Greek yoghurt is thicker in consistency and has considerably more protein per serving (Image: Getty)

Greek yoghurt - what is it?

When you strain regular yoghurt through a fine cloth or filter to remove much of the liquid whey, you make Greek yoghurt.

This straining process takes several hours and may be repeated more than once to achieve the desired consistency, resulting in a product that is noticeably thicker and denser than standard natural yoghurt.

‌



This additional step produces a thicker, creamier product with a more concentrated nutritional profile.

Because a significant portion of the whey is removed during straining, Greek yoghurt contains considerably more protein per serving than natural yoghurt — often around twice as much.

The straining process also reduces the carbohydrate and lactose content, which can make it a more suitable option for those who are lactose intolerant or following a lower-carbohydrate diet.

‌



However, it is worth noting that the removal of whey also means Greek yoghurt tends to be lower in calcium than its unstrained counterpart.

How do they compare?

Both natural and Greek yoghurts make for wholesome additions to a well-rounded diet. Greek yoghurt is a good choice for those looking for a higher protein content and a denser, creamier texture.

Its elevated protein levels make it particularly beneficial for those looking to build or maintain muscle, manage hunger between meals, or follow a higher-protein diet.

‌



The lower lactose content also makes it a more comfortable option for those with mild lactose sensitivity. Its thick consistency means it holds up well under heat and works beautifully as a base for dips such as tzatziki, as a marinade for meat, or stirred into sauces in place of cream.

Natural yoghurt, on the other hand, is the preferred option for those who enjoy a lighter consistency and a more subtle taste. Its higher calcium content makes it the stronger choice for supporting bone health, and its slightly thinner texture means it blends more seamlessly into everyday foods.

It is particularly well-suited to stirring into cereals, blending into smoothies, and folding into desserts. Natural yoghurt also lends itself more readily to baking, as well as being added to cereals, smoothies and desserts, and to salad dressings, where its pourable consistency makes it easier to work with.

Article continues below

Ultimately, neither yoghurt is definitively superior — both offer genuine nutritional value and culinary versatility. For those who are undecided, keeping both to hand and using each where it performs best is a perfectly practical approach.

News.title: 'I'm a binman — you can only leave rubbish beside bin if you do one check first'
News.content:
'I'm a binman — you can only leave rubbish beside bin if you do one check first'

A binman has settled the debate on whether excess rubbish can be left beside wheelie bins

View 2 Images A binman has settled the debate over where excess rubbish goes (Image: Ray Orton/Getty)

Rubbish quickly builds up in homes across the UK because it can be hard to wait weeks for the next collection. Recycling items such as plastics, glass bottles and cardboard can soon fill up a wheelie bin.

‌



Many homes prefer to keep the rubbish out of sight and have it collected as soon as possible, so it is tempting to leave it beside the wheelie bins on collection days. However, it sometimes isn't collected.

‌



A binman has now explained why that happens and if it is actually acceptable to leave rubbish beside bins in the hopes it gets collected.

‌



The No.1 Binman, whose real name is Ashley, often takes to social media to share tips and tricks with the public. He confirmed that the answer all boils down to what your local council says.

Ashley said: "It depends on your council, every council will say something different. Some will allow it, some won't."

He added: "Some councils allow it, maybe paper, but it is how you get it into the lorry, you can't just lean in and add it in. Check your council, if they allow it then you can and follow the guidelines they tell you."

‌



The binman said the council he works for doesn't allow collections of excess waste as if anything smashes, or mess is caused, he would be at fault.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Not everything can be recycled

He has previously urged households to take care with their recycling for another reason. Ashley explained that while items such as polystyrene may display the recyclable symbol, this doesn't necessarily mean they're appropriate for household recycling bins.

‌



The common mistake could result in your recycling bin being left full and uncollected, while collectors wait for you to sort your recycling correctly.

"It can be recycled, you just have to find out where it can be recycled," he said. Ashley said the same principle applies to items like batteries, crisps packages, and carrier bags.

The everyday items cannot be placed in household bins, but instead must be taken to designated locations. He explained: "So you just need to find out where things can be recycled. And just like at home, you have separate recycling bins."

‌



Placing something in the incorrect recycling bin, such as food in the paper recycling bin, would contaminate everything and prevent it from being properly recycled.

Major changes to recycling

View 2 Images You can face fines for disposing rubbish wrong (Image: coldsnowstorm/Getty)

This year, there has been a major change to recycling across England. The UK's Simpler Recycling reforms, under the Environment Act 2021, have introduced uniform recycling for businesses and households in England.

‌



There are now separate collections for food waste, paper and card, glass, metal and plastic. Local authorities need to provide clear information about what can and can't be recycled, with some councils exempt until at least 2040.

Don't risk a fine

The Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs states that penalties can be issued when households don't follow waste collection rules. Not following the rules could cause a nuisance and negatively affect local amenities.

Putting waste out that causes an obstruction to neighbours, restricts access to the pavement, is likely to attract vermin or is unsightly is all grounds for councils to issue fines.

Article continues below

Fixed penalties are issued in the form of a written warning to explain why the rules have been broken. If the household doesn't comply, a notice of intent can be issued.

A final notice can be sent 28 days after the notice of intent, and it will include the amount the household must pay. The government states that the maximum full penalty is £80.

News.title: 'I spent £4,100 on jabs and lost just 11lbs but one diet actually worked'
News.content:
'I spent £4,100 on jabs and lost just 11lbs but one diet actually worked'

Karen Lay says the injections won't work for everyone but she found a way to lose three stone

'I spent £4,100 on jabs and lost just 11lbs but one diet actually worked'

A woman who paid more than £4,100 for weight loss jabs says she lost just 11lbs in 15 months and was left 'heartbroken' Karen Lay, 56, says she was tempted to try the jabs after friends lost up to six stone.

‌



The 56-year-old gradually increased her dose in line with medical guidance, having started taking the medication at 16 stone and while wearing a UK size 18. After only losing 4lbs in nine months on one jab she switched to a different one – but didn’t lose more than another 5lbs in the six months that followed.

‌



Now, she is speaking out to warn other users not to assume they are a “miracle fix” – having gone on to lose more than two stone with a more traditional diet plan. “I turned to injections out of sheer desperation,” said Karen, from Essex.

‌



View 3 Images Karen couldn't lose weight on jabs

“I had spent decades dieting, regaining and feeling completely defeated by my weight. I was also suffering from a respiratory issue, which I knew my weight would exacerbate."

‌



Karen said she suspected from the start that the jabs weren't working for her. She said: "S omething wasn’t right, but I kept pushing through because I assumed I must be doing something wrong, My appetite reduced slightly at first, but not enough to make a meaningful difference, so I increased the dosage each month."

Even when she switched the weight wouldn't drop - while friends were having success. Karen said: “It was especially difficult when, during the same period, I watched friends lose five or six stone on the same medication. I realised the injections simply weren’t effective for me and something had to change.”

The financial services worker was advised to stop treatment by her doctor, as they were concerned that she wasn’t eating enough. By that stage, Karen had spent £4.100 while losing just 11lbs overall.

‌



View 3 Images Karen before her weight loss

Karen said: “It was emotionally exhausting and honestly quite soul‑destroying. We all know that comparison is the thief of joy, but it’s incredibly hard not to compare when people who were much larger than me were seeing their weight melt away.

‌



“Everywhere I looked, people were having huge success on these medications and I felt like the only one failing. It made me feel broken, like my body wasn’t responding the way it should. It was deeply disheartening.

“It’s hard when you’ve spent thousands and you’re seeing other people lose six to seven stone in less time. It made me question whether it was worth it and what was wrong with me because it didn't really work.”

One of the most difficult experiences came when she had to stop treatment for four weeks while transitioning between the two medications. She said: “I had to stop for four weeks to allow the drug to clear my system. That was the worst food noise I have ever experienced.

‌



“It was constant, overwhelming and I gained over seven pounds in that short period. When I stopped the injections for good, the food noise returned, but this time I had support through starting The 1:1 Diet plan.

View 3 Images Karen has lost three stone

‌



“Understanding the why behind my eating made a huge difference, and I was far better equipped to manage it. Once the medication was fully out of my system, I began to feel genuinely better. My energy returned, my digestion improved, and the constipation disappeared.”

Within a year, Karen reduced her body fat percentage from 42% to 31% and dropped to a size 12, the smallest dress size she had worn in 17 years – weighing in at 13st 5lbs. Today, she describes herself as fitter, leaner and healthier than she felt while taking the injections.

Karen, who has recently trained as a 1:1 Diet consultant, believes one of the biggest misconceptions surrounding weight loss jabs is that they are a guaranteed solution. She said: “I think there’s a misconception that jabs are a magic fix. For some people, they work brilliantly, but for others like me, they just don’t.

‌



“What changed for me wasn’t medication. It was proper nutrition, structure, accountability, and rebuilding my relationship with food. For me, it's what’s next after taking the medication, as they stop you medically from eating but don't provide you with that 'why'.

“I feel that without that support to understand 'why' there's a high risk of regaining the weight lost. That's the concern that I hear from my friends who are on jabs.

“As for me, I feel the best I’ve felt in years, and I want people to know there is hope to break the diet cycle even if the injections don’t work for them. I also noticed that once I started fuelling my body properly and losing weight, my other medications, including asthma treatment, reduced or stopped entirely.

Article continues below

“On The 1:1 Diet, once the GLP‑1 drugs were out of my system, I rarely experienced the extreme food noise I’d had on previous diets. With structure and proper nutrition, I felt more in control than I had in years.”

News.title: Ryanair CEO hits back at 'nonsensical claims' man was sucked out of window mid-flight
News.content:
Ryanair CEO hits back at 'nonsensical claims' man was sucked out of window mid-flight

Ljubisa Karović was asleep on board flight FR1879 from Greece to Germany on July 10 when he was woken by the sound of a window shattering - CEO Michael O'Leary has apologised for the incident

View 3 Images Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary (Image: PA)

Ryanair's top boss has played down an incident on one of the budget airline's flights in which a man was reportedly sucked out of a window which shattered in mid-air.

‌



Speaking to The Travel Expert, Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary claimed the passenger was not sucked out of the aircraft, which was operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air.

‌



Describing the incident, Mr O'Leary said: "The window shatters, the oxygen masks come down, the pilots immediately take the aircraft steeply down to a non-pressurised altitude so it is a very upsetting, traumatic experience for everybody on board."

‌



Mr O'Leary apologised to the passenger. "We're very sorry to the passenger who was seated in row 11F," he said.

"He did not, however, get sucked out the window and all these kind of nonsensical claims."

Sixty-one-year-old Ljubisa Karović of Serbia was asleep on board flight FR1879 from Greece to Germany on July 10 when the deafening sound of the window shattering woke him.

‌



View 3 Images

Sitting in 11F, objects flew through the air and out the window as other passengers desperately tried to hold him in place.

Mr Karović sustained burns and bruises on his right arm, which stretch from his armpit to his chest. Now, with his head supported by a neck brace.

‌



"The explosion is what I remember," Mr Karović previously told The Guardian.

"Its the noise before the chaos, the noise that is always there when I close my eyes to sleep."

Mr Karović claims he was partially sucked out of the window before being pulled back in. He fainted between two or three times during the ordeal.

‌



His wife, Svetlana Grković, who was seated three rows behind, recalled the moment oxygen masks came down and how passengers held her husband in place.

View 3 Images Emergency services met the aircraft upon landing in line with standard procedures (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

She said a passenger used a bag, then a suitcase, to plug the hole.

‌



Mr Karović was rushed to hospital once the plane landed, but says he is living with pain.

His lawyer, Vasilis Tsiaras, claims Mr Karović's being alive was nothing short of a miracle.

"Ljubisa dipped in and out of death," Mr Tsiaras told the outlet.

Article continues below

"When the cabin lost pressure he was hurled out of the window from his chest up and immediately lost consciousness. He was on that plane heading to Germany to celebrate his brother's birthday.

"Instead, at 15,000ft he ended up with his head and right arm outside the aircraft as it moved at a speed of more than 600km/h. Imagine that."

Mr. O'Leary said lawyers are "making more claims by the day," and the airline will "deal with that in due course."

News.title: Fifty women come forward saying they were pressured into swinging
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual acts

Fifty women have spoken out saying they were pushed or coerced by their partners into swinging.

They contacted us following a BBC News investigation which told the story of a woman who said she had been pressured into having sex with more than 100 strangers.

Many of the women who came forward said they had sex despite not wanting to, either because they feared the consequences of refusing or felt they had to keep their partners happy.

They spoke of deep, long-lasting trauma.

"I remember many nights of my partner keeping me up all night screaming at me, threatening me, and attempting to gaslight me into believing this was something I wanted," said one woman. "It was never what I wanted."

Another told us: "I felt like I had been given away. I felt used. I felt so dirty."

Most encounters were arranged via the website FabSwingers, say the women, which claims to have more than half a million UK active monthly accounts.

Six women told BBC News they had been raped by men met through the site.

One said her partner had forced her to have sex with more than 90 men through FabSwingers. On one occasion, he held her down by the ankles, she told us.

Sixteen said intimate photos of them had been uploaded to the website without their permission.

News.title: PM to spend first day working from northern branch of No 10
News.content:
Andy Burnham will hold his first meeting at the new No 10 North in Manchester later on Friday.

The branch of Downing Street in the North West will form part of the prime minister's aim to shift power from Whitehall and Westminster to regions across the country.

Ministers Lucy Powell and Louise Haigh will also operate regularly from the new site, with up to 300 civil servants expected to join them by the end of next year.

On Friday in Manchester Burnham will chair a meeting of the National Economic Council, a cabinet committee first launched in 2008 to respond to economic challenges around the UK.

The meeting will bring together senior ministers and regional mayors to "put devolution at the centre of the government's mission to make Britain better".

Ahead of that meeting, the prime minister said: "For 40 years, power and resources have been sucked into the centre, and too many communities have felt forgotten, without the attention and investment they deserve."

He added: "The days of Whitehall resisting devolution are over, for good."

Strategic decisions about devolution and local economic growth will shift from the Treasury and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government to No 10 North, although both departments will have input in these areas.

Angela Rayner, whose constituency is in Greater Manchester, is also expected to work from the new site for the first time on Friday.

News.title: UK complacent about war threat, warns BAE boss
News.content:
The UK has been too complacent about the risk of foreign attack, the boss of Europe's biggest defence contractor BAE Systems has warned.

Dr Charles Woodburn told the BBC in an exclusive interview that the level of threat was the highest he'd seen in his lifetime.

He welcomed the recent boost to defence spending but said much more would be needed to hit the government's commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.

He also warned we were not far from the use of autonomous lethal weapons by countries that may not follow the UK's policy of maintaining human control.

In a rare interview, Woodburn told the BBC the reality of modern warfare had "changed quite profoundly" and that UK defence spending had to change with it.

He said Russia and Ukraine had become "incredibly adept" at using autonomy in the form of drones and counter drones.

"It's something that we now have to really understand and make sure that we're able to provide the capabilities that can counter that and deter aggression," he said.

News.title: King's Tardis entrance as Commonwealth Games begin
News.content:
One of the louder cheers came for the Falklands Islands â in the news recently following Argentina's victory over England in the football World Cup semi-finals â and another followed when the Samoa team emerged and performed a haka in front of the dignitaries in the Royal Box.

But nothing compared to the noise which greeted the arrival of the Scotland team, who entered the arena last in their white shirts and kilts and lifted many in the capacity crowd from their seats.

A large Loch Ness Monster representation then emerged, before, backed by bagpipers and drummers, a rousing rendition of Flower of Scotland followed.

The next section of the evening featured theatrical performances â a show billed as "a love letter to Glasgow and the Commonwealth".

It began with a performance by Scottish folk and country singer Nathan Evans and a dance under a replica of Glasgow Central Station's iconic clock.

The saying "Meet me under the clock" is famous in these parts.

Singer Callum Beattie's rendition of Baccara's Yes Sir, I Can Boogie â the 1970s disco tune recently adopted as Scotland's unofficial anthem - had the Scottish athletes dancing in their seats.

Held indoors in front of about 10,000 people, this was a more intimate ceremony than the last time Glasgow hosted the Commonwealth Games, when a 40,000-strong crowd witnessed the opening of the Games in 2014 at Celtic Park.

There was a point, after the Australian state of Victoria withdrew as hosts in 2023, when some thought these Games would not happen. Glasgow stepped in at short notice to ensure otherwise.

There are eight fewer sports involved compared to 2014, given the short build-up, and venues from 12 years ago have been repurposed.

But Commonwealth Sport president Donald Rukare, wearing a tartan kilt in the colours of his home country Uganda, said this edition has been made possible by the "extraordinary legacy of 2014 and by a city that once again welcomes us with warm hearts and open arms".

News.title: Heat health alerts issued in parts of UK as rain returns for some this weekend
News.content:
Yellow heat health alerts come into force across central and southern England on Friday morning with temperatures forecast to reach 30C (86F) in places.

The alerts, issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover the East and West Midlands, eastern England, London, south-east England and south-west England and are valid from 09:00 BST on Friday until 09:00 on Sunday.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

It comes as parts of the UK prepare to see much-needed rain this weekend - although amounts are expected to be relatively small, especially in the south.

A drought was officially declared for large parts of north and mid-Wales on Thursday.

The rest of Wales, along with much of central, southern and eastern England, is in "prolonged dry weather" category - one stage below a drought.

Hosepipe bans are in force for millions of customers.

News.title: UK mortgage rates rise to highest level for a month
News.content:
UK average mortgage rates have risen back to the level of a month ago as renewed tensions in the Middle East feed through to homeowners.

Lenders' funding costs have increased as markets judge that a prolonged conflict reduces the possibility of interest rate cuts by central banks.

The five biggest High Street banks are among a host of lenders which have increased their interest rates on new fixed deals in recent days.

Recent projections by the Bank of England suggest just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028.

Mortgage rates had been falling as a ceasefire between the US and Iran initially appeared to hold.

But fresh strikes and Houthi militia attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea reignited fears over global energy supplies.

Oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May on Thursday after several days of increases, stoking fears of higher inflation and a lower likelihood of interest rate cuts.

News.title: Hero swimmer helped two children during beach tragedy
News.content:
Witnesses say a heroic day-tripper managed to haul two children back to shore during an incident where a mother and daughter drowned.

Beverly Smit, 60, described the unnamed rescuer swimming out to sea three times as the tragedy unfolded in West Mersea, near Colchester, on Wednesday evening.

Shally Rahman, 41, and Samiha Rahman, 15, were trying to rescue a seven-year-old boy from the water when they got into difficulty and died.

Essex Police said the group, from Barking, east London, were all related to each other and the boy remained in hospital, fighting for his life.

Recalling the moment the "Good Samaritan" sprung into action, Smit said: "They were calling for help and the children and adults were out there.

"He swam out, I think, three times. Two of the children he brought back were not in good condition.

"It's not an easy swim when the tide's coming in - you're swimming against the tide. The water [on Wednesday] was particularly quite cold."

News.title: The new $4.5bn bridge which is a symbol of a strained US-Canada relationship
News.content:
Almost 15 years ago, Canada agreed to fully pay for the bridge's construction to bypass US political resistance and get the project, seen as necessary infrastructure to fix a trade bottleneck, moving.

The bridge will help support more than C$1bn ($710m; Â£530m) worth of goods that pass through Windsor-Detroit crossing each day.

When Canada first took on the construction project, which will be owned by both Ottawa and Michigan, it agreed to share toll revenue with the US state only once its costs were paid.

Then, early this year, shortly before a planned ribbon-cutting ceremony, Trump said he would block its opening until Canada agreed to "share authority" and ownership.

"We should own, perhaps, at least one half of this asset," he said at the time.

The bridge has long faced pushback from the Moroun family in Michigan, who own the neighbouring Ambassador Bridge, the busiest commercial border crossing in North America and one of the few that are privately owned.

Billionaire Matthew Maroun, who is also a Trump donor, met with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick hours before the president's comments, according to a New York Times report.

In June, Carney announced that Canada agreed to a US request to delay the opening of the bridge to allow for further negotiations.

Keen to get the vital trade link open, Ottawa accepted to now split half of the bridge revenues for the next 15 years with an economic development fund "solely controlled" by the US government.

Trump touted in a recent social media post the new agreement was "MUCH BETTER" for America.

The bridge fallout comes against a backdrop of a challenging trade dispute with Canada and the US. While he was running to be elected prime minister, Carney vowed to solve it with an "elbows up" approach - referencing a combative style of hockey coined by the late Gordie Howe himself.

Now Carney is facing pushback for conceding to a US administration that many Canadians view as treating their country unfairly.

"We're dealing with an administration like we've never seen before," Colin Robertson, a former Canadian diplomat and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, told the BBC.

"They renege on deals. They don't follow agreements. It's like dealing with pirates."

News.title: King and Queen emerge from Tardis to open Glasgow Commonwealth Games
News.content:
King Charles and Queen Camilla emerged from a Tardis at the start of a spectacular Commonwealth Games opening ceremony in Glasgow.

The royal couple drew gasps and cheers from the audience at the Hydro as they appeared on a stage that had been turned into a giant garden.

Flags from 74 nations and territories were carried into the arena during the event, which also featured the Loch Ness monster and performances from Nathan Evans, Tom Walker and KT Tunstall.

The show celebrated the story of Glasgow - from its industrial past to its vibrant nightlife - ahead of a Games that will see 215 medals awarded across 10 sports.

News.title: Wildfire spotted from space as helicopter brought in to tackle blaze
News.content:
Satellite images have captured plumes of smoke and damage caused by a wildfire in north Wales.

Data gathered by BBC Verify suggests an estimated 951 hectares (2,350 acres) of the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd have been burned by a wildfire that broke out earlier this month.

Nasa's satellite-based fire monitoring system has also detected heat signatures from four areas of Wales where wildfires have broken out.

It is showing heat sources at Blaenavon in Torfaen, Presteigne in Powys, and Pentre Halkyn in Flintshire.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said a specialist firefighting helicopter would be deployed to Rhinogydd on Friday morning after calls for "aerial support".

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana moved to psychiatric hospital
News.content:
Axel Rudakubana, who murdered three children at a dance class in Southport, has been moved from prison to a secure psychiatric hospital.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed he was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, the high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Rudakubana murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

The then Attorney-General Lord Hermer said Rudakubana's sentence was the "second-longest sentence imposed by the courts in English history".

A spokesperson for the MoJ told PA: "The families of those murdered and injured in Southport will be in this country's heart forever and our thoughts remain with them.

"Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act. Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison.

"Officials have approved this transfer, on behalf of Ministers. This transfer does not change his sentence â which remains at 52 years â and of which he will serve every single day."

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The law requires he be transferred back to prison when he no longer requires treatment in hospital. His sentence is not being converted into a "hospital order", which would mean he stayed at Broadmoor.

The cost of keeping Rudakubana in hospital is likely to be much higher in Broadmoor than a prison.

According to the Centre for Mental Health the average secure hospital bed costs around Â£270,000 a year.

The average cost of keeping a prisoner in Belmarsh is Â£97,740 according to figures for 2023.

In May 2025 there was an investigation after Rudakubana, now 19, allegedly attacked a prison officer with boiling water.

The Southport Public Inquiry has heard evidence about his past mental health conditions.

A senior clinician at Alder Hey Children's Hospital described his "lack of empathy" combined with a "fascination with violence" and neurodiversity, which he said added up to a "really toxic mix".

According to West London NHS Trust, Broadmoor specialises in "providing assessment, treatment and care in conditions of high security" for men.

Is is the oldest of England and Wales's three high-security hospitals and has held some of the UK's most high-profile criminals.

It was renovated in 2017 and the BBC obtained pictures from inside the hospital. They show that older prison-like cells were replaced by more spacious rooms, though still with locks on the doors.

News.title: Burnham pauses plan to release some prisoners early from September
News.content:
Andy Burnham has announced he is pausing a scheme which would have seen thousands of prisoners in England and Wales eligible to be released early.

It came after criticism of the scheme from survivors and victims' families, including the widow of PC Andrew Harper who described the possibility of his killers' early release as "deplorable".

The Sentencing Act, which was due to come into effect in September, would have seen some offenders let out at varying stages in a bid to ease prison overcrowding.

The new Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the pause aimed to "give victims and survivors certainty" and the government wanted to make sure it got "the implementation of this policy right".

He added a review would also look at the information given to survivors and victims' families as part of the early release process.

Burnham earlier said: "No prisoners will be let out under this policy until we have conducted an urgent review and done everything we can to minimise risk to the public."

He added: "Where changes are needed, we will not hesitate to make them."

Under the act, some offenders would have been let out after serving a third of their sentence, rather than half.

The rest of their sentence would be spent in the community, where they would be monitored and could be returned to prison if they offended again.

More serious offenders would have been released after serving half of their sentence, rather than two-thirds.

The policy was brought in to ease overcrowding in the prison system but has been criticised by opposition parties, as well as victims and their families.

The scheme would have seen around 700 prisoners released in early September, the BBC understands.

The decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added to the scheme.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie, called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

His mother, meanwhile, said her son had not been given "proper justice" and "every victim will be feeling the same" about the early prison release scheme.

Thousands of letters had been sent to victims in recent weeks, warning them that the early release scheme was coming in September.

Norris, who voted in support of the Sentencing Act under Starmer's government, later said the decision to pause was made after "listening to victims" and he hoped to provide them "certainty as soon as we can".

He said: "The prime minister and I have heard from victims and survivors and from people across the country about their concerns about the implementation of some very important elements of the Sentencing Act."

One element the government needed to get right was the information provided to victims before prisoners were released, Norris added.

Norris refused to be drawn on why he did not raise concerns when the Sentencing Act was first introduced but said Burnham was "quite right" to review the scheme.

Jade Belgrove, a survivor of sexual assault who has been campaigning against the early release scheme, said it was "such a relief that we've been heard".

She told BBC News that when she received a letter informing her that her attacker might be released early "it was horrific".

Belgrove said it even led her to question whether reporting the assault in the first place was worth it.

News.title: Wildfires and record dry conditions trigger drought in parts of Wales
News.content:
"We've had really dry weather but also it's been really hot - and those things combined if you're a livestock farmer means excessive pressure on livestock," said Abi Reader, president of NFU Cymru.

"You have to make sure they have enough water and shade, and we are getting farms with springs and streams drying up," she told BBC Walescast.

"If you're an arable farmer the heat and dry weather have also forced a lot of the crops to come to ripening a lot earlier than they normally would.

"It's unprecedented early harvesting this year and farmers are going to see lower crop yields."

Welsh Water emphasised that NRW's drought declarations were different to its own announcements.

The company has already brought in a hospipe ban for 33,000 properties in west Wales.

"NRW's drought status reflects environmental conditions, including factors such as rainfall, river flows and groundwater levels," a spokesperson said.

"By contrast, Welsh Water's Temporary Use Ban is an operational measure based on local water demand and our ability to replenish service reservoirs with drinking water at the same rate, or faster, than customers are using water.

"It is driven by the capacity of the local treatment works and distribution network to keep up with sustained demand.

"This means different parts of Wales can experience different operational pressures, even if they are not in the same environmental drought category declared by NRW."

Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd, said: "This is an environmental drought classification. It's about the state of water levels in our rivers.

"It does not speak to public water supplies which I can assure people are there, there is sufficient supplies but we would of course urge people to be careful and diligent in their use of water so that that can be protected."

News.title: Rayner rules out repaying severance cash after making cabinet return
News.content:
A lump sum, equivalent of 25% of the annual ministerial salary, is payable when a minister stops holding office. Departing ministers who are aged over 65 or are reappointed within three weeks do not qualify.

The 2025/26 accounts, external for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government record the severance payment for Rayner.

In her first interview since returning to government, Rayner was pressed on whether she would return the money.

She told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live: "No, my severance payment was given to me at the time, I had worked in government for a period of time and then I came out of government for just under a year."

She added: "I will be delivering in government again."

Rayner earlier said her criticism of the Conservatives over severance payments came at a time when there was a "revolving door" which saw ministers return to government "after 40-odd days".

The Conservatives earlier this week said Rayner had "quit in disgrace and took a Â£17k payout" last year.

The party added: "Now she's got her old job back, will she return the cash? Or is it one rule for Labour, and another for everyone else?"

Rayner's departure last September came after the prime minister's ethics adviser, Sir Laurie Magnus, said she had "acted with integrity" but concluded that she had breached the ministerial code.

Sir Laurie said she did get legal advice when buying the property, but failed to seek further expert tax advice as recommended.

In May, Rayner resolved her tax affairs with HMRC following an investigation, settling Â£40,000 in unpaid stamp duty.

The MP for Ashton-under-Lyne said she had been "exonerated" of the accusation that she had "deliberately sought to avoid tax".

Rayner told Matt Chorley: "The situation I went through last year was really difficult, it was difficult for my family, but I felt I'd let people down and I never want to let people down, I want to fight for them."

Rayner also said she has "unfinished business" in government, including on building council houses and supporting local government.

Burnham has said he wants to deliver "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period".

Asked for details to explain what this will look like, Rayner said she would not provide an "exact figure" or provide a date for when she considers the post-war period to have ended.

She said: "We want to aspire to get as far as possible and what we've done as a government is put more investment in that, the Â£39bn for social and affordable housing grant funding that we want to get out the door."

News.title: Mum and daughter who died at beach were trying to save boy, 7
News.content:
A woman and her 15-year-old daughter who died after getting into difficulty in the water on the Essex coast were trying to help a seven-year-old boy, police have said.

The child remains in a critical condition in hospital after the incident at West Mersea, near Colchester, on Wednesday evening. Three others were taken to hospital.

The victims have been named by a family member as Shally Rahman, 41, and teenager Samiha Rahman. Police said all the people involved knew each other.

Shally's brother-in-law Matiur Rahman said the family was enjoying a seaside holiday when a "big wave came and took them".

"My whole family, we are, like, speechless," said Matiur Rahman, who used to live in Bradford, but spoke to the BBC from Bangladesh.

"We are very shocked. We can't explain [what has happened]."

He said his niece was a "very, very good person" and his sister-in-law was "a very helpful person".

News.title: Gary Lineker among millionaires asking Andy Burnham to tax them more
News.content:
Millionaires including former footballer Gary Lineker and music producer Brian Eno have written to new prime minister Andy Burnham asking to be taxed more.

In an open letter, 120 well-off Britons told Burnham: "We can afford it. We're not talking about higher taxes on those who get up and go to work for their income every day, but on the very richest whose income is derived from the wealth they hold."

Organised by Patriotic Millionaires, the letter said it would lead to a more equal society, and urged a "devolution of wealth and power from the very richest".

People can already give money or stocks voluntarily to the Treasury using a donation facility.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Lineker is "very welcome to pay more tax he can write a cheque to the Treasury, no one is stopping him."

Patriotic Millionaires support a 2% tax on wealth over Â£10m.

"Millionaires are a patriotic bunch," the letter states. "We love this country and we want it to succeed.

"But success requires investment and a primary source of untouched capital investment is sitting with us, in untaxed potential."

Other signatories include Richard Curtis, who wrote the film Notting Hill, and Ian Gregg, the former managing director of Greggs and son of the bakery chain's founder. Scottish crime writer Val McDermid and former financial trader-turned-equality campaigner Gary Stevenson also signed the letter.

Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said she would welcome UK millionaires increasing the amount of tax they pay but said any major changes would be announced during a Budget.

"I welcome the fact that people of good means are saying that they want to pay more. They can pay more," she said and pointed to the Treasury's donation link.

The renewed call for higher tax on the wealthy follows a similar campaign in previous years.

Burnham did not rule out a wealth tax when asked about it by Lineker - formerly the BBC's highest paid presenter - a few days before he became prime minister.

He suggested he may have "to ask for a little more" tax at some point.

Lineker was paid around Â£1.3m a year before he left the BBC. He is worth a reported Â£30m.

In 2023, Lineker won his appeal against HMRC over a Â£4.9m tax bill, after the UK tax authority pursued him over taxes on income from both the BBC and BT Sport, from 2013 to 2014, and 2017 to 2018.

The latest call from Patriotic Millionaires said there is a "need to embrace a new kind of devolution of wealth and power, from the very richest in order to reinvest back into our greatest asset in every region".

It added that in its own poll, the majority of millionaires wanted a higher tax on themselves.

"There are a few people left with outdated economic thinking and few others desperate to hold onto every penny they can... Those that can't see past the end of their own self interest have no place in designing a Britain for the future," the letter said.

Musician Brian Eno told BBC Radio Lincolnshire the tax system was "very generous to rich people".

"If you're wealthy you don't pay very much tax but hire a clever bunch of accountants who somehow get you off that," he said.

He also dismissed the idea that lots of millionaires would leave the UK if they were taxed too much.

UK defence spending "falls well short" of what is required to protect the country, the chief executive of BAE Systems has warned.

Charles Woodburn described the current climate as “the most threatening time I’ve seen” and warned Russia's military advances before and during its war with Ukraine were a key concern.

Despite the Government announcing an additional £15 billion for defence in June, the then defence secretary John Healey resigned, citing inadequate military funding.

At the time, Mr Healey wrote to Sir Keir Starmer to say he had been “unable, and the Treasury has been unwilling, to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats”.

Mr Woodburn said the extra funding still “falls well short of what is needed to protect the country”.

“This is by far the most threatening time I’ve seen,” he told the BBC. “Even when I joined the company in 2016, I was amazed at what we saw Russian submarines doing, the cyber attacks.

“I think that’s come a long way sadly as a result of the Ukraine conflict; we’re much more aware of the proximity of a hot war in Europe.”

Keir Starmer speaks with the CEO of BAE Systems, Charles Woodburn ( AFP/Getty )

He said modern warfare had “changed quite profoundly” and described Russia and Ukraine as becoming “incredibly adept” at the use of drones and counter-drones.

“It’s something that we now have to really understand and make sure that we’re able to provide the capabilities that can counter that and deter aggression,” he said.

Shares in BAE Systems rose by 3.25 per cent, with other defence companies also seeing a rise following the appointment of Mr Healey as Chancellor on Monday, with expectations he will commit to further defence spending.

“The fact that he understands the requirements of defence we see as a very positive thing”, Mr Woodburn said.

BAE Systems announced this week the Ministry of Defence has given it a contract extension worth £708 million to continue developing a next-generation combat aircraft.

New Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: “This investment in advanced combat air technology for the UK Armed Forces will strengthen our defence and deterrence, and shows our clear commitment to backing British workers with our defence investment, creating jobs and supporting communities across the UK.”

President Donald Trump is pressing ahead with new double-digit tariffs on dozens of US trading partners, as existing stopgap levies expire this Friday.

The United States will impose taxes of 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 countries, accounting for 99% of US imports.

The administration alleges inadequate enforcement of bans on goods produced by forced labour.

These new tariffs take effect at 12:01am on Friday, precisely as the temporary 10% worldwide tariffs – introduced by Trump after the Supreme Court struck down his biggest tariffs in February – expire.

"The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

“Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere.”

open image in gallery The new tariffs will take effect just as temporary 10% worldwide tariffs expire on Friday ( AFP/Getty )

Trump is tapping more durable tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in “unjustifiable,” “unreasonable” or “discriminatory” trade practices.

Trump used Section 301 to impose big tariffs on China in his first term, and they survived court challenges.

Are more tariffs on the way?

More Section 301 tariffs are likely coming: The U.S. Trade Representative’s office has launched a probe into whether 16 countries — accounting for 70% of U.S. imports — have overproduced goods, pushing down prices and putting U.S. companies at a disadvantage in global markets. The administration has yet to complete that investigation.

Trump, who argues that high tariffs will revive American manufacturing, last year overturned decades of U.S. policy that favored lower tariffs and ever-freer trade. Invoking the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), he imposed double-digit tariffs on imports from almost every country on Earth, saying America’s longstanding trade deficit amounted to a national emergency.

But the Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA did not authorize tariffs. The decision forced the administration to pay refunds to importers that had paid the tariffs.

In response, Trump announced 10% worldwide tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. But he can only use Section 122 levies for 150 days; time runs out on them Friday.

The administration initially proposed the forced labor tariffs last month. Since then, some countries have tightened forced labor enforcement and qualified for lower tariffs, said a senior administration official who spoke under condition of anonymity. For example, the official said, the tariff on imports from India initially was set at 12.5% but now will be 10%.

open image in gallery U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the move ‘will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice’ ( REUTERS/Daniel Becerril )

Some products — including oil and gas and fertilizer — are exempted from the new tariffs announced Thursday. Also being spared are products that qualify for duty-free status under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the North American trade pact Trump negotiated in his first term.

Tariffs are paid by companies in the United States that import foreign products. The importers usually try to pass along the cost by charging consumers higher prices. Americans are already frustrated by the high cost of living. So the administration is taking a risk in rolling out new tariffs ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

What is the reason for the tariffs?

Human rights watchers say that it’s reasonable to be skeptical of the motivation behind the tariffs. But they say the levies could make an impact on the problem of forced labor.

Forced labor is defined by the International Labor Organization Forced Labor Convention of 1930 as “all work or service which is exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty and for which the said person has not offered himself (or herself) voluntarily.”

According to the latest statistics from the ILO, which is a U.N. agency focused on human and labor rights, about 27.6 million people were in forced labor worldwide on any given day in 2021.

“We’ve gone on record for years now advocating for import bans, not as a magic bullet, it’s not a silver bullet, but as a potentially effective tool in combating forced labor across the globe,” said Martina Vandenberg, founder and president of The Human Trafficking Legal Center.

“It’s possible to be extremely critical of tariffs, as we are, and to be very concerned about blanket tariffs used as bludgeons against countries,” she said. “And yet I think it’s undeniable that there is a significant response in terms of the adoption of import bans.”

open image in gallery Human rights watchers say that it’s reasonable to be skeptical of the motivation behind the tariffs ( AFP/Getty )

However Vandenberg and her organization urged in testimony that the tariffs be implemented in a phased approach to give countries time to implement a ban or a plan for enforcement.

“Our concern is that the import bans will be thin slips of paper with no enforcement,” she said. “Countries need time to build import ban mechanisms that are meaningful and enforceable.”

Kenya Davis, partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, said the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, a U.S. federal law passed in 2021 that prohibits the importation of goods made wholly or in part in China’s Xinjiang region or by designated entities, is the most significant legislation related to forced labor that the U.S. has passed before the tariffs.

“The level of effectiveness is certainly up for debate, but it certainly has drawn attention to the issue of labor trafficking and forced labor,” she said. “And so, if nothing else, these import bans will serve that function of bringing greater awareness to forced labor.”

But without a “comprehensive approach,” that provides transparency about what the investigations consisted of, and programs that provide countries aid in enforcing bans, “I’m very cautious in my enthusiasm about the (tariffs),” she said.

Isabelle Glimcher, senior research scientist for global labor at the NYU Stern Center for Human Rights, said one flaw in the tariffs is that they focus on levying the tax on countries based on goods they import — not goods they make domestically.

But she said the impending tariffs threat has spurred several countries — such as India — to amend their foreign trade policies to include a forced labor import ban. European Union forced labor regulations due to go into effect later next year are also contributing, she said.

“Not all of these things are necessarily or wholly attributable to the Section 301 investigations, but does seem like countries are responding and starting to take all of this seriously,” she said.

A yellow heat health alert has come into force across parts of the UK despite forecasts of rain this weekend.

The warnings are in place from 9am on Friday to 9am on Sunday, and covers the East Midlands, West Midlands, South East, South West, the east of England and London.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the hot weather could have an impact across health and social care services and put vulnerable people at risk.

Health chiefs also warned water‑related incidents may increase, including risks from cold‑water shock and drowning.

open image in gallery UKHSA issue heat health alerts from Friday 24 to Sunday 26 ( UKHSA )

Temperatures are set to hit 29C on Saturday in London and 28C in Birmingham and Norwich. But rain is also forecast.

It comes after three consecutive heatwaves and one of the driest springs on record with hosepipe bans in place across the country.

Showers are expected to roll in across Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland on Saturday evening, before spreading further across the UK on Sunday.

Steve Willington Met Office chief forecaster said: “The high pressure has been a key feature of the UK’s weather forecast over the last few weeks, bringing above-average temperatures and extremely dry conditions for many.

“However, we will begin to see a modest change as a weak weather front pushes south across the UK on Saturday bringing some much-needed rain, albeit it light and mainly concentrated in the north and west. Behind the front a showery air mass will bring potentially heavy showers some of which may be thundery.”

open image in gallery Met Office forecast temperatures will reach 29C on Saturday in London ( Met Office )

Greg Wolverson, Met Office deputy chief forecaster, explained cooler weather can be expected from Sunday onwards, but temperatures will still remain average for the time of year.

“Although there is a return to rain in the forecast, we have just come out of an exceptionally dry spell and the forecast rain is unlikely to be widespread or substantial. Many areas are likely to continue experiencing prevailing dry conditions for the foreseeable future, especially in southern England,” he said.

Five-day Met Office weather forecast

Today:

Dry with plenty of sunshine for much England and Wales. Cloudier across parts of Northern Ireland and Scotland with patchy rain, although some brighter spells developing at times. Feeling warm for many and hot towards the southeast.

Tonight:

A weakening band of cloud and rain moving across Scotland and Northern Ireland this evening, with further rain arriving into Scotland overnight. Remaining dry with clear spells elsewhere.

Saturday:

Band of rain across Scotland moving southeastwards and turning increasingly showery. Remaining dry, sunny and very warm across southern areas, with brighter and fresher conditions following across Scotland.

Outlook for Sunday to Tuesday:

Fresher for all on Sunday with sunny spells and some showers. Remaining changeable early next week across the north, but potentially turning dry and very warm again in the south.

The BBC has demanded that Donald Trump hand over his personal text messages in a £10bn (£7.5bn) defamation lawsuit over his alleged involvement in the January 6 riots in Washington.

The broadcaster’s lawyers are seeking to prove in court that the US president should be held responsible for encouraging his supporters to storm the US Capitol following his 2020 election defeat.

His lawsuit was launched after it was revealed that a BBC Panorama documentary, aired in January 2021, had spliced together two parts of his speech to appear as though he was directly inciting the mob.

In the broadcasted clip, he can be seen telling the crowd to walk down to the Capitol to “fight like hell”. In reality, Mr Trump had said they would walk to the iconic US building to “cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women”.

Later in his speech, he said, Mr Trump told the crowd: “If you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country any more.”

open image in gallery The storming of the US Capitol on January 6 2020 occurred after Mr Trump lost the election to former President Joe Biden ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Trump has accused the BBC of damaging his reputation, despite the fact the Panorama episode was not available on the BBC’s US platform.

Lawyers for the BBC have now applied to the US government to receive evidence gathered in a report last year, which concluded that “the violence was foreseeable to Mr Trump, that he caused it, that it was beneficial to his plan to interfere with the certification, and that when it occurred, he made a conscious choice not to stop it and instead to leverage it for more delay”.

This includes messages sent between Mr Trump and his advisers in the three hours before his speech and calling for the rioters to disperse.

In their legal document, the BBC said: “In [his] lawsuit, President Trump claims that the BBC defamed him by editing his speech at the White House Ellipse on January 6, 2021 in a manner that he claims conveyed the allegedly false implication that he fomented the violence that followed at the Capitol.

open image in gallery The US president has accused the BBC of damaging his reputation ( Getty )

“Thus, as the BBC explained and the government does not dispute, President Trump cannot prevail in his case if he cannot establish the falsity of that alleged implication.”

It also noted that they had served subpoenas on third parties, with his lawyers so far refusing to supply documents under the conditions of “executive privilege”.

A federal judge in Florida ruled on Wednesday that Mr Trump must provide detailed information about his companies’ finances in response to a motion filed by the BBC.

First reported by Politico, the ruling will likely be appealed by the Trump legal team. But if it holds, the decision will open the door to discovery motions targeting the financial data of roughly 400 companies and business interests controlled by the Trump family’s blind trust, according to the news outlet.

The BBC declined to comment.

Hot weather boosting clothes and air conditioning purchases and summer discounting helped lift UK retail sales last month, official figures show.

Online shopping has also rebounded to a five-year high, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The ONS said the total volume of retail sales, which measures the quantity bought, increased by 1% in June.

This compared with a 1.2% rise in May, which was unchanged from a previous estimate.

It was also an unexpected increase for most economists who had been predicting a 0.1% monthly decline.

Retailers suggested that June’s hot spell and more sales promotions helped increasing shopping in clothing stores and online.

The ONS also said sports sales were higher last month and pointed to an increase in alcohol and tobacco sales amid the early matches of the Fifa World Cup helping drive spending.

Between April and June, retail sales are estimated to have risen by 0.6% compared with the first three months of the year, according to the ONS.

ONS senior statistician Hannah Finselbach said: “Internet retailers did especially well, with businesses telling us that this was because of promotions and the warm weather, with strong demand in June for outdoor products, air conditioning and clothing.

“Sports merchandise also sold well online.

“With internet retailers faring well, the proportion of online sales has risen to its highest since spring 2021 when coronavirus restrictions were ending.”
