Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —The strike. A drone launched from Sudan hit a funeral gathering in Tiné, Chad, on 18 March 2026, killing 17 Chadian civilians. —The pattern. This is the fifth cross-border drone strike affecting eastern Chad since December 2025, and the fourth in or near Tiné. —Responsibility. Both the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces deny involvement and blame each other for the attack. —The money trail. The UAE has provided over $700 million in financing to Chad since 2023, even as it faces allegations of arming the RSF through Chadian territory. —Human cost. More than 1,000 civilians have been killed by drone strikes in Sudan in early 2026, with hundreds of wounded treated across the border in Chad.

A drone strike from Sudan killed 17 civilians at a funeral in eastern Chad on 18 March, the fifth such cross-border attack in months, exposing how Sudan’s civil war is spilling into its neighbour and testing Chad’s fragile balance between sovereignty and financial dependence on Gulf patrons.

What happened in Tiné

On 18 March 2026, an armed drone crossed from Sudanese airspace and struck a residential compound in Tiné, a split border town in Chad’s Wadi Fira province. The compound was hosting a funeral gathering, and all 17 people killed were Chadian nationals attending the ceremony.

Multiple people were injured, according to UN-linked monitors and the Chadian government. The strike was the fourth drone attack in or near Tiné since late 2025, and humanitarian agencies describe a pattern of near-daily drone activity along this stretch of the 1,300-kilometre border.

Chad’s government confirmed the drone was launched from Sudan and pledged to pursue those responsible. Officials warned they would retaliate against any further cross-border attacks, framing the incident as a serious breach of sovereignty.

A pattern of cross-border drone strikes

The funeral strike did not happen in isolation. In December 2025, a drone strike near Tiné killed two Chadian soldiers, marking the first clearly documented lethal cross-border drone attack of this cycle.

On 7 February 2026, drones struck Al-Tina again, killing 10 people and injuring 25. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) teams treated 29 wounded at Tiné hospital, and UN flash reports attributed the strikes to Rapid Support Forces (RSF) units targeting gatherings of displaced Sudanese and local traders.

On 12 March, a drone hit the Adikong market near the Adré crossing, killing at least 11 people and wounding 23, including seven children. Though the strike landed on Sudanese soil, MSF teams in Adré, eastern Chad, treated many of the wounded, including Chadian traders and refugees. Counting these incidents alongside the 18 March funeral strike yields at least five distinct cross-border or border-adjacent drone attacks affecting civilians in eastern Chad within roughly four months.

Who is launching the drones

Both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF operate armed drones, and both publicly deny responsibility for the Tiné funeral strike. The RSF condemned the attack and blamed the SAF, calling it a violation of Chad’s sovereignty. The SAF denied involvement and accused the RSF of a repeated pattern of cross-border strikes.

Operational evidence from UN flash reporting and MSF field testimony points more frequently to RSF-linked assets for recent cross-border attacks near Tiné and Adré. However, specific attribution for the 18 March drone remains contested. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project documented 198 drone strikes by both factions in early 2026, with at least 52 involving civilian casualties and 478 fatalities overall.

Amnesty International and other monitors have traced recently manufactured weapons entering Sudan from China, Russia, Turkey, Yemen, Serbia, and the UAE. The SAF’s drone capabilities draw partly on Iranian armed drones, while the UAE is repeatedly cited as a key supplier of armoured vehicles and other systems to the RSF.

Chad’s double bind: sovereignty versus solvency

President Mahamat Idriss Déby faces an uncomfortable equation. RSF-linked drones are killing Chadian soldiers and civilians, making a hardline response popular domestically and necessary for regime legitimacy. Chad closed its border with Sudan on 23 February 2026 after earlier clashes killed five soldiers and three civilians near Tiné.

Yet the same great-power patron accused of arming the RSF is also underwriting Chad’s budget. Since 2023, the United Arab Emirates has provided a $200 million financing package, including $50 million in grant aid, followed by a $500 million loan from the Abu Dhabi Fund for Development in October 2024 at a preferential 1 percent interest rate over 18 years. The International Crisis Group notes that Chad’s political stability now appears to hinge on its partnership with the UAE.

Multiple investigations allege that UAE-supplied arms reach the RSF via Chadian territory. A UN Security Council briefing in December 2025 described an extensive military air-bridge run by the UAE, flying weapons to the RSF through client regimes in Chad, Libya, the Central African Republic, South Sudan, and Somalia’s Puntland region. The Council on Foreign Relations notes that weapons from the UAE have been funnelled to the militia through Chad, even as Abu Dhabi provides billions in investment and loans to N’Djamena.

The great-power contest and the new Scramble

Eastern Chad now sits at the intersection of gold, fuel, and logistics corridors linking Sudan, Libya, the Central African Republic, and the wider Sahel. The drone campaign has systematically targeted fuel depots, markets, and transport hubs crucial to local commerce and humanitarian logistics. At Adikong, drones repeatedly hit the fuel market, destroying stockpiles, vehicles, and food supplies, and killing traders including women and children.

This is drone-enabled warfare driven by mid-tier powers’ defence industries, debt-based influence where loan terms translate into tolerance for external meddling, and a scramble for critical minerals and trade routes. For readers following Africa: The New Scramble, the Chad-Sudan borderlands represent a textbook case of how external money and technology are reshaping the balance of power across the Sahel and Horn of Africa.

The UAE, Iran, Turkey, Egypt, Ethiopia, and Russia all pursue strategic and economic interests in Sudan’s war. The UAE backs the RSF to secure gold and energy routes and expand political influence. Egypt and Eritrea align with the SAF, viewing the RSF as a threat to regional order. Ethiopia reportedly leans toward the RSF as a counterweight to Cairo and Asmara. Iran provides armed drones to the SAF, anchoring Tehran’s growing security footprint in the Red Sea corridor.

What to watch next

Chad’s border closure and threats of retaliation signal a desire to reassert sovereignty, but the financial leash from Abu Dhabi limits how far N’Djamena can go. The Africa Center for Strategic Studies warns that Chad risks greater instability from its engagement in Sudan’s war, having already lost nine soldiers to cross-border violence since December 2025.

For investors and policymakers, the key question is whether Déby can maintain his balancing act. A single high-casualty strike on a major Chadian town could trigger domestic pressure that forces a break with the UAE, jeopardising the concessional financing that keeps the regime afloat. Alternatively, continued drone strikes may push Chad deeper into the conflict, transforming its eastern provinces from a transit hub into a proxy battlefield.

The UN Human Rights Office estimates that more than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes in Sudan in the first five months of 2026. MSF reports that since early February, 457 people injured in attacks along the border have been treated in Tiné alone. A new surgical unit at Tiné hospital has treated nearly 300 patients, over 90 percent wounded by drones. These numbers are likely to rise as both factions acquire more advanced systems and external sponsors deepen their involvement.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was responsible for the drone strike from Sudan that hit Chad?

Both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) deny responsibility and blame each other. UN-linked monitors and MSF field reports attribute most recent cross-border drone strikes near Tiné to RSF units, but specific attribution for the 18 March 2026 funeral strike remains contested. Both factions operate armed drones supplied by foreign backers including Iran, the UAE, and Turkey.

How many cross-border drone strikes have hit eastern Chad?

At least five distinct cross-border or border-adjacent drone incidents have affected civilians in eastern Chad since December 2025. These include strikes in December 2025, February 2026, early March 2026, 12 March 2026 at Adikong, and the 18 March 2026 funeral strike in Tiné. Humanitarian agencies describe a pattern of near-daily drone activity along the Chad-Sudan border since early 2026.

Why does Chad not break ties with the UAE despite RSF drone attacks?

Chad is financially dependent on the UAE, which has provided over $700 million in concessional financing and grants since 2023. The International Crisis Group notes that Chad’s political stability now hinges on its partnership with Abu Dhabi. Breaking ties would jeopardise the loans and investment that keep President Déby’s government afloat, even as the UAE faces credible allegations of arming the RSF through Chadian territory.

World.content:
Africa · Northern

The money funds rails, switches, and supervision on the Kenitra–Marrakech corridor and Casablanca hub. —Bigger picture. Morocco’s total railway investment programme is valued at roughly 96 billion dirhams ($10 billion). —Multi-lender stack. The World Bank, European Investment Bank, France, Spain, and South Korea are all providing parallel financing. —2040 target. Morocco aims to grow its high-speed network from 320 km to over 1,280 km by 2040.

The African Development Bank has approved a €205 million loan for Morocco high-speed rail infrastructure, locking in a critical piece of the kingdom’s $10 billion railway expansion ahead of the 2030 FIFA World Cup.

What the AfDB loan actually finances

The board of the African Development Bank approved the financing on 8 July 2026 under the Rail Infrastructure Development Support Project, known by its French acronym PADIF. The €205 million ($234 million) package targets the physical track layer: rails, track components, switches, plus engineering supervision and results monitoring.

The works concentrate on the Kenitra–Marrakech corridor and the Casablanca rail hub. This is the “permanent way” layer where construction delays and supply-chain bottlenecks most often derail large rail programmes.

Morocco’s national rail operator ONCF will implement the project. The loan covers both the conventional network and the high-speed line on the same axis.

A $10 billion railway programme takes shape

The AfDB money is a single tranche inside a far larger investment cycle. Morocco’s wider railway programme is valued at about 96 billion dirhams, or roughly $10 billion, and centres on extending the high-speed line south from Tangier–Kenitra toward Marrakech via Rabat and Casablanca.

The new line is planned at 430 kilometres with an operating speed of 320 km/h. ONCF has also signalled plans to purchase 150 trains, and France has already committed a €781 million loan for 18 Alstom high-speed units.

Spain and South Korea are providing additional concessional financing for rolling stock. This multi-lender approach spreads political risk and gives several manufacturing nations a long-term stake in Morocco’s rail backbone.

Why the World Cup deadline concentrates minds

Morocco will co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup with Spain and Portugal. The tournament has become a hard deadline that forces infrastructure decisions to move from planning to procurement at unusual speed.

Rail is the most visible piece of that push. The government is using the event to demonstrate state capacity, investor readiness, and the ability to deliver complex projects on time.

The rail plan is also a statement about Morocco’s role as a gateway between Europe and West Africa. A modern, bankable transport network reinforces the kingdom’s pitch as a logistics and manufacturing bridge.

The great-power and lender contest behind the tracks

The AfDB loan is not arriving in isolation. In roughly the same period, the World Bank approved a $350 million package for the Greater Casablanca Mobility and Logistics Hub, and the European Investment Bank signed a €365 million transport package in Rabat on 30 June 2026.

The EIB deal included €50 million for ONCF rail rehabilitation and a €15 million European Union grant for climate resilience. France, Spain, and South Korea are all financing train purchases, while the AfDB, World Bank, and EIB cover the fixed infrastructure.

This layered financing model is a deliberate strategy. It reduces Morocco’s dependence on any single external patron and gives multiple powers a reason to see the programme succeed. The pattern mirrors what we track in Africa: The New Scramble, where infrastructure has become the primary arena for great-power competition on the continent.

What the numbers say about African infrastructure appetite

AfDB president Akinwumi Adesina said in Rabat in December 2024 that the bank was overseeing nearly 37 investment projects in Morocco worth $3.6 billion. At the same Africa Investment Forum, investors offered more than $13 billion against ONCF’s target of $8.8 billion for its railway plan.

The oversubscription is a signal. It suggests that Morocco’s rail programme is seen as one of the more bankable infrastructure plays on the continent, combining sovereign creditworthiness with a clear revenue model and a fixed deadline.

Morocco aims to grow its high-speed network from 320 kilometres today to more than 1,280 kilometres by 2040. The total rail network is projected to reach about 3,800 kilometres, connecting more cities and a larger share of the population.

The South-South and BRICS read-through

For Latin American and BRICS-focused readers, the Morocco case offers a direct comparison with Brazil’s own infrastructure financing challenges. Both countries are using multilateral development bank money to close gaps that purely commercial lending cannot fill on acceptable terms.

Morocco is also deepening its role as a hub for continental capital mobilisation. Moroccan institution Ithmar Capital has been strengthening ties with the AfDB and other African sovereign investors under the New African Financial Architecture for Development agenda.

The kingdom is not simply a borrower. It is positioning itself as a bridge between African, European, and Gulf capital networks, using infrastructure as the visible proof of that role.

What to watch next

The next milestone is whether ONCF can keep the Kenitra–Marrakech high-speed line on schedule for the 2030 deadline. Track-laying contracts and signalling tenders will be the clearest indicators of progress.

The train procurement sequence also bears watching. The mix of French, Spanish, and South Korean suppliers will shape Morocco’s long-term industrial partnerships and maintenance dependencies.

Finally, the AfDB’s growing Morocco portfolio suggests the bank is betting heavily on the kingdom as a creditworthy anchor for its North African operations. Any sign of fiscal strain or project delay would ripple well beyond the rail sector.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the AfDB financing in Morocco’s rail expansion?

The African Development Bank approved a €205 million ($234 million) loan on 8 July 2026 for the Rail Infrastructure Development Support Project (PADIF). The money covers rails, track components, switches, and engineering supervision on the Kenitra–Marrakech corridor and around the Casablanca rail hub. ONCF, Morocco’s national rail operator, is implementing the project.

How does this loan fit into Morocco’s wider railway programme?

The AfDB loan is one piece of a roughly $10 billion railway investment programme tied to the 2030 FIFA World Cup. Morocco is extending its high-speed line 430 kilometres from Kenitra to Marrakech, with trains running at 320 km/h. The World Bank, European Investment Bank, France, Spain, and South Korea are all providing parallel financing for different parts of the programme.

What are Morocco’s long-term rail expansion targets?

Morocco aims to grow its high-speed network from 320 kilometres today to more than 1,280 kilometres by 2040. The total rail network is projected to reach about 3,800 kilometres, connecting more cities and a larger share of the population. These targets are embedded in ONCF’s long-term planning and have attracted over $13 billion in investor interest.

World.title: Latin America Visa Runs Are Dead: Residency Now Required
World.content:
Latin America · Immigration

Key Facts The shift. Five popular hubs are closing the tourist-stay loophole at the same time.

Five popular hubs are closing the tourist-stay loophole at the same time. Argentina. Insurance and purpose are checked at entry; a “false tourist” can be refused.

Insurance and purpose are checked at entry; a “false tourist” can be refused. Brazil. The 90-day extension is reportedly refused more often; the fix is the nomad visa.

The 90-day extension is reportedly refused more often; the fix is the nomad visa. Mexico. The tourist permit is no longer automatically 180 days; overstays draw one-to-five-year bans.

The tourist permit is no longer automatically 180 days; overstays draw one-to-five-year bans. The rule. Hold a status that matches how you actually use the country.

For years, the cheapest way to live in much of Latin America was to never get residency at all — just renew a tourist stamp with a border hop. That era is closing, in several countries at once, and the fix is the same everywhere: get a status that matches how you live.

Across the region, rolling tourist entries are increasingly treated as misuse. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Argentina: checked at the border

Argentina now checks health insurance and a sworn statement of purpose when non-residents enter, and its officers can refuse a “tourist” they judge is really residing, under the 2025 migration reform. Temporary residency also lapses after six months abroad.

The durable route is formal residency, most commonly the rentista or investment paths, which lead to permanent residency. Carry compliant insurance whenever you cross the border.

Brazil: the tourist extension tightens

Brazil grants visitors 90 days, extendable to 180 in a year, but visa-service reporting says those extensions are being refused more often, leaving overstayers in a legal grey zone. Treat the trend as reported, and confirm the current rule with the Federal Police.

If you live in Brazil, the answer is the digital-nomad visa, the VITEM XIV, which needs about US$1,500 a month in income or US$18,000 in savings, plus health insurance valid in Brazil.

Mexico: no more automatic 180 days

Mexico no longer automatically grants the full 180-day tourist permit; officers set the length based on your stated plans and documents. Overstaying is logged, and the immigration institute increasingly issues re-entry bans of one to five years, plus fines.

Border runs to reset the clock are being scrutinised, so anyone settling in Mexico should move to a proper residency — the income or savings route, or a family tie — rather than rely on tourist entries.

Peru: the 90-day norm

Peru’s officers usually grant 90 days, and while up to 183 is possible at their discretion, staying beyond 183 days in a year can lead Migraciones to refuse you at the next entry. Overstays carry a small daily fine, paid on exit.

For a long stay, use a residency route rather than stacking tourist entries. The digital-nomad permit exists in law but still cannot be filed, so remote workers use other categories.

Chile: apply before you arrive

Chile does not let you switch from a tourist stamp to residency inside the country in the ordinary case. The temporary-residence visa is applied for from abroad, through the SERMIG portal, before you travel.

New arrivals also get a valuable tax runway, three years of foreign-income exemption, extendable to six, which rewards planning the move properly rather than drifting in as a tourist.

The common thread

The pattern across the region is the same: authorities now expect foreigners who actually live somewhere to hold a status that matches how they use the country, whether that is rentista, digital-nomad, professional or investment residency. Rolling tourist entries are treated as misuse.

Enforcement still varies by officer and keeps evolving, so confirm each country’s current rule with its immigration authority before you travel. This is general information, not legal advice.

03

What to See & Do

FRIDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — LAST-CHANCE ART Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel Masterpieces, Brought to São Paulo’s Floor The touring immersive exhibition “Michelangelo: O Mestre da Capela Sistina” is open this Sunday at MIS Experience, Rua Cenno Sbrighi 250, Água Branca, and Friday is your most serene window to experience it before the weekend rush. Using licensed high-definition photography, the show projects the Vatican’s frescoes onto vast surfaces and floors, allowing a close-up, contemplative look at The Creation of Adam and The Last Judgement without a flight to Rome — a profound date with Renaissance genius. Hourly entry slots run from 10am to 8pm; tickets from R$40 (half-price for students and seniors) are sold online and, subject to availability, at the door — booking ahead on Fever is genuinely wise for a Friday. Reach it via CPTM Linha 7-Rubi (Água Branca station plus a short walk) or bus corridors from Avenida Santo Amaro — factor in thirty minutes from Pinheiros by app car, as the late afternoon rodízio distorts traffic in the expanded centre. Afterwards, debrief over an espresso and a pão de queijo at Santo Grão Café (Rua Oscar Freire, Jardins), a short trip north, and let the Baroque drama settle before the evening programme begins.

OUTDOORS — A CENTRAL STROLL A Sé-to-República Walk, No Clouds Needed Put the weather’s moody cloud to work as soft, natural light for photographing Centro’s architectural heft — start at the Catedral da Sé, walk west under the monumental Edifício Martinelli, and cut through the mosaic-lined Galeria do Rock. The open-air Praça da República, with its weekend hippie-craft fair previewing late in the day, is a breezy spot to sit with a caldo de cana, watching São Paulo’s relentless, chaotic choreography unfold against a wintery grey sky.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — REPÚBLICA & JARDINS Quiet Corners for a Friday Brainstorm For a morning deep-work session with excellent Brazilian single-origin, go to Por Um Punhado de Dólares (Rua Dr. Cesário Mota Jr, República) — its quiet back-room library vibe and reliable Wi-Fi are a nomad’s secret shelter until 8pm. Later in Jardins, Coffee Mais Prosa (Rua Haddock Lobo) blends co-working spirit with a leafy pavement terrace: take noon calls at a shaded outdoor table over a R$12 espresso and a tapioca, plugged into a generous no-rush weekend rhythm.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — A QUIET SUBURBAN EVENING Mooca’s Italian Lullaby, Far from the Friday Crowds If the thought of Vila Madalena’s nocturnal roar is too much, head east to Mooca for a dinner that feels like a São Paulo still untouched by time — Castelões Cantina (Rua Javari, 100) serves 1920s-era pizza and beer in a tiled, family-thronged room. Walk it off through the tranquil streets past the old factories and Italian social clubs, ending with a quiet glass at the understated Adega do Rigo, where Friday feels less like a release valve and more like a slow, savoured breath.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Football Screens, Samba Circles, and Rooftop Talk As the air cools by sunset, Vila Madalena stirs: Beco do Batman’s open-air graffiti walls drain the last tourists, and nearby bars raise the volume on a big Paulista football clash. Catch the match in full voice at São Cristóvão Bar & Futebol (Rua Aspicuelta) — a temple to the game with cold Original on tap, screens in every corner, and a mixed-allegiance crowd that makes every goal a riot, plus Pirajá (Avenida Brigadeiro Faria Lima) out west for a more polished watch party. For a samba pulse with no cover, trail the players of Samba da Vela into a wedged Vila Madalena boteco where the weekly roda de samba erupts — expect tight percussion and a midnight crowd singing every lyric.

ALSO ON TODAY Michelangelo: O Mestre da Capela Sistina — MIS Experience, Água Branca — terça a domingo 10h–18h (sábados, domingos e feriados até 19h), ingressos grátis às terças, a partir de R$30. Exposição “Lasar Segall: Um Modernista Brasileiro” — Museu Lasar Segall, Vila Mariana — 11am–7pm, free entry, a serene walk through a master modernist’s painted and printed world. Amanhã: Feira de Antiguidades do Bixiga — Praça Dom Orione, Bixiga — Saturday 9am–5pm, free entry, the city’s most charismatic vintage and bric-a-brac crawl. Pôr do Sol at Praça Pôr do Sol — Alto de Pinheiros — 5:42 pm sunset; bring a blanket, a thermos, and watch the skyline silhouette against a winter citrus glow. Cinema: Mostra de Retrospectiva Italiana — CineSESC, Rua Augusta — 6pm & 8:30 pm screenings, tickets R$10 (SESC), a Fellini double-bill in a historic cinema. Aula Aberta de Forró — Bar do Alemão, Pinheiros — 8pm, free, a welcoming beginner forró class with live trios later; dance shoes not required.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

This Friday falls under normal rodízio rules: the municipal vehicle restriction is in force across the Centro Expandido, banning cars with plates ending in 9 and 0 during the morning peak of 7am–10am and the evening crush of 5pm–8pm, with a fine of R$130.16 for violations.

Metrô and CPTM lines are running regular Friday timetables; riders on Linhas 11-Coral, 12-Safira and 13-Jade should, however, expect possible residual delays following yesterday’s power interruption near Brás–Engenheiro Goulart — check the TOP app before departing.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: A Centro duo: Bar do Mané (Rua Aurora) for a plate-of-the-day PF at R$35, its old-school counters humming; or Copanzinho (Rua Avanhandava) for a relaxed R$50 grilled-sandwich and a cold chope.

Dinner: West-side splits: authentic pasta magic at the cramped, red-checked Taberna Santo Antonio (Pinheiros, around R$80/person); or modern Brazilian plates at Jiquitaia (Paraíso), where R$120 buys a tasting menu and a fine caipirinha.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a light jacket for the post-sunset drop and keep a small umbrella in your bag for the slim chance of a cold-front drizzle; Pix is near-universal across bars and museums, but having R$50 in small notes is wise for street feiras and caldo de cana stalls.

Book Michelangelo tickets online via Fever before heading to Água Branca to avoid a sold-out slot; for the night’s samba and football bars in Vila Madalena, arriving by 7:30pm secures a table before the 8pm crush.

Stick to well-lit, populated routes when filing out of Centro’s Praça da República after dark — the area empties quickly after offices close, so order a ride from a café or bar porch rather than waving the phone on the street.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Digital nomads on the SP Friday loop should look to the “Expats SP – Coffee & Coworking” WhatsApp group, whose members routinely post up at Coffee Mais Prosa on Fridays for a low-key afternoon brainstorming and happy-hour segue.

The “São Paulo Nomads” Meetup holds a casual English-language happy hour tonight at O Pasquim Bar in Pinheiros from 7pm — it is the single best plug-in point for a newcomer hunting an apartment lead, a weekend hiking squad, or a fellow football neutral.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

São Paulo’s football weekend ignites with the city’s rival clubs vying early in the Série A return: tonight, Corinthians face a tough away clash, a game that will pack every Allianz Parque-adjacent and Vila Madalena bar by 7pm.

Kickoff times and venues were fluid as of press, but the standard 8:30 pm BRT Friday slot means the watch-party energy assembles from 7pm — look to São Cristóvão Bar (Rua Aspicuelta, Vila Madalena) for a cathedral of football with a raucous crowd and cold Original.

A refined alternative is Pirajá (Avenida Brigadeiro Faria Lima, Pinheiros), whose large patio screens and crisp caipirinhas offer a less elbow-to-elbow viewing experience for neutrals and the shirt-averse.

With Palmeiras and São Paulo FC also in weekend action, expect a rolling festival of green, white, and tricolour colours across pub screens through Sunday night, cementing this as a perfect weekend to absorb local football passion.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The last settled session on 2026-07-23 produced losses across all the main Americas equity and currency boards printed in the panel (Business & Markets / WEEK IN FIGURES): the S&P 500, Ibovespa, Merval, and IPSA all fell, while Latin American currencies broadly weakened against a stronger dollar, with notable 1%+ softness in the Chilean peso.

The mood reflects a global end-of-week caution as the market prices in an extended period of elevated U.S. interest rates; Brazil’s Ibovespa was dragged by commodity weight, and the broader risk-off saw the Mexican peso give up 0.75%, while a puzzling 0.37% USD/COP dip bucked the regional trend.

For the expat professional in São Paulo, the board underpins a cautious near-term macro backdrop: a firm USD/BRL at mid-5 levels crimps overseas remittance power, and signals that Faria Lima desks will open Monday scanning for fresh rate rhetoric out of the Fed and the Copom.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD Sat July 25 — Bixiga antique fair from 9am, dry winter light; Paulista Ave open to pedestrians; football watches from 4pm. Sun July 26 — Michelangelo exhibition at MIS Experience; Ibirapuera morning bike ride; midday feijoada in Vila Madalena. Mon July 27 — New week exhibitions open at IMS Paulista; rodízio resumes 9/0; Brazilian Série A midweek previews. Tue July 28 — Fresh corporate week: expat coffee mornings in Itaim;

Museu do Futebol open late; rodízio plates 1/2. Wed July 29 — Midweek samba at Ó do Borogodó; a cooler evening low near 13°C; check the board for fresh data.

Background: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — July 23, 2026.

Background: São Paulo Daily Brief — Thursday, July 23, 2026.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

I just landed in São Paulo this morning. Can I drive my car today and where am I restricted?

Today, Friday, the rodízio is in normal operation and applies to the Centre Expanded area bounded by the Minianel Viário. If your car’s number plate ends in a 9 or a 0, you are prohibited from driving in this zone between 7:00 am and 10:00 am, and again from 5:00 pm until 8:00 pm — violating it means a R$130.16 fine and 4 points on your licence. Motorcycles are exempt, as are cars on weekends and holidays. If your plate ends in any other digit, you are free to drive all day. For plates 9 and 0, the best alternative during the evening window is the Metrô or a ride-hail app; order one from your café and wait inside.

What is the one unmissable thing I should do this specific weekend in São Paulo?

Go to “Michelangelo: O Mestre da Capela Sistina” in Água Branca — open until 19:00 on Sundays. This is a licensed, high-definition projection exhibition that spreads the Sistine Chapel’s entire ceiling and Last Judgement across vast floors and walls, letting you see every finger of The Creation of Adam from centimetres away. Tickets start at R$40 on Fever, and a Friday visit dodges the weekend rush. Afterwards, take a car north to Jardins for coffee, and you have a culturally perfect winter day without braving a line or a crowd.

I want to watch the football with locals but I don’t know which bar I’ll feel comfortable in as a foreigner.

Lapa’s cultural strip calls tonight with live samba at Rio Scenarium (confirm the current cover ahead) and an ever-changing line-up at Circo Voador.

Latin American equities broadly dipped yesterday; check the board for the real’s move against the dollar as you budget your weekend.

A day made for a waterfront museum morning, a leisurely Centro lunch, and an evening pivoting from forró to vintage samba.

Today feels properly carioca — warm sun breaking through high clouds, around 31°C at the peak, but humidity will make it feel a few degrees heavier. A quick, isolated shower may pass in the late afternoon, so don’t let the blue morning fool you entirely.

Lightweight trousers or a sundress work best; carry a light jacket or hoodie for air-conditioned museums and the evening breeze off the bay. Sandals are fine for the calçadão, but closed shoes will serve you better on Lapa’s cobblestones tonight.

The weekend settles into mostly sunny, slightly cooler comfort — ideal for Sunday’s Feira Hippie de Ipanema. Monday brings a slightly higher shower risk before Tuesday returns to a pleasant, partly cloudy rhythm.

Sunset today: 5:25 pm · Zona Sul beaches sit at a refreshing 23°C with small half-metre waves; yellow flags are flying — swim only between the lifeguard posts as rips are lurking near the channels.

A day to move slow, stay curious, and let the city’s old port carry you into its loud, joyful night.

03

What to See & Do

FRIDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — CENTRO & THE OLD PORT From the Museum of Tomorrow to a night of Northeastern forró Start your cultural Friday in Praça Mauá, where the futuristic Museu do Amanhã explores sustainability and science across immersive exhibits. Entry is R$40 (R$20 half-price), and you’ll want a timed ticket online to skip any queue — aim for 10am to have the space almost to yourself before the lunch crowd descends. Next door, the Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR, R$20) offers a grittier, deeply Brazilian take on urban history and contemporary art. Both museums close by 6pm, leaving you a perfect window for a cold chopp on the square as the golden winter light hits the bay. Grab a VLT tram (buy a R$4.30 card at any stop) and ride the sleek, cable-free light rail through the revitalised port to the rodoviária stop. Twenty minutes north by taxi or ride app sits the Feira de São Cristóvão, an indoor universe of Northeastern culture. For a R$10–R$15 entry, you get endless food stalls piling high with carne de sol, baião de dois, and tapioca, plus live forró stages where couples dance close well past midnight. It’s a state of mind, not just a market. This is a day of two Brazils: the sleek, forward-looking Centro and the raw, beating heart of the Northeast diaspora — all within a single humid Friday. Wear comfortable shoes, bring cash for the feira’s smaller vendors, and let the accordion-led trios tell you where the night is heading.

OUTDOORS — BAYSIDE STROLLS & LATE SUN Before the sun drops at 5:25 pm, walk the recently extended Orla Prefeito Luiz Paulo Conde along Guanabara Bay, starting from Praça Mauá towards the MAR. The wide promenade offers a breezy, traffic-free stretch with views of the Niterói bridge and the occasional capybara sighting in the mangroves. For a more athletic outdoor dose, hire a bike from one of the Itaú stations and pedal the dedicated lane from Flamengo Beach to Botafogo. The Aterro do Flamengo park is in its winter prime — lush, uncrowded, with cooling sea spray that takes the edge off the 30°C warmth.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO & LAPA Remote workers with a taste for history should post up at Confeitaria Colombo (Rua Gonçalves Dias, Centro). The palatial belle-époque room opens at 12pm on Fridays, offering strong espresso, reliable wifi, and a pastel de nata that justifies the premium price (cover varies by night). Arrive early to secure one of the marble tables near a power outlet. For something grittier and open late, head to Café Cultural Sacrilégio (Avenida Mem de Sá, Lapa) from 5pm. The wifi holds up, the crowd is a mix of laptop-toting freelancers and pre-samba drinkers, and the transition from work to play is seamless when the roda de samba strikes up later.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — ZONA SUL SERENITY If Centro’s density doesn’t appeal, let Leblon’s polished calm be your antidote. Walk the leafy streets of Jardim Pernambuco, then settle at the beachfront kiosk Praia do Leblon for a gentle afternoon of fresh coconut water and a book, with the sound of small winter waves as your background track. This is the Rio of quiet money and unhurried living, where a late lunch at a sidewalk restaurant on Rua Dias Ferreira stretches into the evening. The sunset will silhouette Dois Irmãos softly — a far cry from Lapa’s roaring amplifiers.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Lapa takes over once the sun sets. Start with a caipirinha on the steps of the Arcos da Lapa, where street vendors and informal capoeira circles create a free, electric pre-show. Then make your way to Rio Scenarium (Rua do Lavradio, cover varies by night) — a multi-storey antique-filled mansion where live samba, choro, and MPB play across three floors from around 8pm. A ten-minute walk away, Circo Voador (Rua dos Arcos) typically opens doors around 8pm for whatever touring act or themed party is booked tonight; tickets range R$40–R$120 depending on the headliner. Check their online agenda earlier in the day and grab a ticket before they sell out. For a less structured, more local crawl, drift between the open-door bars along Avenida Mem de Sá. The street fills with a cross-section of cariocas from all walks, cold bottles of Antarctica, and impromptu pagode circles lasting until 3am. Wear closed shoes — the pavement gets sticky.

ALSO ON TODAY Exhibition — CCBB Rio — Rua Primeiro de Março, Centro — 10am–8pm, free. Rotating contemporary art in a grand Belle-Époque hall; the current show is worth a quiet hour before your train out. Feira de São Cristóvão — Campo de São Cristóvão — from 10am, R$10–R$15 entry. Massive Northeastern food hall and forró dance floor; best visited from 7pm onward when the trios are at full tilt. Bip Bip — roda de samba — Rua Almirante Gonçalves, Copacabana — typically 7pm–late, free entry (buy a drink). An intimate, old-school circle where choro and samba purists squeeze around plastic tables on the pavement. Cinema at Estação Net Rio — Rua Voluntários da Pátria, Botafogo — various session times, R$20–R$30. Independent and Brazilian cinema in a beloved art-house setting; air-conditioned respite with a good café attached. Bar do Mineiro happy hour — Rua Paschoal Carlos Magno, Santa Teresa — 12pm–midnight. The feijoada is the daytime draw, but Friday evening brings a caipirinha-fuelled crowd spilling onto the steep street. Nuth Lounge rooftop — Avenida Nossa Senhora de Copacabana, Copacabana — 6pm–late. Drinks R$35–R$55. A polished rooftop crowd watches the lights flicker on across the Zona Sul shoreline.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

MetrôRio lines 1, 2, and 4 are scheduled for normal Friday operations, but riders should follow MetrôRio’s social channels before descending — recent weeks have seen sporadic signal and energy-related delays across the network. A single journey card costs R$7.50, and trains can be crowded between 5pm and 7pm as the Centro workforce heads home.

The VLT Carioca is a smooth way to hop from Praça Mauá to the edge of Lapa; buy a R$4.30 card at any tram stop machine, though note the trams are slow during peak evening hours. If rain arrives suddenly, ride-hailing surge pricing kicks in hard — consider ducking into a bar in Lapa or São Cristóvão and waiting 30 minutes for fares to normalise.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: A casual Centro lunch at Bar Luiz (Rua da Carioca) delivers old-school German-Brazilian dishes like chope and salsichão for around R$60–R$80. Alternatively, the pay-by-weight buffet at Grão Integral (Rua da Quitanda) offers fresh salads and grilled meats for roughly R$55 per kilo, popular with local office workers.

Dinner: For a pre-Lapa feast, Santo Scenário (Rua do Lavradio) serves polished Brazilian comfort food like moqueca and grilled picanha for two at R$140–R$180 in a soft-lit courtyard. In Ipanema, the Argentine-inflected Frontera (Rua Barão da Torre) offers excellent bife de chorizo and malbec for R$90–R$130 per person with a quieter, date-night murmur.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a small daypack with a water bottle, sunscreen, and an ultra-light rain shell — the late-afternoon shower can appear suddenly and pass within twenty minutes. Cards are widely accepted in Centro and Zona Sul, but Pix is the payment norm even among street vendors; set it up via your Brazilian bank app if you haven’t yet. For the Feira de São Cristóvão, bring R$100–R$150 in cash to avoid stall-level payment hiccups.

Book a timed entry for Museu do Amanhã online before leaving home to guarantee your slot, especially on a Friday when school groups sometimes visit until mid-afternoon. For Rio Scenarium, arriving before 8:30pm usually means a short queue; after 9:30pm the line can stretch for an hour.

After dark in Centro and on the Lapa-to-Cinelândia corridor, keep your phone tucked away and walk with purpose on the main streets; the area between the VLT stop and the Arcos gets gritty, not dangerous, but pickpockets work the crowd flow. Stick to well-lit, populated stretches and use ride apps for longer hops after midnight.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

The weekly Mundo Lingo language exchange (typically Thursday, but verify on their Facebook page) has likely just happened, so tonight is for practising your newly acquired Portuguese in the wild at Rio Scenarium — cariocas are generous with learners and a badly pronounced ‘mais uma cerveja, por favor’ will earn smiles. The Internations Rio chapter also lists a casual after-work mixer on their app, often at a rooftop in Botafogo or Copacabana.

New arrivals plug in fastest via the WhatsApp groups for ‘Rio Expats Meetup’ and ‘Digital Nomads Rio’ — ask at any Selina or coworking lobby in Lapa or Flamengo for an invite link. The Muralzinho de Ideias space in Glória occasionally hosts free Friday afternoon co-working with a creative, bilingual crowd.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

With no Rio Série A fixtures confirmed for tonight, the football focus shifts to the weekend’s likely match-ups. Flamengo, sitting second on 34 points and stuttering slightly after two winless league outings, expects to play a weekend fixture still to be confirmed by the CBF; the stakes are unusually sharp with Palmeiras opened up a gap at the top. Reliable expat watch spots include Belmonte (Rua Dias Ferreira, Leblon) with its wall-to-wall screens, or the rowdier Bar da Frente (Rua Barão de Iguatemi, Praça da Bandeira), where boteco charm meets fervent debate.

Fluminense, third on 31 points, carries strong form into whatever fixture drops in the coming days; maracanista expats can catch that game at Boteco Belmonte in Flamengo, where the post-beach crowd merges with shirt-wearing tricolores. For any Série A game confirmed by Friday, kickoff times are typically 4pm, 6:30pm, or 9pm BRT across the weekend.

No major tennis or F1 events affect the Rio calendar this week, leaving the beach-side altinha circles and sunset volleyball on Ipanema’s Posto 9 as the participatory sporting highlights. The real action is the carioca championship’s boardroom wrangling over stadium allocations, which will shape where and how fans travel to the big games next week.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Latin American equities broadly moved lower yesterday, with the Ibovespa tracking regional caution alongside the IPC in Mexico and the IPSA in Chile. The full verified levels and percentage moves are on the inserted board — look to the real’s close against the dollar there to gauge local purchasing power for the weekend.

The structural story continues to be the hollowing out of the B3, as Brazilian companies delist or move primary listings abroad in search of deeper liquidity and lower regulatory friction. For the expat professional, this matters: a shrinking local equity market pushes more wealth into dollarised assets and keeps long-term pressure on the real, even on days when the spot rate feels calm.

Looking ahead, any fresh commentary from Brasília on fiscal targets or trade policy — particularly any US tariff threat on Brazilian steel or ethanol — could swing the Ibovespa sharply, as seen earlier this month when similar fears sliced nearly a full percentage point off the index. Weekend reading: monitor the Friday evening news cycle from the Fed and the Brazilian finance ministry for signals that will hit Monday’s opening board.

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is it safe to swim at Copacabana or Ipanema today?

Yellow flags are flying, which means caution is required — the sea is not closed but is rated as a moderate risk. Waves are modest at around 0.5 to 1.0 metre on the Zona Sul shore, but winter rip currents run strongly near the drainage channels and rock formations. Only enter the water directly in front of an active lifeguard post, where the bombeiros can see you. If you feel yourself being pulled, don’t fight the rip — swim parallel to the beach until you’re out of the current, then make your way back to shore at an angle.

How do I get from Centro to Lapa after dark without using my phone on the street?

The simplest route is to walk with the crowd along Avenida Mem de Sá from the Arcos da Lapa, under the brightly lit aqueduct. The path is heavily trafficked on Friday nights with partygoers heading to the same samba venues, so you’re part of a river of people rather than a solitary target. If you’re alone or nervous, a ride-hailing car from Praça Mauá to the door of Rio Scenarium costs around R$15–R$20 and takes ten minutes — wait for the car inside the museum lobby or a bar entrance, not on the kerb. Once inside Lapa’s main strip, the area is loud, crowded, and well-policed until about 3am.
