World.title: Electric Cars in Costa Rica Face a Higher Sales Tax
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Finance Ministry has increased the selective consumption tax applied to electric vehicles, a change Finance Minister Rodrigo Chaves announced Wednesday evening and which the country’s electric mobility industry says was already mandated by legislation approved four years ago.

Chaves, who also serves as Minister of the Presidency, said in a television interview that he had signed the decree that day. He gave two figures in the course of his remarks. He said electric vehicles had been paying a 6% rate and that the government intends to bring that figure to 30%, and he said separately that the rate applied immediately is 7.5%.

The minister defended the measure on the grounds that Costa Rica’s potential contribution to combating climate change is minimal. He questioned the electric vehicle incentive policies pursued by previous administrations and said the country should concentrate its resources on measures that produce direct benefits.

Silvia Rojas, director of the Costa Rican Electric Mobility Association, known by its Spanish acronym Asomove, disputed the characterization of the change as a government initiative. She said the 2022 reform to the Green Transport Incentives Law had already established that electric vehicles would begin paying 25% of the full 30% selective consumption rate, the figure of 7.5% that Chaves announced, and that the schedule called for that step to take effect last year rather than this week.

“The announcement is not about new taxes,” Rojas said, describing the decree instead as the law being carried out as written. Rojas also set out the remaining schedule the legislation establishes. By 2028, electric vehicles would pay half the selective consumption rate, equivalent to 15 percentage points of the 30. By 2031 the proportion rises to three quarters, or 22.5 points.

In 2034, the full 30% applies. The same law governs reduced value added tax and customs valuation rates for electric vehicles alongside the selective consumption levy. The minister did not address how vehicles already imported or awaiting customs clearance will be treated, and publication of the decree in La Gaceta, the official gazette, has not been confirmed.

Electric vehicle registrations have been rising steadily. Figures compiled by Asomove recorded 1,064 new electric vehicles registered in April 2026 alone, of which 1,007 were passenger cars, with the remainder made up of motorcycles, specialised vehicles and work vehicles.

The decree emerged from a wider fiscal package the Finance Ministry presented Wednesday, comprising more than 15 bills covering electronic invoicing, penalties for tax evasion, the regulation of exemptions and a reform of income tax. Chaves has said the government does not intend to create new taxes, and the ministry has indicated that applying the 13% value added tax to the basic food basket remains under consideration, subject to conditions.

Chaves said in the same interview that the ministry will file a separate bill in September to simplify and reduce the taxes levied on alcohol and cigarettes. He did not specify the size of the proposed reduction, saying only that the initiative would cover both categories.

World.title: Grief turns to protest in Troy
World.content:
Placard-bearing residents in Troy, Trelawny, on Thursday protesting againt the arrest of a man in connection with fatal mobbing following murder of 10-year-old Shani Coke.

TROY, Trelawny — Still mourning the murder of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke on Tuesday residents of the usually quiet district took to the streets on Thursday after one of their own was reportedly arrested by the police in connection with the mob killing of the man believed to have attacked her.

According to residents the man was taken into custody by the police who are probing the death of Shani and the fatal attack on the suspected child killer Delroy Coke, and the brutal beating of his father.

The placard-bearing residents used debris to block the Troy main road — which links part of south Trelawny to northern Manchester — as they charged that the police had no reason to arrest the man, whose identity has not been released.

The residents also expressed their anger at the murder of Shani.

“We want justice. Protect our children. Children are the future. Let us protect them. The justice system failed us. We want justice for the brutal murder of Shani,” some of the placards read, while other called for the freeing of the man they said had been taken into custody.

Some of the protesters also took to social media platform TikTok to express their frustration and disgust.

“We a protest, because the police lock up a man and we want him to be freed…. We want justice,” one of the protesting residents told the Jamaica Observer.

Shani partially nude body was found with her throat slashed in bushes on Tuesday. Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on the father and son in the community.

Residents told the Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. They accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father was left with major wounds.

When contacted head of the police Area One Assistant Commissioner Glenford Miller said the investigators are seeking those involved in the mob attack.

“I know we are investigating to know who were the persons involved in that mob killing. I cannot say at this time if we have made any arrests,” Miller said mid-morning on Thursday. Subsequent efforts to get a further update were unsuccessful up to press time.

A heavy pall of gloom and anger clouded over Troy on Thursday with one resident telling the

Observer that the community remains grief-stricken.

“The whole of Troy is in mourning. We can’t stop thinking about the little girl and how she died so awful,” said the resident who requested anonymity.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday, Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

On Wednesday relatives remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night [Tuesday] we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” her aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

World.title: ‘The best yet’
World.content:
Kevin Downswell.

Award-winning Jamaican gospel artiste Kevin Downswell says his upcoming album is the most personal project of his career, describing it as his “the best yet” and the most vulnerable he has ever allowed himself to be in his music.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer’s Spalsh ahead of his Pre-Album Launch Worship Experience on Sunday, July 19 at Victory Tabernacle, Bayside, Port Henderson Road, Portmore, Downswell revealed that the unnamed album was largely written during the COVID-19 pandemic, with its songs inspired by seasons of uncertainty, disappointment, perseverance, and renewed faith.

“I wrote most of these songs in the pandemic, when we were feeling all the pressure and the battles, the tears, the pain and the disappointment,” he said. “Wherever you are in your process, one song will connect with you.”

Asked to describe the album in three words, the gospel minister replied simply: “The best yet.”

Downswell said listeners can expect what he considers his strongest songwriting to date.

“I think this is the realest I’ve ever been in my songs,” he said. “This is the most vulnerable I’ve ever been with my tracks… and I think this is the best I’ve ever written.”

He added that fans will hear pieces of his own testimony throughout the album: “You’ll hear my story in every song. You’ll know that I couldn’t write like this if I hadn’t been through something like this.”

The first taste of the project came with the release of Higher (From the Fire) on Tuesday, July 14, an Afro-soca anthem centred on overcoming life’s trials.

“Sometimes what was meant to destroy you actually lifts you higher,” Downswell explained, pointing to the biblical story of Joseph as one of the inspirations behind the song.

The singer also disclosed that the album moves beyond traditional gospel, blending worship music with reggae, Afro-soca and calypso influences.

“I’ve always tried to stay away from limitations,” he said. “It’s a beautiful mixture.”

The event, which formed part of the Portmore New Testament Church of God’s 50th anniversary celebrations, served as an opportunity for fans to hear songs from the upcoming album before its official release.

“There’s nothing like live performances,” he said. “I’ve worked all my life to make the live experience better than the recordings.”

Beyond the music, Downswell said his greatest hope is that listeners encounter God in a fresh way.

“I’ve fallen in love with God all over again,” he said. “I just want people to experience His presence and His love. I want God to meet people wherever they’re at.”

World.title: BPO’S US$220-M SLIDE
World.content:
Key points:

Local spending fell 22 per cent from about US$1 billion to US$780 million as another 5,000 jobs disappeared.

Government data put employment at 50,000, while the GSAJ estimates about 40,000.

A working group is pursuing new investment, better skills and a shift towards higher-value KPO services.

JAMAICA’S global digital services (GDS) sector spent an estimated US$780 million in the local economy in the fiscal year ended March 2026, down US$220 million from about US$1 billion a year earlier as the industry lost another 5,000 jobs.

The estimate — which measures spending in Jamaica rather than export earnings — was higher than the US$612 million earned from bauxite and alumina exports in 2025 and was equivalent to about 47 per cent of the country’s US$1.65 billion in total merchandise exports.

The spending covered wages, office-space leases, utilities and other operating expenses.

Employment in the sector fell to approximately 50,000 in March 2026 from 62,000 two years earlier, while the number of companies declined from more than 90 to about 70.

The sector had already missed Government’s March 2025 target of 70,400 jobs by 15,400. By March 2026, the gap had widened to 20,400 jobs.

“This decrease in employment is attributed to a variety of factors which include: Onshoring/reshoring, geopolitical considerations, technological advancements, the impact of Hurricane Melissa and the local challenges of cost of doing business,” the Government of Jamaica stated in its annual report on Form 18-K for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission.

The report said Hurricane Melissa compounded those pressures.

“Hurricane Melissa, in particular, had a disruptive impact on Jamaica’s GDS sector, primarily through damage to critical infrastructure and interruptions to essential utilities. Widespread outages in electricity and telecommunications networks constrained business continuity across BPO (business process outsourcing) and other digitally enabled services, limiting firms’ ability to meet international client demands and maintain service-level agreements. In addition, damage to transportation networks and displacement of workers further affected operational capacity and productivity,” the annual report added.

However, Global Services Association of Jamaica President-elect Yoni Epstein has placed employment in the sector at about 40,000 for two consecutive years. The

Jamaica Observer reported on August 1, 2025, that Epstein said the sector employed about 40,000 people, a figure he repeated to the

Financial Gleaner earlier this month. The Government, by comparison, reported approximately 55,000 jobs in March 2025 and 50,000 in March 2026, leaving differences of 15,000 and 10,000, respectively. It was not immediately clear whether the discrepancies reflected different reporting periods, industry coverage or methods of counting workers. Epstein is the founder and CEO of Outsourcing Management Limited, trading as itel.

Since 2012, the Development Bank of Jamaica Limited (DBJ) has committed US$92.66 million in financing to the GDS sector and disbursed US$90.01 million to 20 BPO ventures covering approximately 1.18 million square feet of operating space. The ventures had a combined capacity for 27,513 jobs.

The report said DBJ financing also facilitated US$152.72 million in private-sector investment. However, the Government’s latest report gives a different account of the occupancy of the DBJ-funded projects.

The 2025 annual report said all 20 projects had been completed, leased and occupied and had reported total employment of 22,598. However, the 2026 report said only 19 projects were leased and occupied and had provided 22,598 jobs at their peak. It said the remaining project had been completed with capacity for another 1,200 jobs, but the developer was still seeking an operator. The reports do not explain the change in the stated occupancy of the projects.

The sector’s contraction has also affected the Port Authority of Jamaica (PAJ), which recently postponed plans to monetise its BPO real estate assets through an initial public offering on the Jamaica Stock Exchange.

A CariCRIS report on the PAJ noted, “The authority decided that prevailing market conditions were not conducive to achieving favourable valuation outcomes and therefore postponed the transaction.”

The Government has responded by establishing a working group comprising representatives of the GDS sector, the PAJ, Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) and the Jamaica Special Economic Zone Authority (JSEZA) to develop and implement an action plan aimed at growing the industry.

The working group’s mandate was limited to three areas in the Government’s 2025 annual report. The latest report expands the mandate to six areas. One of the six areas is changing the industry’s mix of BPO and KPO (knowledge process outsourcing) jobs from 80:20 to 60:40. This would reduce the sector’s concentration in basic queries and routine tasks while expanding its participation in more advanced, higher-value activities.

Other focus areas include enhancing job-readiness and digital-skills curricula, optimising processes, institutions, regulations and the incentives framework, strengthening the sector’s value proposition, and developing incubator and accelerator programmes for small and medium-sized enterprises. These initiatives build on work being done with the HEART/NSTA Trust, the United Kingdom Trade Partnerships Programme and the Inter-American Development Bank to better prepare GDS firms and their staff to take on new global opportunities.

“Jamaica, through Jampro (the government agency responsible for the promotion of business opportunities in export and investment), has actively engaged international KPO operators to get them to expand their business to Jamaica. Additionally, Jampro continues to work with local universities and key stakeholders, sharing opportunities for employment as well as establishing partnerships for training in the KPO and ITO (information technology outsourcing) space,” the annual report stated.

World.title: CASH SQUEEZE
World.content:
Jamaica Football Federation headquarters in New Kingston (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts has outlined what he considers a harsh financial reality facing the body, which is managing a tight cash-flow situation after putting significant resources into national team programmes that ultimately missed out on major qualification payouts.

International football is a high-stakes business, and Ricketts says the JFF is counting the cost of an aggressive push for global recognition that fell short on the pitch.

Failing to qualify for the 2026 FIFA World Cup cost the JFF a guaranteed minimum payout of at least US$10.5 million to US$12.5 million (under J$2 billion) — a windfall tied to FIFA participation and preparation fees.

For a federation historically hampered by tight budgets, a capital injection of that size could have cleared existing debt, reduced reliance on government subventions, and fully funded grassroots facilities, coaching development, and youth travel across all age groups.

“Right now, it’s challenging,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer. “We would’ve invested heavily in so many of the World Cup qualifiers. The U-20s leave [today] to participate in the last round. The ladies will play their last game against Costa Rica in November, and of course the senior men’s team didn’t do as well as we would’ve thought; hence, we did not get the returns based on the investment.”

The immediate strain comes as national squads continue to compete. While the senior men missed their target, the federation must still fund ongoing campaigns, including the departure of the national Under-20 team and the senior women’s team’s crucial November fixture.

Should the Reggae Girlz win that Concacaf W Championship game against Costa Rica, they qualify not only for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but also for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil. At the latter, they would receive a financial payout for competing in the group stage at the very minimum. FIFA has however not yet shared an exact breakdown of monetary prizes for this tournament.

Ricketts defended the heavy spending as a necessary cost of doing business in modern football, where federations must spend aggressively across all age groups just to remain competitive on the world stage.

“There were so many teams vying for global recognition that it cost us a lot of money,” Ricketts said. “So, we are struggling right now financially, simply because we would’ve invested heavily in these programmes and the senior men’s team didn’t qualify.”

Despite the short-term financial challenge, Ricketts says staying visible on the global stage remains the JFF’s best path forward. Mentioning long-term commercial goals, such as Jamaica’s interest in hosting the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup, Ricketts says the high cost of international football is a necessary investment in the country’s social and technical future.

He believes the star power of players like Khadija “Bunny” Shaw and Jody Brown demonstrates the return on investment that numbers alone cannot capture.

“This is to ensure that we impact the lives of every Jamaican,” Ricketts said. “Everybody wants to be like Bunny Shaw, everybody wants to be like a Jody Brown, everybody wants to be like a Jamaican player. So, we’re very hopeful, we’re optimistic that this will, from a commercial standpoint, from a technical standpoint, from a social standpoint, certainly help our country.”

World.title: Addison adds up victory
World.content:
Chris-John Addison celebrates his second win in the Drift Ruption series at Falmouth Cruise Ship Pier on July 19.(Photo: Rory Daley)

Chris-John Addison was the winner of the second round of Drift Ruption, which was held on Sunday, July 19, at the Falmouth Cruise Ship Pier, Trelawny.

“This victory is a great feeling, because we were leading the competition from round one, and nevertheless we came out today to execute, and that’s what we did,” Addison told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

Addison worked his way through a field stacked with major drift talent from across the island.

In the Drift Ruption format, entrants are whittled down to the highest-scoring eight, and then the highest-scoring four to determine the winner.

It is not a timed event, but a pure drift event in which the drivers have to display maximum slip angle while navigating and interacting with various obstacles for points.

So tough was the competition that several drivers posted perfect runs, leading to multiple ties. When it came to the final four Addison was tied with Sheldon Johnson at the very end. It was his consistently high scores throughout the event that eventually gained him the win.

“This round we didn’t do anything different, because we have an engine being built for high-speed drifting, so we decided to use the stock motor for this, the last car park event. Other than that, no major upgrades. That happens next event,” explained Addison.

Following Addison and Johnson were Cleve Ottey and Nicholas Barnes.

The current standings put Addison at the top of the leaderboard with 200 points. Johnson sits in second with 176 points. Barnes is third on 128 points, while Ottey is fourth on 124 points.

“The event went very well for me and my team,” said Kingsley Scott, event organiser and conceptualiser.

This event marks a change for Drift Ruption as it shifts to high-speed tandem drifting and a move to circuit venues, such as Dover Raceway in St Ann and JamWest Speedway in Westmoreland. The Drift Ruption finale is for a to-be-determined date in December.

World.title: WATCH: Troy residents protest amid man’s arrest following fatal mobbing over slain 10-year-old
World.content:
Placard-bearing residents protesting in Troy, Trelawny on Thursday morning.

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Placard-bearing residents of Troy, Trelawny on Thursday morning mounted a roadblock as they demanded the release of a man who they say was arrested in relation to a fatal mobbing two days ago following the gruesome murder of 10-year-old Shani Coke.

The residents also protested over Coke’s death. The child’s partially nude body was found with her throat slashed in bushes on Tuesday.

Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on a father and son in the community.

READ: Family grieves bright 10-year-old killed in Troy, as man accused of her murder beaten to death by mob

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. They accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father, who was also attacked by the mob, was admitted to hospital.

Subsequently, police arrested a man in connection with the mob attack. However, residents are demanding his release as they claim he is innocent.

“We blocked the road this morning, and police came and clear most of it. The police came and lockup [a man] and he is innocent, because the guy never went to the mobbing with any machete,” a resident who requested anonymity told Observer Online.

“The whole Troy is in mourning. We can’t stop thinking about the little girl and how she died so awful,” added the resident.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: A light extinguished
World.content:
Shawna Williams-Stevens (left) shows off trophies her niece, 10-year-old Shani Coke, received from Troy Primary School. Looking on is Shani’s mother, Ackeem “Kim” Williams. Kasey Williams

TROY, Trelawny — Huddled on the verandah of their family home, relatives of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke, whose partially nude body was found with her throat slashed on Tuesday, remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“Shani was born here and lived [with her grandparents], because her [mother] has to work. When Shani goes to school she doesn’t play around. She took her education seriously. From Shani a go basic school she was always first [in her class]. She was always putting out her best. She is from an educated background. Her father is educated and so is her mother,” the child’s aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens told journalists on Wednesday as she stood beside her grieving sister, Shani’s mother Ackeem “Kim” Williams.

The aunt’s hands could not hold the many academic trophies and certificates earned by Shani during her tenure at Troy Primary School.

“From grade one her teachers rewarded her, whether with a stamp in her book or sweets, or you know the teachers always try to elevate her for her to know that she does good. Her mother would always buy her gifts to encourage her,” said Williams-Stevens.

“Right now she was [among] the top students at Troy Primary. If school was keeping it would have to lock today, because of Shani,” added the aunt, while pointing out that up to last Friday Shani was recognised for her participation in summer school.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on a father and son in the community.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. Angry residents accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father, who was also attacked by the mob, was admitted to hospital.

Police identified the dead man as Delroy Coke, but did not provide any other information.

Shani’s father, Aston Coke, otherwise called Junior, told journalists that his daughter was well-loved and admired by many in her community.

“Her grandmother sent her to the shop and she did not make it back home. Someone stopped her on the street and disturbed her somehow and slashed her throat… She was loving and caring in the community growing up. Everybody knows her. She knows everyone. She can see you and call you by your full name. She had a sense of humour. She was doing well in school and she got a lot of academic awards,” said the heartbroken father.

“She decided that she wanted to make something out of herself growing up, because we were driving that into her head, but things just happened overnight,” added Coke as he alleged that the man believed to have killed his daughter was a habitual offender.

“It is an act that should never have happened in this neighbourhood,” declared Coke, who is battling his own health problems.

He recounted the last encounter with his daughter over the weekend.

“She came by Saturday afternoon and my uncle was putting on a back-to-school treat up by the community centre and she went there to get bags and food. She was very polite. She stopped by and I said to Kaidra, ‘What you doing here? Aren’t you supposed to be up by the treat?’ She said, ‘Yes, Daddy’ and she walked off and said, ‘Daddy, later when I am coming back I will show you what I get.’ I called her back and went in my wallet to give her money to buy juice,” Coke said.

“That was the first time my uncle and some of my aunts met her. I didn’t get to see her Sunday morning when she went to church and I didn’t get to see her yesterday (Tuesday), because she didn’t come all the way out here to the store,” he said as he reflected on the precious memories and proud moments he spent with his daughter.

“She was always smiling and you never saw her sad. You always saw her happy. Those are the things I remember about her at all times. When it comes to the academics you go by her grandmother’s house, trust me you will see a lot of achievements — trophies — that she got at school. Even sometimes when her mother and grandmother are not around I go by the church to collect them,” he said.

“It is a very sad story to know that this neighbourhood of Troy, Trelawny, has come to this. I don’t know if it is because it reached my doorstep [why] I feel it so pressuring, but things have been happening around here a long time and nobody gets justice,” charged Coke.

World.title: Too late to explain?
World.content:
Chairman of Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee Julian Robinson speaks during Wednesday’s sitting of the parliamentary oversight committee.

PERMANENT secretary in the Office of the Prime Minister Ambassador Rocky Meade has defended the Government’s decision to preserve Hurricane Melissa cash donations for longer-term recovery, insisting the auditor general’s finding that only 1.8 per cent of the funds had been spent did not reflect the Government’s full recovery strategy.

However, after hearing the detailed explanation from Meade during Wednesday’s sitting of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), Chairman Julian Robinson argued that the explanation should have been communicated much earlier and clearer to prevent the public alarm and loss of confidence that followed the audit report.

The discussion emerged as the committee reviewed the auditor general’s compliance audit into governance and procurement under the Hurricane Melissa relief programme, which found that the National Disaster Fund Committee had been non-functional for more than two years.

As members questioned officials about how the committee now operates, the conversation shifted to the controversy sparked by a separate auditor general’s report showing that only 1.8 per cent of the roughly $1.44 billion in Hurricane Melissa cash donations had been spent by February 23, prompting Meade to again defend the Government’s recovery strategy.

Seeking to place those findings in context, Meade told the committee that the Government deliberately prioritised distributing food, medical supplies, building materials and other items donated in kind during the immediate aftermath of the hurricane, while preserving cash donations to support the country’s transition from emergency relief to long-term recovery.

“The point about the percentage of donations that were deployed needs to be put into context. We were getting donations in kind and we got cash donations. The decision that was taken was in the immediate aftermath of the hurricane, while persons were in need of physical items, giving them money would not help them at that time necessarily. They were interested in getting physical items. The funds that we had, the idea was to reserve those funds to acquire and provide for these [modular] units that would give people the recovery,” he explained.

He argued that focusing solely on the amount of cash spent failed to capture the extensive use of donated goods, which he said formed the backbone of the initial relief effort.

“The bottom line to the point is that the totality of the donations we got included cash and kind, and the priority was to use up the resources in kind first. So by reporting that at a certain point, only a small percentage of the donated funds were used, it doesn’t capture the fuller picture that of all the donations, including the kind… we did substantially use up the donations in kind to provide for the immediate need, and it was a part of the plan that most of the funds that were donated would be used for the more medium-term sustainable recovery, including the housing solutions, [and] that’s the context,” he said.

While acknowledging that approach, Robinson said the public had not been given sufficient information to understand why the money remained largely untouched months after the hurricane.

“It’s important to note because people did fundraisers, people went out of their way, and so if you hear eight months post a hurricane that only two per cent of the money has been used, come next hurricane, people aren’t going to be inclined to run and support a fund of this nature… So the communication on that particular issue, I believe, should have been done earlier, probably immediately after the report came out so that there was some greater understanding of what the plan was,” said Robinson.

Meade accepted that the Government could have done more to communicate its strategy, although he maintained that information had been shared through several channels.

“I certainly accept the point that if you saw a gap in communication, it means we didn’t do enough. I can assure you that communication was done, but clearly if there are persons who didn’t hear it, we didn’t do enough… I accept your point in principle, and we will do even more than we did,” said Meade.

Updating the committee on the recovery programme, Meade said the cash donations are now being used to support the modular housing initiative, including the construction of foundations and installation of utilities.

He disclosed that the Government had initially targeted the procurement of 2,500 modular units, with about 1,200 already in Jamaica for families who suffered total or near-total loss of their homes during Hurricane Melissa.

World.title: Will Europe warm to Britain’s new prime minister?
World.content:
He’s the seventh British prime minister to walk through the famous black door of Number 10 Downing Street since the Brexit vote 10 years ago. Can Andy Burnham refresh relations with Europe and rescue a reset with Brussels that feels like it has been kicked into the long grass?

Host Anne McElvoy talks to two guests who know the knotty relationship between Britain and the European Union. Sylvie Boulard was France’s defense minister in 2017. She was previously an MEP who joined Emmanuel Macron’s En Marche party and advised him on the fallout from Brexit.

Sir Simon Fraser led Britain’s Foreign Office between 2010 and 2015. He knows his way around Brussels, having served as Peter Mandelson’s chef du Cabinet when he was EU trade commissioner and held a senior position at the British Embassy in Paris. Now he leads the business consultancy Flint Global, where he worked with James Purnell — who’s just become Andy Burnham’s chief of staff.

World.title: Merz ally challenges Germany’s far-right firewall ahead of crucial state elections
World.content:
With those comments, Kretschmer stirred up tensions that Merz has stubbornly sought to avoid.

Merz rules out cooperation with the far right — invoking the country’s Nazi past — but the political realities of eastern Germany are piling on the pressure for a rethink. Polls show that the AfD has a chance of winning an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 and is poised to perform well in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin later that month.

At the national level, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the AfD as the single most popular party with 28 percent support, with the Christian Democrats on 22 percent.

For now, however, Merz is sticking to his line that Germany has a special historic responsibility that means it cannot follow the course of other EU countries where the far right has worked with the centrist mainstream.

“If a far-right party were to enter the government in Germany, it would have a completely different significance than if that were to happen in another country,” he told reporters at a press conference. “This is also tied to our history, and that’s why, for me, it’s neither a benchmark nor an example, nor something to learn from. It is, quite simply, something different. I will do everything in my power in Germany to prevent it.”

Instead, Merz said the government’s goal had to be to seek to create a climate where the far right could be defeated.

World.title: EU’s Google fine risks triggering Trump as he gears up for more tariffs
World.content:
European officials insist that the two-part fine on Google that includes €460 million for favoring its own search services and €430 million for the unfair way the Play Store is installed on smartphones, has nothing to do with trade policy. Brussels says the penalties reflect normal enforcement of EU law, like a similar fine against China’s Alibaba earlier this week. They also note that the total penalty is relatively modest, amounting to around 0.22 percent of the global annual turnover of Google’s parent company, Alphabet.

“We'd rather have a very friendly relationship with all our partners but we are not going to refrain from acting because one of our partners doesn't like our law,” said Teresa Ribera, the European Commission's executive vice president for competition policy.

But that European attempt to keep the Google case separate from trade policy is unlikely to count for much in Washington as Trump gears up for his new tariff round.

U.S. trade czar Jamieson Greer said the “EU’s recent actions ... pose a real risk to the continuation of transatlantic stability with respect to trade” while Andrew Puzder, the U.S. ambassador to the EU, called the Google fine “the latest example of Brussels using regulation as a blunt instrument against American innovation.”

U.S. lawmakers this week also called on Trump to push back against the EU’s “discriminatory” digital policies and keep up the pressure on Brussels in order to defend American interests. The Republican legislators thanked the president for his “recent threat to impose tariffs” on countries imposing a digital service tax. The appeal underscored how the EU’s regulation of U.S. tech firms has become intertwined with domestic politics, particularly ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.

The expiration of the temporary 10 percent tariffs on Friday opens the way for the administration to rebuild its tariffs against Europe using other legal mechanisms.

World.title: L’UE inflige à Google une amende de 890 millions d’euros pour son moteur de recherche et son app store
World.content:
Ces sanctions sont prononcées plus de deux ans après l’ouverture des procédures par la Commission en mars 2024, parallèlement à des enquêtes visant Apple et Meta, qui se sont soldées par des amendes en avril 2025.

La Commission avait pris une décision en interne dès le mois de mars, ce qui avait suscité des critiques de la part d’organisations professionnelles et de la société civile, qui reprochaient à Bruxelles de freiner l’application de la réglementation pour éviter de s'attirer les foudres de Washington.

L’amende la plus élevée, d’un montant de 460 millions d’euros, concerne la pratique dite de “self-preferencing” ou autopréférence : la Commission a en effet constaté que le moteur de recherche affichait de façon plus visible les propres services de Google en matière d’e-commerce, d’hôtellerie, de transports et de sport que ceux de ses concurrents.

La seconde, d’un montant de 430 millions d’euros, concerne le Play Store installé sur les smartphones fonctionnant sous le système d’exploitation Android. La Commission a constaté que Google empêchait les développeurs d’applications d’informer les utilisateurs de l’existence d’offres moins chères disponibles en dehors de l’app store, et que, par ailleurs, elle facturait des frais liés aux redirections des utilisateurs vers les applications dépassant les limites autorisées par la loi.

Ces amendes, bien que substantielles, sont nettement inférieures à celles infligées par Bruxelles à Google pour pratiques anticoncurrentielles : la Cour de justice de l’UE a récemment confirmé une amende de plus de 4 milliards d’euros, décidée en 2018 par la Commission européenne, après avoir conclu que Google avait abusé de sa position dominante via Android.

Cela vient du fait que le DMA cherche d’abord à lutter contre les positions dominantes sur le marché en collaborant avec les entreprises pour qu’elles modifient leur mode de fonctionnement.

World.title: Linnemann wird offenbar neuer Gesundheitsminister
World.content:
Linnemann war bereits zu Beginn der Legislatur im Gespräch für ein Ministeramt. Der 48-Jährige sollte ursprünglich Wirtschaftsminister werden, lehnte die Position aber ab. Er wäre lieber Arbeitsminister geworden, wie er der „Welt“ sagte (hier). Das Ressort ging aber an die SPD. Am Ende blieb Linnemann Generalsekretär seiner Partei. Er ist seit 2009 Mitglied des Deutschen Bundestags für den Wahlkreis Paderborn.

Warken hinterlässt ihrem Nachfolger eine abgeschlossene Finanzreform der Gesetzlichen Krankenversicherung und eine angestoßene Pflegereform, die nach der Sommerpause ins Kabinett kommen soll. Auch hier muss ein Milliardendefizit ausgeglichen werden. Warken hat zudem eine Strukturreform für das deutsche Gesundheitswesen angestoßen. Hierzu soll die Finanzkommission Gesundheit erste Vorschläge gegen Jahresende machen.

Die Nominierung Warkens zur Gesundheitsministerin im vergangenen Jahr galt als Überraschung. Die Juristin kam als Quereinsteigerin in das Ressort. Durch die noch kurz vor der Sommerpause verabschiedeten GKV-Reform hatte sie sich dann zwar Respekt innerhalb der Union verschafft. Warken gilt als ideal für den Posten der Kanzleramtschefin, bei dem sie im Hintergrund agieren wird.

Das zeigen die Worte von Kanzler Friedrich Merz nach dem Kabinettsbeschluss des GKV-Beitragssatzstabilisierungsgesetzes (hier). „Sie hat mit sehr viel Mut, mit Augenmaß, mit Ehrlichkeit, mit Empathie eine Reform vorgelegt, die beispielhaft ist für all die großen Reformen, die wir in der Koalition noch leisten wollen“, so Merz über Warken. Ihrer Entschlossenheit und dem Tempo gebühre „allergrößte Anerkennung“.

World.title: Beethoven versus birds: ECB shortlists designs for new euro banknotes
World.content:
The first set of potential banknotes features American-Greek opera singer Maria Callas, German composer Beethoven, French-Polish scientist Marie Curie-Skłodowska, Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra, Italian polymath Leonardo da Vinci, and Austrian pacifist Bertha von Suttner. The reverse of the notes depicts generic European cultural spaces including libraries, universities and public squares.

The ECB said the figures represent “iconic European personalities who have contributed to building Europe’s cultural heritage” whose accomplishments “resonated around the world.”

Wildlife fans can instead go for the option featuring rivers and birds, which the ECB says “highlights the resilience and diversity of Europe’s natural ecosystems” to showcase “the importance of nature and environmental protection.”

Those note designs feature such combinations as a mountain spring with a wallcreeper, a waterfall with a kingfisher, a confined river valley with bee-eaters, a meandering river with a white stork, a river mouth and an avocet, and a seascape with a Northern gannet. The reverse depicts EU institutional buildings such as the European Parliament and European Commission.

In a twist of fate, the eurozone and Britain could both end up with kingfishers on their legal tender, as the Bank of England has also put forward a series of animals for a public vote.

The ECB shortlisted ten design proposals which the public can give feedback on until September 21.

World.title: Environment ministry chaos tears France’s centrists apart
World.content:
Roughly one-third of lawmakers from the president’s own party on Monday either voted against or abstained from voting on the law, after amendments were added at the last minute allowing France’s food and drug safety watchdog to approve the use of a controversial pesticide, acetamiprid, for nut producers and doubling the amount of water farmers can store over the next decade despite the threat of more climate change-induced droughts.

“Politically, we’ve managed to turn a law with more than 70 articles into a fruitless, dogmatic debate,” said Jérémy Decerle, a member of the European Parliament representing Macron’s Renaissance party, and the former head of the Young Farmers union.

But the drama within parliament also showed just how nasty the infighting has gotten in the overcrowded field of presidential candidates. Two of Macron’s former prime ministers, Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, are running for the presidency and threaten to split the centrist vote, thereby costing their camp a place in the runoff of the two-round race.

During parliamentary debate on the bill, Attal, who fell out with Macron after the ill-fated decision to call a snap election in 2024, asked why it was used to hastily reopen the explosive debate over pesticides.

After Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard declined to answer publicly, Attal texted her to complain, according to someone who saw the message and was granted anonymity to share sensitive private correspondence without fear of reprisal. Genevard appeared to mistake Attal for current Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, a nominal political ally of the duo.

Genevard replied: “But Sébastien, you’re the one who told me not to answer him,” before quickly deleting the message and sending a corrected response, said the individual who saw the texts.

World.title: Short breaks set the tone for Greek travellers, new data reveals
World.content:
Short breaks are now setting the tone for Greek travellers' choices, while citizens over 65 make up the age group with the sharpest increase in their trips. This emerges from the latest data released by the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT) for 2025.

 

The strongest growth was recorded in trips lasting one to three nights. Their number rose by 26.7% compared with 2024, reaching 2.1 million. Overnight stays for these trips increased by 27.8%, while spending was up 21.6%.

This trend does not mean that short breaks have replaced more traditional holidays. Trips of four to seven nights remained the largest category, accounting for 41.5% of the total. However, their increase was limited to 9.8%, significantly below the growth in trips of up to three nights.

The change was even more modest for trips lasting 15 or more nights, which increased by just 1.6%. Despite this almost stagnant picture, they still account for more than half of all overnight stays, indicating that long holidays continue to carry significant weight.

Over-65s are travelling more

The second key trend concerns travellers over the age of 65. The number of people in this group who made at least one personal trip rose by 24%, while the total number of trips by the same age group increased by 28.5%. Their spending was up 21%, and overnight stays by 12.1%.

Travellers over 65 accounted for 16.6% of personal trips but concentrated 28.7% of all overnight stays. The figures suggest that older travellers tend to stay longer at their destinations than other age groups.

Trips and spending on the rise

In total, 4.56 million residents aged 15 and over made at least one personal trip in 2025.

The number of personal trips increased by 13.7% to 7.93 million, while overnight stays rose by 7.4% to 73.3 million.

Total spending came to 3.68 billion euros, up 13.3% on the previous year.

Food and drink was the biggest spending category, absorbing 32.1% of the total, followed by transport, other expenses and accommodation.

Domestic destinations remain the primary choice

The vast majority of personal trips, 85%, took place within Greece.

However, trips abroad grew at a faster pace, by 18.8%, compared with 12.8% for domestic travel.

Italy was the most popular destination outside Greece, followed by Albania, Germany, the United Kingdom and France.

Despite the rise in short breaks, the seasonality of Greek tourism remains pronounced.

August alone accounted for 31.3% of personal trips and 34.9% of overnight stays, and together with July represented almost half of all trips made in 2025.

World.title: Spain coach slams Argentina's World Cup final behaviour as 'unacceptable’
World.content:
The head coach of the Spanish national team, Luis de la Fuente, has strongly criticised the behaviour of several Argentina players following Spain's victory in the World Cup final.

 

In an interview with Spanish public broadcaster TVE, de la Fuente described Argentina's actions after the final whistle as "intolerable and unacceptable" and praised his own players for keeping their composure.

"At the time I didn't realise, because I was celebrating with other people, hugging team-mates. In any case, I find it intolerable and unacceptable from players of that calibre, whom I had been praising in the days before and who have a magnificent coach," de la Fuente said.

The Spain boss said he was disappointed by the conduct of several Argentine players, referring to the closing stages of the game, when a number of on-pitch incidents created a highly charged atmosphere and led to the dismissal of Argentina's Enzo Fernández.

"It cannot be allowed," he added.

De la Fuente also commended his players for the way they handled the situation.

"I want to highlight our behaviour in the face of that kind of aggression and provocation. Our players always kept their composure and behaved like true professionals," he told the outlet.

His comments come after FIFA announced the opening of a disciplinary investigation into the incidents at MetLife Stadium.

Looking back at the tournament

During the interview, de la Fuente looked back on Spain's path to the trophy, dishing out particular praise for certain players and stressing that the biggest challenges extended beyond the opposition.

"It has been 24,000 kilometres, humidity, little rest... All of that process, beyond the opponents, is what you have to overcome," he said.

Speaking about Rodri, the tournament's Golden Ball winner, he added: "To 'doubt' the Manchester City midfielder is 'an insult to footballing intelligence.'"

On Lamine Yamal, de la Fuente said the tournament had helped the young star mature, especially in terms of his willingness to sacrifice for the team.

Spain's Lamine Yamal (19) and Argentina's Lionel Messi (10) embrace after during the World Cup final soccer match between Spain and Argentina in East Rutherford, N.J. Seth Wenig/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved.

Looking ahead, de la Fuente added that leading Spain at the 2030 World Cup would be "the greatest source of pride for any coach", although he insisted that his immediate priority was Spain's upcoming fixtures in September and October.

He ended by thanking supporters for their backing during the tournament: "I want to thank the whole country for being so invested in us. Even from afar we have felt your support. It is a huge source of pride to be Spanish. Thank you, Spain."

World.title: ‘Less than a minute of your time’: Driving the speed limit could save you money and cut emissions
World.content:
Sticking to the speed limit can “dramatically curb” fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions while saving drivers billions of euros annually.

 

Researchers at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities have analysed more than 120 million real-world vehicle trips in the US to understand the true impacts of speeding.

The study, published in the science journal Communications Sustainability, found that if drivers across the US complied with posted speed limits, it could save an average of $22 million (approximately €19.26 million), more than 25 million litres of fuel and 57,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide every single day.

These savings apply for light-duty engine-powered vehicles (LDVs) such as cars and small vans which account for 14.6 per cent of total energy consumption in the US.

According to a 2024 report by Odyssee-Mure, a project supported by the EU to monitor energy efficiency trends, LDVs consume around half of the energy used in European road transport.

‘Real-world fuel savings potential’

Along with the cash and climate savings, which could increase further following the soaring price of gas amid the war on Iran, researchers found that sticking to the speed limit added less than a minute to the average daily commute.

“While internal combustion engine-powered vehicles have become significantly more efficient in the past decades, they have also become much more powerful,” says William Northrop, University of Minnesota mechanical engineering professor and corresponding author on the paper.

“Driving fast is easier than ever. Our study examines an obvious yet difficult-to-implement intervention for major fuel savings that can be achieved without replacing our cars: driving slower.”

Researchers say that the next step of their research is to expand their framework to cover more diverse roadways and understand the impacts of “aggressive accelerations” on fuel use and emissions.

“Exploring both speed and acceleration reductions will give us an even more complete picture of real-world fuel savings potential,” Northrop says.

EV sales surge across EU

The war on Iran’s disruption of global energy supplies has triggered an electric vehicle (EV) boom across Europe, as more drivers wean themselves off fossil-fueled cars.

New battery-electric vehicle (BEV) registrations across the EU rose 48.9 per cent in March compared to the same period last year, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).

Battery electric cars reached more than 20 per cent share of the total EU market in March and a 19.4 per cent share for the first quarter. This compares with 15.2 per cent in the first quarter of 2025.

ACEA's report explained that the shift was significantly bolstered by new and revised tax benefits and other incentive schemes introduced across major European countries.

While electric cars are gaining ground rapidly, hybrid-electric vehicles (HEVs) still hold the largest individual share of the market at 38.6 per cent, and registrations surpassed one million units in the first quarter.

At the same time, internal combustion engine vehicles continue to dwindle in popularity. Petrol car registrations decreased further across the EU in the first quarter, dropping significantly from last year’s 28.7 per cent, and diesel followed a similar path, with its share shrinking to just 7.7 per cent.

Italy led the race, with a 65.7 per cent increase in BEV registrations during the first quarter, followed by France, then Germany.

How much will I save with an EV?

According to the UK’s Energy Saving Trust, a full charge in an EV will give a typical range of around 220 miles (354 km) and cost approximately £17 (€19.91) if charging at home.

Driving a petrol or diesel car for the same length would cost more than double, coming in at £45 (€52.69).

As EVs produce zero tailpipe emissions, drivers will also be significantly cutting their carbon footprint.

Energy giant EDF calculates that traditional petrol cars emit around 165 grams of CO2 per kilometre, and diesel cars emit about 170 grams of CO2 per kilometre. EVs average just 50 grams of CO2 per kilometre, including consideration of the electricity generated.

Of course, producing EVs does use a lot of energy. Typically, the emissions created during EV productions tends to be higher than petrol cars due to the manufacturing of lithium-ion batteries which release heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions.

While advances in technology are making this process more efficient, drivers can opt for a second-hand EV which are often priced on par with petrol alternatives.

World.title: ‘Like a bird flying’: You can now soar on a giant swing over the Swiss Alps
World.content:
Attention adrenaline seekers, there’s a new reason to visit the Swiss Alps this summer.

 

Perched at an altitude of 2,110 metres on the Grand Chamossaire peak at the Villars ski resort is a giant swing.

The towering V-shaped structure catapults visitors out over a gaping void with a breathtaking Alpine panorama stretching before them.

The 12-metre-high swing opened earlier this month and is the latest effort by Alpine ski resorts to attract off-season visitors as snow becomes less reliable due to climate change.

‘You feel like a bird flying’

The swing, which is accessible to anyone with a ski lift ticket, can take three people at a time.

Each person straddles a saddle affixed to a metal structure made to look like an Alpine Ibex, their hands clenching handlebars as they are strapped down tightly.

Then an elaborate system of cables and pulleys is used to draw them as far back as a 90-degree angle, leaving them suspended face down, perpendicular with the metal platform far below.

The swing hopes to attract tourism beyond the ski season. Télé-Villars-Gryon-Diablerets

When the security cable is suddenly released, the swing plunges forward out over the sharp, jagged drop to exalted screams, before a spectacular view of the valley below against a dramatic backdrop of rocky and snow-dusted Alps rushes in.

"The feeling of hanging up there, and then being released, it's an amazing sensation," Yannick Boudouin, 38, told AFP.

"I had a bit of a pit in my stomach" before getting strapped in, acknowledged Alexandra Henchoz, 37, who tested the new swing with her husband and 10-year-old daughter.

"But once it is happening, it is just incredible. You feel like a bird flying."

Alpine resorts prepare for less snow

The Grand Chamossaire swing is part of efforts to introduce year-round appeal and make use of ski lift infrastructure when snow is scarce.

"We are really trying to diversify our offering," Martin Deburaux, head of the Villars-Gryons-Diableret ski area, told AFP.

The new structure "provides us with a source of attraction that can function independently of snow conditions", he said.

Deburaux stressed that the resort had seen record numbers coming during the past two ski seasons, as visitors who usually skied lower-lying slopes sought higher ground and more snow.

"But we know we are facing climate change," he said. "We are looking for substitutes to conserve jobs, the dynamism and the tourist economy built up around our ski lift facilities."

Currently, the resort draws more than 700,000 people during the winter season, but just 100,000 in summer.

It aims to triple its summer season numbers in the next couple of years, Deburaux said, adding that doing so would require offering a multitude of activities.

Nearby hikers filled the grassy paths, while mountain bikers sporting helmets and protective gear sped down a separate, steep dirt trail.

They wind past an ephemeral land art fresco painted by French artist Saype across an entire hillside showing a child drawing.

Deburaux said the new swing had intentionally been erected in a spot that had already been brimming with activity, while leaving other parts of the resort untouched to appeal to those seeking a pristine nature experience.

World.title: Safeguards for new EU members need objective criteria, Montenegro's ambassador says
World.content:
Montenegro backs new safeguards to stop future EU members backsliding on the rule of law and democratic standards, but only if they rest on objective criteria for assessing systemic breaches, the country's ambassador to the EU has told Euronews.

 

Montenegro is the most advanced candidate country in the accession process, aiming to become the 28th EU member state in 2028. But its bid might be complicated by a string of proposals to overhaul how enlargement works.

Chief among them: five of the six EU founding members have called for stronger safeguards against democratic rollback after accession — a lesson drawn from Viktor Orbán's Hungary.

Petar Marković, Montenegro's head of mission to the EU, told Euronews his country supports tougher safeguards, noting that Podgorica already outperforms some member states on rule of law reforms, according to the European Commission's periodic review.

"Montenegro has an interest in introducing guarantees meant to maintain EU standards. But the potential breaches would have to be assessed on a case-by-case basis against objective criteria to prove systematic backsliding," he said.

Marković argued the criteria must be agreed before membership begins, and should not be used to pre-emptively curtail a new member's voting rights through a transitional period — a move he called politically and legally dubious, warning it could effectively create a second-class membership.

At the same time, the ambassador acknowledged that one of Montenegro's main incentives for accepting new safeguards is that they could smooth the ratification process, providing additional reassurance, particularly as the political spectrum in some founding members shifts rightward and grows more sceptical of enlargement.

Reform of the methodology

Another proposal on the table is "gradual integration," pushed by France and Germany, which would let candidate countries reap early benefits of EU membership as they advance through the accession process.

"For far too long, there has not been a real discussion on the enlargement methodology," Marković said, welcoming the return of enlargement as a top political priority in European capitals.

But he argued that after 14 years of intensive work in the accession process, it would be unfair to change the rules this late — especially since Montenegro was the first country to accept, and the most advanced country approaching the finishing line under the current methodology.

"This is not about what we deserve. This is a rational choice. Discussions on a new methodology should focus on the candidate countries for which the current methodology has not worked. For Montenegro, it clearly has," Marković added.

"Strategically, the stakes could not be higher. The EU has a real chance to reverse the Brexit effect and return to expanding again," Marković concluded.

World.title: 'Respect the City': How Dubrovnik is managing overtourism without losing its charm
World.content:
Dubrovnik has spent almost a decade tackling one of modern tourism’s biggest challenges: how to remain a popular destination without being overwhelmed by its own success, especially when popularity shows no signs of slowing down.

 

Over that time, city officials have shifted focus from responding to crisis-mode overtourism to sustainable management.

From the start of the year until mid-July, the city has already welcomed almost 650,000 arrivals and two million overnight stays. Travellers from the UK, US, France, Germany, Poland, Ireland, Spain, Canada and Australia are among the largest markets so far, with the city also proving popular as a domestic tourism destination.

So, the trouble isn’t attracting visitors. Instead, the city’s leaders are focused on ensuring tourism can grow sustainably while protecting its heritage and preserving locals’ quality of life.

“Here, it’s not just about the numbers,” Mato Franković, Mayor of Dubrovnik, told Euronews Travel. “Also important is how the flow of numbers is spread throughout a day and across the week.”

According to the city’s mayor, tourism once grew with little coordination.

“For years, tourism in Dubrovnik wasn’t managed, it simply just ‘happened’ on its own,” he said.

Mayor Franković: 'Respect for Dubrovnik is something we ask of everyone' City of Dubrovnik

“Previously, there would be days where five or six cruise ships would arrive at once, bringing with them so many day-trippers from nearby destinations. That’s when we realised we needed to manage tourism differently, so we divided it into different sectors.”

The Dubrovnik native, who has been in the role since 2017, has centred much of his tourism strategy on the “Respect the City” (RtC) initiative, which initially launched that same year in response to the immense strain on the UNESCO-listed Old Town.

“Respect for Dubrovnik is something we ask of everyone: citizens, people working in the city, those who come to enjoy Dubrovnik – this is our message to everyone,” he said.

Balancing popularity with preservation

Throughout the 2010s, the Old Town, which stands as a living stage of Dubrovnik’s history along the Dalmatian coast, bore the immense brunt of the city’s increasing popularity.

Through an influx of cruise arrivals, wallet-friendly flight tickets, and the destination’s global profile boosted by the success of HBO’s Game of Thrones series, this created summers of severe congestion and left the “Pearl of the Adriatic” struggling to cope with peak visitor numbers. “So much so, you could hardly walk or go around to enjoy the city,” Franković told Euronews Travel.

Rather than treating tourism in a catch-all fashion, the Dubrovnik mayor explained that it is instead managed across different sectors: namely cruise tourism, day visitors and overnight stays.

As part of the RtC initiative, no more than two cruise ships can dock at the city’s port at a time with a maximum of 4,000 passengers. Cruise calls must also last for at least eight hours.

By encouraging longer port stays, Franković explained that passengers are more likely to spread their travels across the city and surrounding region, rather than converging on the historical centre all at once.

“We’ve seen that visitors are now choosing to explore more excursions elsewhere,” he said. “Of course, they still visit the Old Town at some point, but the traffic is now not all at the same time, compared to previously when six cruise ships would arrive and dock for just four hours.”

Figures from the Dubrovnik Port Authority show cruise tourism remains resilient, with 2026 expecting to receive more than 661,000 cruise passengers across 461 ship calls by the end of the year.

Beyond cruise tourism, Dubrovnik’s RtC initiative also turns its attention to how day visitors and overnight guests move through the city.

Coach operators bringing visitors from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and nearby Croatian islands must now reserve arrival slots before entering the city under the bus webshop scheme. The booking system allows officials to stagger arrivals throughout the day and adjust capacity depending on when events are being held and as arrival demand fluctuates.

While for visitors staying longer, the city’s Dubrovnik Pass is both a gateway to sightseeing as well as a visitor management tool. Alongside entry to the city’s museums and granting access to public transport, the pass also allows Dubrovnik to recommend the best times to visit popular attractions.

“Because it's digitalised, we are able to message visitors with the best times to visit attractions, such as the Old City,” Franković said.

“This is something we are especially working to fine-tune: avoiding situations where hundreds and hundreds of people are walking the city at the same time. We want people to choose the best times so they can enjoy the city with their families.”

Franković also said the city is increasingly relying on data to shape coming policies. People counters have been installed throughout the Old Town to monitor footfall. Tourism data is then shared with and analysed by the University of Dubrovnik to identify trends and recommend further improvements to the city’s visitor management.

What’s next for sustainable tourism?

Despite Dubrovnik’s global appeal, Franković said that there are still corners of the city and its surroundings that remain overlooked by visitors. He said: “There are many areas that are still undiscovered, take Mount Srđ, for example.”

Rising above Dubrovnik, the hills offer sweeping views across the Old Town, Adriatic Sea and surrounding islands, with the AllTrails outdoor activities guide platform recommending hikers to venture out closer to the end of the day to catch the sunset.

Views of the Old Town from Mount Srđ Copyright Mike Starling/Euronews Travel

Rather than creating new tourist hotspots, the mayor said the city’s priority is encouraging visitors to explore what already exists while improving the overall quality of offerings.

This is also the framework shaping future development plans, as the city earmarks underdeveloped tourism zones to be replaced with affordable housing for locals and residents to sustainably inhabit. A challenge Franković said extends beyond Croatia.

While other cities across Europe also grapple with overtourism, he argued that a broader challenge lies in protecting communities from the influx of too many holiday homes.

“Short-term rentals are killing cities because step by step, they push residents out and turn living neighbourhoods into tourist apartment zones,” he said. “It's going to be just like a generic Disney-land experience, and who wants to visit a ghost town?

“That’s not what people want – they want to see and meet the citizens. But if we let this continue, our citizens will be forced out of the major cities and into the far away suburbs.

“I hope in the future this won’t continue to be an issue where locals struggle to find good places to live. In fact, there are many villages around us that are now abandoned and they have potential to become great living zones.”

In the Old Town, for example, the permanent population has dropped to just 1,500 people in stark comparison to 1991's figures of 5,000.

Croatia’s approach has drawn interest elsewhere across the continent and Franković said that European cities are increasingly learning from one another’s experiences, saying that his office collaborates a lot with other regional counterparts.

For the future of the city, his ambition is not for Dubrovnik to necessarily become bigger, but to remain recognisably itself. He said while he looks forward to the country developing a comprehensive, reliable nationwide rail system, he also wants most of its charm to remain intact.

“My hope is that someone will return in 30 years’ time and find the same Dubrovnik. The same beauty, the preserved historical site and clear sea.”

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.content:
Skip next section Trump says Iran will pay for damage to shipping

07/24/2026 July 24, 2026 Trump says Iran will pay for damage to shipping

Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been at risk [FILE: July 16, 2026] Image: REUTERS

US President Donald Trump said Iran would be held responsible for the financial cost of any damage to ships or cargo amid the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz.

He said he would use seized Iranian assets to pay for any damage to shipping.

"From this point forth, any and all damages done to Ships, Cargo, or anything related thereto, will be paid for by Iranian Money that the United States has in its possession, and controls," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

"These damages may be very substantial but, nevertheless, this is the fair and equitable thing to do," Trump added.

Trump's statement comes after Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked two Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea.

In response, Iran warned that Trump's threat to use seized Iranian assets would set a dangerous precedent.

"Seizing another nation's assets to pay for unrelated future claims is an incendiary precedent," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X.

World.title: Wildfires in Europe prompt tens of thousands to evacuate
World.content:
Spain has declared a national emergency in the Madrid region. In neighboring France, meanwhile, President Emmanuel Macron has invoked the EU's civil protection mechanism to ask for help.

Tens of thousands of people were urged to evacuate on Thursday as forest fires continued to tear through Spain, France and Italy.

The latest fires come as Europe prepares for another heat wave, with temperatures of up to 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) forecast in some areas.

So far in 2026, wildfires have burnt more land in Europe than the annual average over the past two decades.

Climate change is making extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and the forest fires that ensue, more frequent and more severe.

Heat waves fuel wildfires across southern Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Spain declares national emergency in Madrid region

To better tackle several out-of-control wildfires, Spain declared a national emergency in the Madrid region and in the province of Avila, near the capital, late on Thursday.

The measure aims to speed up the deployment of resources to fight the blazes, which have forced some 10,000 people in the region to evacuate.

The decision also transfers the crisis response to the military emergency unit of the Spanish Armed Forces, which is specialized in disaster relief.

Earlier on Thursday, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez posted on X that "the government has deployed every available resource to stop the terrible fires currently affecting numerous areas: Avila, Leon, Toledo, Madrid and other parts of Spain."

Sanchez also visited a fire-ravaged area in Guadalajara, northeast of Madrid, where more than 30 villages were evacuated.

"Year after year we clearly see how climate change kills and destroys wealth in our communities," he said. "This isn't politics. It is science, it's about facts."

France seeks EU civil protection mechanism

Across the border in France, President Emmanuel Macron said that France has invoked the EU's civil protection mechanism to ask for help to tackle forest fires.

"We will soon have support from two Croatian Canadair aircraft, two Portuguese Air Tractors and two heavy-lift Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia," Macron posted on X early on Friday morning.

Authorities evacuated 7,000 people "as a precaution" on Thursday north of Cap Ferret, near the tourist hub of Arcachon Bay, bringing the total number of evacuees in the area to 12,000.

Fires had ravaged around 2,000 hectares (nearly 5,000 acres), authorities said on Wednesday.

French authorities said firefighters were battling 'house by house' to protect the tourist hub of Lege-Cap-Ferret Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

Italian officials blame 'malicious' arsonists

Around 6,000 firefighters, forest guards and civil protection officials have been deployed across Sicily after fires have raged for days.

Regional president Renato Schifani said about 50 fires were still burning despite the deployment of water-bombing aircraft.

And on the mainland of Italy, in Calabria, more than 160 fires have been recorded.

Local officials in Calabria have accused "malicious individuals" of arson, pointing to rags doused in flammable liquid that were tied to the tails of stray cats to spread fires.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko and Karl Sexton
