World.title: RSPCA investigates deliberate attacks on kangaroos in Albany
World.content:
The RSPCA is investigating reports of kangaroos being deliberately run over in Albany, Western Australia.

Warning: This article contains details and an image readers may find distressing.

Warrenup resident Mary Saunders told the ABC kangaroos had been targeted in the area for several years.

"As an animal lover it's just become overwhelming, to the point now I drive into the estate and I'm just filled with this overwhelming feeling of sadness," she said.

Mary and Robert Saunders have spent years advocating for the safety and protection of Australia's native wildlife. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

Ms Saunders called the police when she came home late last Saturday night and saw a female kangaroo with its legs severed and bones sticking out.

"I looked inside the pouch and sure enough there was a beautiful little joey still attached to the teat, suckling," she said.

" Severing that teat and taking the joey out was probably the most heartbreaking thing I've ever had to do. "

Mary Saunders rescued this joey after finding its mother injured. (Supplied: Mary Saunders)

Ms Saunders said she found a kangaroo and its joey dead on her property during Easter and that in June she and her husband, Robert, saw three dead joeys lined up on the side of the road.

"No sign of road trauma, but the three lined up obviously placed there by someone," Ms Saunders said.

'Far too many' deaths to be accidental

RSPCA inspector Shaye Barrow said the incidents were concerning and that "quite a number" of kangaroos had been found dead and injured, leaving joeys orphaned.

"There was at least one where we've had a joey that was deliberately targeted, but the joeys that have been left orphaned have been taken in by wildlife carers, thank goodness," she said.

Mary Saunders has reported numerous deliberate acts of violence towards kangaroos in Warrenup. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

Wildlife carer Maggie van Santen said Ms Saunders did the right thing on Saturday night.

"She's a hero in my eyes, rescuing that little baby," Ms van Santen said.

"She brought her to me on Sunday morning and yeah, she saved the little one's life."

Maggie van Santen rehabilitates injured kangaroos. (Supplied: Maggie van Santen)

She said it seemed as if there was a "constant stream" of kangaroos being killed.

"And I understand that, yes, kangaroos do jump in front of cars, and I do understand accidents happen, but it's up to the driver then to take responsibility and check," Ms van Santen said.

"But I honestly believe that there are far too many that have been killed in that area in the last couple of months for it to be accidental."

A joey was taken from the pouch of this kangaroo after it was hit by a car. (Supplied: Mary Saunders)

Ms Barrow urged the public to make reports to the RSPCA.

"We've had at least half a dozen reports made since June, including some cases dating as far back as January in relation to people deliberately running down roos in the Warrenup area," she said.

"So we've had a number of witnesses come forward, but unfortunately the CCT footage and witness accounts we have today haven't yielded any concrete information in terms of number plates of vehicles and things like that."

Anyone with information can contact the RSPCA on 08 9209 9300.

World.title: Trump tariffs 'hurting investment and jobs', businesses warn
World.content:
Businesses say a new tariff on Australian exports to the United States will make it harder to compete and could reduce investment.

The Trump administration has confirmed a 12.5 per cent tariff has been imposed on Australian exports to the US, which it says is due to Australia's failure to enforce laws banning goods made by forced labour.

A temporary 10 per cent "global tariff" on the US's trading partners has now expired. That replaced the "liberation day" tariff regime, announced last year, which was scuppered earlier this year by the US Supreme Court.

The firm that shut down Trump's tariffs When a law centre decided to fight Donald Trump's "liberation day" tariffs, it was acutely aware of possible "retaliation" from a president who takes matters "personally".

Legal analysts suspect this approach, applying a fee imposed on foreign countries that engage in unreasonable trade practices, will be more enduring.

The US is Australia's largest two-way investment partner, with total investment exceeding $2 trillion.

"It's just another punch to roll with, to be honest," said swimwear retailer Tom Wilson.

The founder of Nashie told the ABC the rollercoaster of fees for exporting goods to the US made business more difficult.

"Changing prices is a really big deal," he said.

Nashie clothing co-founder Tom Wilson at the company's Brisbane headquarters. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

" You've got goods that are all labelled and have set prices on them, and you might be wholesaling with set prices too. So changing prices is not as flexible and easy as people might think. "

Tariff could reduce Australian goods going to the US

Australian businesses are worried.

Jeffrey Grosset is the owner and founder of Grosset Wines in the Clare Valley, South Australia.

Jeff Grosset has been making wine for 37 years in South Australia's Clare Valley, a region famed for its Riesling. (ABC News: Simon Royal)

He told the ABC's Isabella Kelly that the local wine industry will lose its presence in the massive US market.

"If America decides to become more isolationist, which it appears to be doing through this … then regrettably, it might hurt American consumers because they don't get to see us, but it will hurt us more. That's the reality," he said.

" To lose that presence, that visibility, hurts Australia and our equity disproportionately. "

Disappointment reigns

Trade Minister Don Farrell says Australia is disappointed in the US's decision to raise tariffs on Australia's exports.

Speaking at a press conference in Adelaide, Mr Farrell says the tariffs are "completely unjustified".

He has defended Australia's anti-modern slavery regime, which he says is taken seriously.

"We continue to maintain that these tariffs are unjustified. Australia is a country that deals with the issue of modern slavery seriously," Mr Farrell said.

"And from my point of view, the government's point of view, we will continue to argue very strongly for the removal of these tariffs."

Richard Marles says the federal government will argue against the new tariffs. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Defence Minister Richard Marles added that the federal government is arguing "very forcefully" against US tariffs on Australian goods.

The Business Council of Australia made submissions to the process that eventually determined the tariffs. Chief executive Bran Black said today he was disappointed by the decision, which was made for "no justifiable reason".

"The United States Trade Representative's finding rests on the narrow claim that Australia lacks a US-style ban on importing goods made with forced labour, despite our already strong Modern Slavery Act, and without identifying a single company, enforcement failure, or quantified trade impact," he said in a statement.

Bran Black says the tariffs will make it harder for Australian businesses to compete.

"The Business Council supports free and open trade, and we see no basis for these new tariffs.

"This decision will make it harder for Australian businesses to compete and sell their products into the US market, hurting investment and our jobs."

More to come

Australia is not the only affected country. Tariffs of 10 and 12.5 per cent will be on imports from 59 other economies, which represent all of the US's major trading partners.

As the economics team at Westpac wrote in a note to investors, it probably does not change things. But the injection of uncertainty could slow the US economy.

"This measure replaces the temporary 10% tariff set to expire at 12:00am. As a result, it should have little-to-no net impact on US inflation or growth," Westpac wrote.

"That said, it maintains pressure on US households and businesses at a particularly inopportune time and so is a threat to sentiment."

US to impose 50pc tariffs on most Canadian goods The White House says the tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, meaning there is time for negotiations.

That's something Thomas Foods International chief sales officer Jonathan Bayes sees happening.

The company sells meat and seafood globally and sees particular impact on Australian sheep meat exports.

"It's [prior tariffs] had a significant impact on the sheep meat in particular," he says.

"We've seen demand soften a little bit."

Mr Bayes expects the tariff cost to be passed onto American consumers.

Thomas Foods International sells meat and seafood globally and says the 12.5 per cent tariff will have a huge impact on sheep meat exports. (Supplied)

"In uncertain economic terms in the US, people are watching their spend," he says.

"Ultimately it's going to have a major impact on the consumers and that it could lead to further softening given the US is such a large partner of our sheep meat trade."

World.title: Villagers hold vigil for stranger as PNG boat tragedy victims wash ashore
World.content:
Families had been celebrating a birthday at a Papua New Guinea beach resort when they went missing on their return boat journey last week.

It has been described as one of the nation's worst maritime tragedies in recent years.

WARNING: This story contains images that may upset some readers.

Twenty-seven people, including families with young children, were travelling on two boats when they capsized in rough seas off East New Britain in the country's north-east on Saturday.

The boats were returning from Pangpang Beach Resort, travelling from Pigeon Island to Kokopo, when they overturned shortly after 3pm in the Bismarck Sea.

The only known survivors are the two boat operators, who drifted for six hours before reaching Baai village.

The search for the 27 others has entered the recovery phase, with nine bodies found in neighbouring New Ireland Province.

Vigil for a stranger

Three days after the tragedy unfolded, the first two bodies washed ashore on Djaul Island in New Ireland.

The victims, a mother and her 18-year-old daughter, had been carried more than 200 kilometres north-west by ocean currents from East New Britain.

The mother was discovered during the day by villagers working in their gardens.

The teenage girl was found later that night by a young boy who helped carry her to the nearby home of a village councillor.

It was after midnight, but instead of leaving her alone, islanders gathered around her and began singing hymns.

Djaul Island villagers laid flowers on the body of the 18-year-old victim. (Supplied: Lavina Ono)

Michael Rangrang, a school teacher on the island, said they kept vigil beside her body through the night until authorities could be contacted to retrieve her the next morning.

"It's sort of our culture … when people die, we have to do something," he said.

A large crowd of villagers gathered to see her off when the helicopter arrived.

Mr Rangrang said they placed flowers on her body as a final act of respect, despite not knowing who she was.

"Finding her like that … it was really frightening and sad. We couldn't bear with that," Mr Rangrang said.

"What we are trying to do is show people there's a village here with this type of lifestyle, this type of culture."

Recovery effort against the current

More bodies have been recovered along the coast of New Ireland, another major PNG island.

A woman found near Djaul Island on Wednesday was identified as an East New Britain Provincial Health Authority staff member.

New Ireland health workers formed a guard of honour as she was transferred home from the morgue in Kavieng, the province's capital.

Five more bodies recovered in PNG's Tigak group of islands were taken to the morgue on Thursday night. (Supplied: Robin Anton)

On Thursday, five more bodies were recovered from Enang and Upuas in the Tigak group of islands and taken to the Kavieng morgue. Another body was found on Friday morning, bringing the total recovered to nine.

More than 20 boats operated by police, disaster teams and local communities are searching coastlines and surrounding waters.

But New Ireland Governor Byron Chan said dangerous conditions were making the recovery difficult.

New Ireland search and rescue teams near Djaul Island say rough seas are complicating recovery efforts. (Supplied: Rebecca Marigu/ Siro Media)

Strong winds and rough seas are keeping smaller vessels from reaching open water until the afternoon.

By then, he said, powerful currents may have already carried victims beyond the islands.

"Bodies are bypassing everyone, every island," he said.

"Especially the young ones who are not so heavy, they'll be drifting past."

New Ireland journalist Rebecca Marigu, who joined search teams near Djaul Island this week, said locals reported seeing three bodies near Sumuna village on Wednesday, but a returning boat could not retrieve them because it was already carrying passengers.

"When they came back, they couldn't find any … the waves out here are still quite high," she said.

Mr Chan has requested support from the Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) Navy, saying larger vessels were needed.

The ABC has contacted the PNGDF for comment.

Families waiting for answers

In East New Britain, governor Michael Marum has been meeting with relatives of those missing and recovered.

He said many of those lost came from the same families and villages.

"It is sad to see we lose these families," he said.

" The youngest is two, three years old. Innocent ones that we've lost now. "

Pastors and community leaders have remained in close contact with grieving families since the boats disappeared.

Mr Marum said the disaster was among the worst Papua New Guinea had seen since the sinking of the Rabaul Queen ferry in 2012, which killed at least 140 people.

"It is probably one of the ones with the highest number," he said.

Authorities say accounts from the surviving boat operators point to dangerous sea conditions as the cause of the incident.

Loading...

They say the group left Pangpang Island for Kokopo about 3:30pm when rough seas struck.

A sudden swell lifted the stern of one boat, causing it to capsize and send passengers into the water.

The second boat attempted a rescue but also overturned as people tried to climb aboard.

Police have dismissed speculation of piracy and urged the public to rely on official information while recovery efforts continued.

Calls for safer journeys

The tragedy has prompted renewed calls for stronger maritime safety enforcement across PNG as authorities respond to multiple incidents at sea in recent days.

Mr Chan said his province was already dealing with another maritime tragedy, after a passenger boat carrying nine people reportedly capsized while travelling from Muliama to Anir Island on July 14.

Three people managed to swim ashore at Tefa Island, while six others remained missing.

"I was with the families of those missing from Anir. One body [was] just recovered [on Wednesday]," Mr Chan said.

Pumice stone inundates islands in Papua New Guinea Residents are concerned about access to food and fresh water as pumice makes travel difficult for Papua New Guinea's seafaring communities.

A separate search is also underway in Bougainville, where three people remain missing after a banana boat disappeared while travelling from Nissan Island to Buka on July 18, the same day as the East New Britain incident.

Fisheries and Marine Resources Minister Jelta Wong said existing safety requirements, including compulsory GPS trackers and life jackets, needed stronger enforcement.

"We need to learn some hard lessons from this tragedy," he said.

The PNG National Weather Service has renewed strong wind warnings across the Bismarck Sea, including East New Britain, New Ireland and Bougainville, urging small vessels to remain ashore until conditions improve.

World.title: Calls for change after French apprentice jockey's track work death
World.content:
The family of a French apprentice jockey who died after falling from a horse during track work in the New South Wales Central West is hoping an inquest will prevent similar incidents.

Marina Morel, 30, died on February 8, 2022 after she was thrown from Lina's Choice at the Gulgong Turf Club.

Experts told the coronial inquest in Lidcombe that the most likely cause of the fall was a pre-existing stress fracture in the horse that resulted in a catastrophic fracture on the day of the accident.

Morel's family said in a statement that they did not blame anyone for her death but wanted protocols put in place to spare others the same pain.

"There are foreseeable factors that need to be taken into account," they said.

" We will make sure your departure was not in vain. "

Marina Morel had been riding horses for most of her life. (Facebook)

Morel came to Australia in 2014 to follow her dream of becoming a professional jockey.

The inquest was told she was a "highly competent horsewoman" who had been riding since the age of five.

Morel was working for trainer Brett Thompson at BKB Racing when she died.

Early return to training

The inquest looked at a number of issues, including the return of Lina's Choice to training after an injury in March 2021.

The mare suffered a partial ligament tear in March that year and veterinarian Jack Holman recommended she take six weeks' box rest and 12 months' paddock rest.

The horse returned to work six months and three weeks later.

Dr Holman told the court he was not concerned about the early return to training.

"Brett [Thompson] was a good operator and I trusted his judgement in the case of lame horses," he said.

Brett Thompson has been a full-time professional trainer for more than 15 years. (Supplied: Brett Thompson Racing)

Mr Thompson said that during the spelling period he regularly checked Lina's Choice for signs of lameness but did not find any.

The inquest heard there had been signs of tension in the mare's opposite pectoral prior to the fall, which could have been a sign she was offloading weight due to a stress fracture on the other side.

Experts at the inquest were divided about whether a vet should have been called to perform an assessment before the horse returned to work.

An expert engaged by Mr Thompson said the injury was not reportable, but the former and current Racing NSW chief veterinary officers disagreed, citing state guidelines regarding the potential effect on performance.

Counsel assisting the coroner David Kell said Racing NSW should clarify its policy on reportable injuries.

He said the policy left room for ambiguity about what injuries were notifiable and recommended Racing NSW publish further guidance on the reporting of major orthopaedic injuries.

Since Morel's death, BKB Racing has changed its practice to ensure a vet assesses a horse when returns to training after an injury.

Marina Morel started as an apprentice jockey at the Gulgong Turf Club in 2021. (ABC News)

American veterinary surgeon specialist Susan Stover told the inquest she recommended mandatory exams after an inactivity period of 60 days, but accepted that could capture horses going through ordinary spelling in preparation for a race.

The court heard it was standard practice in NSW to have a veterinary assessment after 150 days, but that was not written policy.

Dr Kell recommended Racing NSW develop and publish a policy to reflect that requirement.

Racing NSW did not oppose any of the recommendations made.

Marina Morel trained as a jockey in Sydney and Mudgee. (Supplied)

Profound loss

The inquest heard that Morel was an organ donor who saved two people's lives after her death.

Her family described her as "passionate, loving, full of courage, determined, sparkling" and possessed of "undeniable elegance".

Deputy State Coroner Derek Lee indicated his appreciation for the family's testimony.

"Policy documents, whilst they are important, they are very much sterile, lifeless," he said.

"The statement you have shared today very much puts into perspective why a coronial inquest process exists."

The findings will be handed down on August 21.

World.title: Families of Sea World crash victims say 'lives changed forever'
World.content:
The family of a British couple who died in a Sea World helicopter crash in 2023 say their "lives changed forever" that day.

Pilot Ashley Jenkinson, UK tourists Ronald and Diane Hughes, and New South Wales tourist Vanessa Tadros were killed when two Sea World helicopters collided near the Gold Coast theme park in 2023.

In statements read out on the final day of an inquest into the collision the families of those that died discussed their grief following the event.

Lewis Ainsworth, the son of Diane Hughes, said: "It is impossible to fully put into words the devastation of that day, or the depth of the loss that has followed."

Ashley Jenkinson was killed in the 2023 crash along with NSW woman Vanessa Tadros and UK couple Ron and Diane Hughes. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Coroner Carol Lee teared up as she made her closing address to the court after the powerful statements had been read.

The inquest has involved multiple sittings in a bid to understand how and why the deadly crash occurred, including what safety systems were implemented at SeaWorld at the time and whether they were adequate.

An earlier report by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau found a litany of issues including a faulty radio antenna and discrepancies between maintenance records and components which had been installed in the helicopters.

The report suggested "this introduced vulnerabilities in assurance of airworthiness of these helicopters."

Army medicine expert and aviation accident investigator Dr Jeffrey Brock told the inquest he agreed with the ATSB report's findings.

He also told the inquest he believed Mr Jenkinson had been "likely mildly impaired" from the use of cocaine at a New Year's Eve party two nights prior.

Sea World Helicopters pilot Ash Jenkinson delivering supplies to flood-affected NSW communities in 2022. (Facebook: Sea World Helicopters)

Dr Brock agreed the airspace around Sea World was an "inherently risky" environment.

'No words can explain the loss'

The heartbroken family of Vanessa Tadros said "no words can explain the loss that we have endured".

"What was meant to be a long-awaited Christmas holiday that we had been saving for and looking forward to, and that we worked hard to make happen, ended up being the worst nightmare of our lives," the statement said.

"Vanessa had that positive energy about her that attracted people. She was always happy and joyful. She was always so loving, caring and compassionate. She had the softest heart, a heart of gold."

Ronald Hughes's family thanked the inquest "for the care and thorough consideration given to these proceedings and to the circumstances surrounding our dad's death".

Diane and Ron Hughes were married just months before the fatal crash. (Supplied: Hughes family)

"Our dad was the kind of person whose presence you never forgot," the family said.

"He was funny, generous, hardworking and a big kid at heart. He was truly one of a kind and lived life to the fullest."

Mr Ainsworth, the son of Ms Hughes, added his mother was "a cool mum, warm, loving and endlessly caring".

"We miss her every day. And we know that everyone who knew and loved her misses her too."

The parties now have until October to draft written submissions to the inquest.

World.title: 'Terrifying' four hour wait for police to reach life-threatening DV incident
World.content:
Queensland police took over four hours to reach a life-threatening domestic and family violence (DFV) call-out in May.

Statistics revealed in budget estimates found it took almost 16 days on one occasion in March to respond to an urgent DFV call-out involving injury or an imminent threat.

In May, the average call-out time for police to respond to a priority one DFV matter involving a threat to life was 42 minutes.

The data dated back to January 2024, with the average priority one response time dropping as low as six minutes, including for the latest figures in June.

Responding to the more than four-hour response incident, Acting Police Commissioner Brett Pointing said the figures provided no context.

Brett Pointing said the figures provide no context. (ABC News)

"In normal circumstances, you respond to a code one as fast as you can," he told budget estimates.

"That is the only figure in the whole table that's high, and it's impossible to comment on it unless you are able to talk to the officers who are involved.

"From January [20]24, code one, they're all, I think very, very impressive responses, that particular event would have a particular story to it."

From January 2024 to 30 June 2026, there were almost 440,000 total call-outs for DFV assistance in Queensland.

Police union president Shane Prior said resourcing had not kept up with demand.

"Police officers in Queensland never want to see a situation where a code one domestic and family violence job, which is clearly urgent, has to wait for hours after service," he said.

Police union president Shane Prior said resourcing had not kept up with demand. (ABC News: Heidi Sheehan)

"Police are bogged down, we can no longer continue and allow this to be the norm, because we're going to see more and more of this, and I fear that more people are going to die unless there are more urgent reforms."

He said police were on average spending three to six hours at a DFV job, often due to red tape.

Calls for help going unanswered for weeks

The average time to reach an urgent priority two call, defined as involving an imminent or present threat of injury, peaked this year in February at 48 minutes.

In that same month, the longest time to reach a DFV call-out was more than 11 days.

Mr Pointing again defended the work of police when questioned by the opposition.

"The circumstances of every case are different. It could be a thousand different hypothetical scenarios why police couldn't attend," he said.

"It would take a review of each specific incident to find out why that outlier was there."

Mr Prior said it was "terrifying".

"This is a symptom of what the community has come to expect of their police.

"If you want police to be mental health workers, social workers, prisoner daycare for Queensland Corrective Services, then the knock-on effect is that we're not going to be there to do the stuff that we need to do now."

Police minister Dan Purdie said the government would continue to listen "to the experiences of frontline officers to ensure they have the laws, resources and support they need".

Meaghan Scanlon is calling for clarity from the government on whether there has been an investigation. (AAP: Jono Searle)

Shadow Attorney-General Meaghan Scanlon said the numbers were incredibly concerning, calling for clarity from the government.

"We want to know what has happened to these domestic and family violence victims. Was there an investigation?" she said.

"And if not, why wasn't there?

"It's quite concerning that we only discovered this information because Labor asked questions of the government, and yet the government seemed to not come with answers today about the circumstances of these cases."

World.title: Aboriginal man died after being handcuffed in Adelaide CBD, police say
World.content:
South Australian Police say they will treat an internal investigation into the death of a 23-year-old Aboriginal man in custody with the "utmost importance".

Police said they were called to the car park of the Elephant and Castle Hotel, on West Terrace, in Adelaide's CBD just after 4:15pm on Thursday.

In a press conference today, Assistant Commissioner Ian Parrott said police responded to multiple reports of vehicles being damaged and two people fighting, "one person particularly being aggressive, that person potentially being armed with a knife".

He said that two "experienced officers" attended the scene and located a man in the driveway of a hotel "armed with a piece of wood or a stick", but that upon direction from police, he dropped it.

"As they moved in to arrest this male he has resisted and a struggle ensued," he said.

"During the arrest, he actually threatened to stab the police officers and he attempted to bite them on numerous occasions as well.

"I don't believe the officers were physically injured."

Assistant Commissioner Parrott said the police officer had received information that the man was "potentially" armed with a knife. (ABC News: Kathryn Bermingham)

Assistant Commissioner Parrott said initially two officers were on scene but they were "shortly after" assisted by another two officers "who assisted in restraining and handcuffing the man".

"It was a physical struggle that lasted a matter of minutes," he said.

“During which time the male was handcuffed and very shortly after became unresponsive."

Assistant Commissioner Parrott said that when the 23-year-old became unresponsive, the officers "immediately rendered assistance" and commenced CPR.

"This was a dynamic incident … he struggled violently and within a matter of minutes they were conducting CPR," he said.

"But, tragically, we were not able to revive this person who died at the scene."

Three investigations underway

SA Police's Major Crime Investigation branch is preparing a report for the coroner.

A Police Commissioner's Inquiry and an investigation conducted by the Ethical and Professional Standards Branch, overseen by the Office of Public Integrity, are also underway.

Assistant Commissioner Ian Parrott said "no taser or other equipment" was used by police. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"The internal investigation will take as long as it takes," Assistant Commissioner Parrott said.

"We treat this with the utmost importance.

" A person has actually lost their life here and we need to make sure that our investigation is extremely thorough. "

Assistant Commissioner Parrott said the man's family, who reside in the Aṉangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands, has been notified of the death.

“It’s unimaginable grief for the family and our condolences certainly do go out to the family," he said.

The ABC has reached out to Aboriginal Legal Rights Movement and community members for comment.

Incident captured on body-worn camera

The assistant commissioner said the incident was captured on one of the police officer's body-worn camera, adding that "no taser or other equipment" was used.

"I have watched the body-worn video, I won't be making any comment in relation to that," he said.

When asked if the officers were still on duty, he responded: "both officers are still on active duty in this point in time".

Assistant Commissioner Parrott said investigations were still underway into the alleged assault they were originally called to investigate.

He said the situation was "extremely traumatic" for the police officers involved.

"It’s also extremely traumatic for our community constables and our Aboriginal employees," he said.

In a statement released on Friday afternoon, SA Police said the alleged fight was at the Gilles Street entrance to the hotel's car park, and have asked anyone who witnessed it to contact police.

Police also said they "believe the deceased man may have interacted with vehicles travelling on West Terrace" about 4pm as he crossed from the road's western side.

"Anyone who may have witnessed an altercation between two men in the hotel car park or who may have dash cam vision of an Aboriginal man wearing dark clothing crossing West Terrace in traffic late Thursday is urged to contact CrimeStoppers on 1800 333 000," they said.

World.title: 'It's home': Victim of alleged gun theft, arson wants to go back to Coles Bay
World.content:
The victim of an alleged violent home invasion and gun theft on Tasmania's east coast says he still considers the area home and plans to spend his "last days" there.

Grant Whelan was found by police injured and tied up outside his Coles Bay property after the alleged attack on July 11, in which 15 firearms were stolen, and he was left to watch his home burn down.

Grant Whelan's house in Coles Bay was reduced to wreckage after the fire. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

The 76-year-old was left not only homeless but with essentially no possessions to his name, and with a "tough road" of physical and psychological recovery ahead of him.

Last week, Tasmania Police charged three men with aggravated burglary, aggravated assault, arson and theft of a motor vehicle over Mr Whelan's home invasion and they were remanded in custody.

Loading...

Speaking to 936 ABC Hobart, Mr Whelan thanked the "wonderful" staff at the Royal Hobart Hospital.

"I'm recovering okay," he said.

" Just slowly. Every day is a little bit better than the one before. "

He said he was having nightmares and was receiving psychological support, and thanked his family and the wider community for the support he had received.

Grant Whelan has said he has been overwhelmed by the generosity of the wider community. (Supplied)

As well as significant financial donations being made to fundraisers online and at his grandsons' football club, Mr Whelan said people had also donated building materials.

"I've seen the very worst in people and I've seen the very, very best in people," he said.

"She's been a tough road, and it's going to get a lot tougher."

But he wants to return to Coles Bay.

"It's home. Once you establish where the last of your days are going to be, it really doesn't matter much what happens; you'll still go back there," he said.

Government data shows uptick in crimes involving guns

The Coles Bay incident has renewed focus on Tasmania's proposed new gun laws, an uptick in some gun-related crimes and calls for the government to impose caps on the number of firearms a person can own.

It also sparked a heated exchange with the state's police minister, Felix Ellis, after a journalist asked him at a press conference last week if gun robberies were more likely to occur if more people owned more guns.

Attacking media a diversion tactic The scolding of a journalist asking a legitimate question about firearm ownership, and the subsequent pile-on which was allowed to run on social media, should ring alarm bells for anyone concerned with democracy.

That was "victim blaming", the minister said, but advocates believe if there were fewer guns legally owned in the community, fewer could be stolen and used by criminals.

In recently published data, Tasmania Police said there was 50 per cent more robbery incidents involving firearms in Tasmania in the year to May, with a jump from eight incidents to 12.

There was also a 19 per cent jump in assault incidents involving a firearm being used as a weapon to 64, while aggravated burglaries were down 13 per cent to seven on the year prior.

The Tasmanian government has declined to impose a limit on how many firearms a person can own. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

During the same period, there were 40 firearm theft incidents with a total of 155 firearms stolen, only 29 of which have so far been recovered, which were similar figures to the year before.

There were more than 150,000 licensed firearms in the state, while more than 4,000 firearms were seized by or surrendered to Tasmania Police in the 12 months to May.

Gun control advocate blames government, not victim

Speaking to 936 ABC Hobart, gun control advocate Roland Browne said he believed Mr Ellis was "hiding from" the issue of stolen guns in the community.

"It's not victim blaming; if anything, it's government blaming," Mr Browne said.

" This is not banning guns; this is just limiting the number of guns in one place to prevent theft of large numbers of guns. "

Tougher penalties, but no gun limit under Tasmania's proposed new laws People who steal guns or possess stolen firearms would face a mandatory minimum jail term under proposed new laws in Tasmania.

He said it was an issue of public safety, and highlighted the murder of Constable Keith Smith, who was killed in June last year with a rifle illegally owned by Leigh Geoffrey Sushames, who did not have a gun licence.

Tasmania Police Commissioner Donna Adams also highlighted Constable Smith's death when she wrote to Mr Ellis in February, urging the government to adopt ownership limits.

"The murder of Constable Keith Smith … was a confronting reminder that the presence of a firearm can change the outcome of even the most routine policing task," she wrote in February.

" You stood with us in the aftermath of the tragic murder of Constable Smith, and we now seek your support as we confront the growing risks posed by firearms in our community. "

Tasmania has recorded a sharp rise in gun crime. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Ellis again defends no gun cap

Speaking on Friday, Mr Ellis said while he welcomed the advice from Commissioner Adams, other states and territories had followed Tasmania's "lead" on not introducing limits to the number of firearms licence holders could own.

He also reiterated that licensed gun owners "were not the problem" and that caps "don't apply to criminals".

Loading...

Labor's police spokesperson, Jen Butler, criticised Mr Ellis for going against Commissioner Adams's advice.

"It absolutely beggars' belief that we have a police minister that is ignoring the concerns of a police commissioner when it comes to firearms," she said.

" We believe in reducing firearms in our community because we will always prioritise public safety. "

"We look forward to working with the parliament to deliver practical reforms that improve community safety while respecting the legitimate needs of primary producers, sports shooters and recreational hunters."

When asked, Ms Butler did not say whether Labor had the support of the crossbench to pass legislative amendments in the minority parliament.

An alleged affair with a married man almost three decades ago could help solve the cold case murder of a Queensland mother, as police double the reward to $500,000 for information and begin retesting evidence from the crime scene. Dianne Angwin was stabbed and killed in her own home in Bowen in the Whitsundays in 1997. The case has never been solved. Queensland Police Dianne Angwin was fatally stabbed inside her own home on Leichhardt Street, Bowen, in the Whitsundays just after midnight on December 2, 1997. She was 50 years old. Her friend and housemate told police she was woken up and confronted by an armed man just moments before. “There are people out there with information,” detective senior sergeant Tara Kentwell said.



“Relationships and loyalties change, and I would encourage anyone with information, big or small, to contact police.” Angwin grew up in Victoria where she was married with four children before moving to Bowen with a new partner in 1995. They separated soon after she arrived in North Queensland, and she lived at various homes in Bowen before moving in with friend Edith Lay – known as Edie – in September, 1997. The unit on on Leichhardt Street, Bowen where Dianne Mary Angwin was murdered, reportedly by an unknown man who had woken up her housemate. Queensland Police The duo were frequently seen together at pubs and clubs across town, and they attended the Bowen Bowls Club along Livingstone Street on the evening of December 1, 1997.



Angwin returned home about 6.30pm and her friend was about an hour behind. We would like to speak to anyone who has information regarding a relationship Dianne was involved in with a local married man Detective senior sergeant Tara Kentwell Lay told investigators she was woken in her bed about 12.30am by an unknown man with one hand over her mouth, and a knife in the other. Angwin appeared in the doorway before running away. The man chased her and fatally stabbed her in the neck before leaving the flat. She was pronounced dead on arrival at Bowen Base Hospital.



Police found no signs of forced entry or disturbance during the investigation, and no property was stolen from the unit. Murdered women Dianne Angwin grew up in Victoria and was married with four children in the state before moving to Bowen in Queensland, south of Townsville. Queensland Police Detective senior sergeant Kentwell revealed on Thursday police had spoken to witnesses who said Lay, who died in 2022, had confided in them she knew the identity of the armed man, but had kept it secret out of fear. “We would like to speak to anyone who has information regarding a relationship Dianne was involved in with a local married man, who had been seen at her unit,” the officer said. “Information suggests that around the time of Dianne’s murder, she was actively encouraging him to leave his wife so they could overtly continue the relationship.”



Police obtained over 100 witness statements at the time of the murder, but never solved the crime. Friend and housemate Edith Lay – known as Edie – told police she was woken up and confronted by an armed man just moments before Dianne Angwin was murdered. Queensland Police The Queensland Homicide Cold Case Investigation Team recently began a review into the death, retesting items from the crime scene including the clothes Angwin was wearing when stabbed. Detectives are travelling to Bowen, Cairns and Victoria to re-interview key witnesses and persons of interest. A mobile police facility will also be set up in Bowen’s CBD to engage with residents. The initial reward of $250,000 was upped to $500,000 on Thursday. There has been very little previous media coverage of the murder, which occurred just months before the high-profile disappearance of teenager Rachel Antonio from the same small town.

World.title: Geelong superstar agrees to a deal for 2027, Pendlebury still undecided
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Geelong superstar agrees to a deal for 2027, Pendlebury still undecided Jake Niall Updated July 24, 2026 — 4:29pm ,first published 10:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Geelong and Patrick Dangerfield have agreed to a contract for 2027, confirming that the Cats’ superstar veteran will play on into his 20th AFL season. The Cats and their skipper have reached agreement on terms for a one-year deal for 2027, meaning Dangerfield will play on as he wished and push towards the 400-game mark, according to industry sources familiar with Dangerfield’s deal, speaking anonymously to discuss player contracts. Patrick Dangerfield has agreed to terms with Geelong to play on in 2027. AFL Photos Dangerfield, who was drafted by the Adelaide Crows in 2007, will suit up for his 12th season at Geelong, an astonishing return for a player and club who joined forces for the 2016 season and helped arrest a potential slide for the Cats. Dangerfield was due to play his 15th game of 2026 on Friday night against the Demons and the 375th of his career, having surmounted a calf injury that saw him miss games from rounds two to five this season.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Should not have happened’: Dillon, Crows denounce booing after coach comes under fire The Cats confirmed he had signed on after this masthead’s report. “It’s exciting for us all to have Pat playing for the Cats in 2027. He continues to lead from the front and remains an important player and person within our football program,” football boss Andrew Mackie said. “Pat drives high standards, cares deeply about the Club and has a positive influence on everyone around him, so we’re pleased to see him continue his career into 2027.” Dangerfield entered Friday’s game with 18 goals and an average of just under 15 disposals, having been deployed mainly as a forward rather than midfielder since 2025, when he was instrumental in Geelong overcoming Hawthorn to reach the grand final with one of his career-best games in the preliminary final (31 disposals, three goals, nine inside 50s). He was second in the AFL for goal assists last year.



Should Dangerfield, who has been carefully managed by the Cats, play all the remaining games and one final, he would need a further 20 games to reach the 400 game mark in 2027. He turns 37 in April. Dangerfield needs four votes in the Brownlow Medal to become the highest polling player for that award in the game’s history, surpassing ex-teammate Gary Ablett (262 votes). Dangerfield, one of the AFL’s most decorated champions with a Brownlow Medal (2016), eight All-Australian jumpers (equal most of any current player with Max Gawn), had signalled his wish to play on 2027 earlier this season. He has captained the Cats for four seasons, and was an influential president of the AFL Players’ Association from 2018 until early 2025. Like several other Geelong greats, including the retired Joel Selwood and Tom Hawkins, Dangerfield has played well into his 30s on significantly reduced dollars in his twilight years – a situation echoed at Collingwood, where Scott Pendlebury, Steele Sidebottom and Jeremy Howe have sustained careers into their mid-30s or beyond.



Geelong’s capacity to keep veterans playing on at a high level in to their 30s on moderate or reduced contracts has assisted the Cats in recruiting select players from rival clubs. They have been the leading contender for Giants’ skipper and free agent Toby Greene should he leave and have remained interested in St Kilda ruckman Rowan Marshall, whom the Saints retained despite Marshall’s bid for a trade to Geelong last October.

- Jake Niall Pendlebury ‘unsure’ about 2027 Steve Barrett Scott Pendlebury is still yet to decide whether his legendary career at Collingwood will continue into a 22nd season in 2027, with the club maintaining it will ultimately be his call.



Pendlebury was among the Magpies’ best at Adelaide Oval on Thursday night as they turned a 27-point deficit into a powerful 34-point win over Adelaide. Scott Pendlebury (right) celebrates a goal with Nick Daicos against the Crows. AFL Photos Playing his VFL/AFL record-extending 439th game, Pendlebury racked up 29 touches and six clearances, while his right-foot snap deep into the second quarter sparked Collingwood’s comeback. Uncontracted for next season and set to turn 39 in January, Pendlebury is averaging 23.9 disposals per game this year, his highest return since 2019. “I’m not sure about next year,” Pendlebury said with a straight bat.



“My focus is still on this year, and performances like this give me belief that this group can do special things this year.” Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Sidebottom set to exit, one of Pendlebury and Howe makes sense This masthead reported this week that, while Collingwood is expected to announce the retirement before the season’s close of Pendlebury’s great mate Steele Sidebottom, it is open to either of Pendlebury or Jeremy Howe (who was also important on Thursday night) to either retire or seek to finish their playing days at another club and then (assistant) coach there. Even as his side struggled early against the Crows, Pendlebury took a moment to appreciate fellow veteran Taylor Walker’s 700th career goal – a sublime free-kick conversion from the scoreboard pocket late in the opening term. “Tex’s goal that he kicked was amazing and the way the crowd celebrated that was unreal,” Pendlebury said.



“Tex is an icon of our game and such a great player. “I knew he’d kick one, so when he had that shot, I was half-hoping that this would be a nice moment for him.” The surging Magpies have now won six straight to suddenly sit just two points outside the top four. While Collingwood’s belief is now being rewarded on the scoreboard, Pendlebury insisted they were never far away, even when results weren’t going their way earlier in the season. “I’ve been around long enough to know it’s a long season and there’s going to be patches where you win close games, patches where you lose close games,” he said.



“Even in that patch of close losses, we felt like we weren’t far away. “It is nice to get some confidence at this time of the year.” While Pendlebury remains undecided about his future, Magpies coach Craig McRae believes the five-time Copeland Trophy winner will ultimately drive the conversation. “Honestly, I think that will be a lot on him – that’s the way I see it,” McRae said. “I’m not a part of contracts – I’ve never negotiated a contract in my life.



“What I’ll say is he’ll lead that narrative more than most.“We’ll see how that plays out.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Stunned by the intervention’: NSW minister under fire over payment to Labor-linked carer
World.content:
NSW Families and Communities Minister Kate Washington ordered her department to pay a Catholic not-for-profit $40,000 to drop legal action against a Hunter foster carer with Labor links. The controversial payment has prompted a former senior Catholic official to level a series of extraordinary allegations against Washington and the Department of Communities and Justice, including that the organisation’s government funding was threatened if it did not “toe the line”. NSW Families and Communities Minister Kate Washington instructed her department to pay $15,000 to a Hunter foster carer with close links to the Labor Party. Peter Stoop In 2024, Washington ordered her department to pay CatholicCare $39,316 in exchange for the not-for-profit dropping legal action against a foster carer it had mistakenly paid an allowance to for almost two years after their status as a carer ended. The minister approved the payment after a recommendation from the department. The minister then went against the advice of the department to authorise a special $15,000 ex gratia payment to the carer, as first reported by The Daily Telegraph.



The carer, whom the Herald cannot name for legal reasons, has close ties to the Labor Party. Related Article Graphic content

Crime Multiple child safety reports before child’s alleged murder by mother Documents obtained by the Herald through a parliamentary order show Washington intervened to use almost $40,000 in public funds to repay CatholicCare on behalf of the carer. A DCJ official wrote to CatholicCare in January 2024 confirming Washington requested the sum be paid by the department. “Accordingly, CCHM will withdraw legal proceedings against [the carer],” the official wrote. The email also stated the department would draft a non-disclosure agreement over the payment.



The department’s payment sparked significant angst with CatholicCare, and prompted a series of crisis meetings within the diocese. The decision was initially taken to quarantine the money while the organisation considered its options. In May 2024, the then-chief executive of the Catholic Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle, Sean Scanlon, wrote to the DCJ to raise his concerns about the department and the minister’s handling of the “highly unusual” case, as well as objecting to signing a non-disclosure agreement. “We were stunned by the intervention,” Scanlon told the Herald. “We took legal advice … I wrote to the department questioning their direction … The matter went to our advisory board [and] we considered reporting it to the ICAC.” In his letter, Scanlon said DCJ had verbally requested CatholicCare staff to scrub any mention of the minister from written correspondence. He also said staff at the not-for-profit had believed there was an “imputation” in its dealings with DCJ that its ongoing funding could be affected if it did not agree to the minister’s intervention.



He also insisted that the diocese would not sign an NDA, saying it “looked like a shut-up agreement”. “I was never going to sign that. I could not believe it.” Another CatholicCare employee, who spoke to the Herald on the condition of anonymity, described the process as “extremely unusual”. “The consensus among senior leaders … was outrage,” they said. In a statement, Washington said the case “warranted an ex gratia payment to ensure a foster carer was not left tens of thousands of dollars out of pocket after continuing to care for a vulnerable young person”.



“The NGO involved was aware the young person remained living with the foster carer. Staff attended the foster carer’s home to meet with the young person during that period,” she said. “I was presented with technical and bureaucratic reasons why this foster carer should personally bear those costs. I did not believe that was fair, and I stand by my decision. “The payment did not provide any special benefit. It simply reimbursed the foster carer for the ordinary costs of caring for a child that would have been paid had the administrative issues not occurred.” She did not have any relationship with the carer, she said. Washington has been under pressure over a series of scandals within her department, including two foster children being allowed to live with a convicted triple killer, and the alleged murder of a child at the hands of his mother, who was the subject of multiple child safety concerns.



Related Article NSW State Parliament ‘Multiple failures’: Urgent review after triple killer found living with foster children When asked on July 14 if Washington acted appropriately in granting the $15,000 ex gratia payment to the foster carer, Premier Chris Minns said he had not spoken to the minister, but was satisfied that it was a “reasonable intervention”. That’s despite the department recommending against the payment, in part because the dispute between the carer and the Catholic not-for-profit was not caused by the government. In advice to the minister, the DCJ said it would set an “unhelpful precedent” and warned it carried “considerable reputation risk”. “The moral justification is limited,” the department said in briefings obtained through parliament. However, the latest revelations are likely to place further pressure on the minister.



Opposition families and communities spokeswoman Natasha Maclaren-Jones said Scanlon’s comments showed Minns “could not look the other way”. “This raises serious questions about whether decisions are being made fairly and consistently, or whether the rules change depending on who has the minister’s ear,” she said. Scanlon told the Herald he and other staff at the Catholic diocese were aware of the carer’s links to Labor. “This whole thing just looked like an old-style backroom deal,” he said. “I thought we were past that.”



Washington, the member for Port Stephens, has said that she did not know the carer despite their links to the Labor Party. The issue was first brought to her attention by another MP, who made two further representations on behalf of the carer in August and September.
