Opposition families and communities spokeswoman Natasha Maclaren-Jones said Scanlon’s comments showed Minns “could not look the other way”. “This raises serious questions about whether decisions are being made fairly and consistently, or whether the rules change depending on who has the minister’s ear,” she said. Scanlon told the Herald he and other staff at the Catholic diocese were aware of the carer’s links to Labor. “This whole thing just looked like an old-style backroom deal,” he said. “I thought we were past that.”



Washington, the member for Port Stephens, has said that she did not know the carer despite their links to the Labor Party. The issue was first brought to her attention by another MP, who made two further representations on behalf of the carer in August and September. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. 

CLARIFICATION This story has been updated with additional context about the approval of the payment.

World.title: Installation features 'forbidden' medicines denied to New Zealanders
World.content:
Locked up medicines on display to highlight unfunded treatments Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Patients waiting for life-changing medicines to be funded say people should not have to fundraise, go into debt, or travel overseas for treatments and therapies that could be administered here.

More than a dozen patient organisations are hosting the Forbidden Pharmacy, online, and this weekend at Auckland's Shed 10.

Supplied/ Forbidden Pharmacy

It's an installation that shows shelves of white medicine packets and bottles locked behind doors - representing what people may need but can't access, because they are not funded by Pharmac.

When Jemma Gerring was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in late 2023 she had no symptoms till the day she went to the doctor thinking she might have appendicitis.

"It was surreal. It was just like being hit by a freight train. It took a long time to process what that meant," she said.

"You start off really optimistic about, okay, that's great, we'll have treatment and be all better. Very quickly you start looking at the statistics and realise it's not going to be that easy."

Jemma Gerring RNZ/ Amy Williams

She has health insurance but that has a cap for the unfunded drug that is buying her more time with her family.

It has so far cost her hundreds of thousands of dollars for the drug and life-prolonging surgeries in Australia; something she said is unfair to anyone without such means.

"I think the thing for me is I feel guilty that I can afford to pay for this. It's inconvenient and it costs money, but I can pay for it and I really do credit this drug with making a difference in my life," she said.

"I'm still working full-time, I'm still being a mum full-time."

Supplied/ Forbidden Pharmacy

Gerring drives six hours from New Plymouth to Palmerston North each fortnight to have the drug she pays for, Bevacizumab, administered.

It is funded in other countries, including Australia and the UK.

"It's that sort of continual guilt that you feel too, of 'Am I taking money away from my children's future, from my husband's ability to live when I'm not here?'," she said.

"But I'm literally in the situation of buying time, and I like to think it's worth it.

"It's certainly worth it for me."

Locked up medicines on display to highlight unfunded treatments Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Tim Edmonds RNZ/ Amy Williams

The Forbidden Pharmacy has the medication on a shelf, and spokesperson for the installation, Tim Edmonds, said for patients waiting for medicine to be funded, the cost of living is a burden.

"This is having to make decisions no New Zealander should ever have to make, remortgaging homes, setting up Givealittle pages, moving to another country," he said.

"There is a financial cost, an emotional cost, but actually for many people those aren't options and the cost is going without, worsening health and less time with family and loved ones."

Edmonds is chief executive of Blood Cancer NZ and said a recent international report found patients in New Zealand have the poorest publicly-funded access to modern medicines out of comparable OECD countries and that the majority, 95 percent, of modern medicines don't make it to the shelves here.

"We want the future government to solve this for New Zealand," Edmonds said.

"We want the medicines that Pharmac have recommended to the government to be funded over three years and clear the backlog, and we want to plan for sustained investment so that we stop getting further behind the countries that we like to compare ourselves to."

Bart Schroder RNZ/ Amy Williams

For Bart Schroder, having access to an unfunded cancer medication means he is still alive after being diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer five years ago.

His health insurance has covered the cost since diagnosis, otherwise he would have had a long wait.

"In my case, I'm still here four years later, which is pretty good, and I'm still feeling really good," he said.

"That wouldn't have been the case, because my cancer is very aggressive... it would have taken me out so the standard treatment wouldn't have been very effective."

Schroder would like to see the medicine funded so everyone with his diagnosis can access it early on.

An engineer, he is still working for the company he founded and recently sold, it sells specialised equipment around the world.

"Five good years of working, contributing, selling stuff all over the place is way better than six months in a hospital. Hospital is much more expensive than just looking after me for five good years," he said.

"So why don't they fund it? It makes a lot of sense."

Looking ahead, Gerring wants more life-changing medicines funded so everyone can have the same chance as she has to enjoy more of their life.

"I was sort of told average life expectancy from diagnosis is two and a half years. I'm beyond that now, so... I definitely feel like I'm living on borrowed time, but every extra month I get with my children at this very formative age for them is worth it."

Politicians from National, Labour, ACT and New Zealand First visited the Forbidden Pharmacy today.

World.title: Police execute search warrants in relation to Wellington homicide investigation
World.content:
Police investigating a homicide in the Wellington region want information about sightings of two cars.

Nathaniel Sturmey, 29, was found dead at a property on Malone Road in Lower Hutt on 9 April.

Police say they have executed a number of search warrants across the Wellington region as enquiries into his death continue.

Detective Inspector Jamie Woods said the investigation team was making significant progress.

Police want to hear from anyone who saw a grey 2007 Audi A4 in and around the Waterloo area on the night of Wednesday 8 April and the early hours of Thursday 9 April. Supplied / NZ Police

Police were focusing on a number of people, including some who were known to Nathaniel Sturmey, he said.

"Thanks to those who have spoken with us - anyone else who has information and has not yet talked with us please get in touch."

Police are seeking sightings of a black 2010 Nissan Qashqai in and around the Waterloo area of Lower Hutt on the night of Wednesday 8 April and the early hours of Thursday 9 April, as well as in the Naenae area on Sunday 12 April.

Police also want to hear from anyone who saw a grey 2007 Audi A4 in and around the Waterloo area on the night of Wednesday 8 April and the early hours of Thursday 9 April.

Anyone with information that may assist the investigation is can call 105, quoting reference number 260409/9927 or provide information anonymously through Crime Stoppers on 0800 555 111.

World.title: Police rescue team phones in local farmer, who saves elderly man and dog
World.content:
Rescuers had grave concerns for an elderly fisherman stranded at night in the cold near a South Island river, until they called in a farmer with local knowledge who was able to locate the man in the dark.

The lost 87-year-old man rang emergency services for help about 8:15pm on Thursday, after becoming disoriented following a fishing trip near Lake Tekapo, at the Cass River mouth, police said.

Search and Rescue teams were swung into action, and police "remained on the phone with the 87-year-old, encouraging him to keep himself moving to stay warm, and provided reassurance while efforts were under way to locate him," they said.

But, they were worried the response would not reach the lost man and his dog in time: "While [he] was dressed warmly, Police were concerned he was not equipped to spend the night outdoors in the cold conditions".

So, looking for a faster way to get help to him, police made a call to a nearby farm manager, Grant Murray, who knows the area well.

Murray agreed to help. And "after 35 minutes on the phone, the lost man was successfully located by Mr Murray".

The elderly man and his dog were taken home to warm up and rest.

The rescue showed the value of local knowledge, and strong community relationships, police said.

World.title: No bridge too far for man behind new Aoraki Mt Cook bridge
World.content:
No bridge too far for man behind new Hooker Valley bridge Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

There is virtually no bridge too far for the man behind the new Hooker Valley suspension bridge at Aoraki Mount Cook.

The marvel of design and modern engineering is due to open next week and replaces the old one that closed due to erosion caused by storms in April last year.

It spans 189 metres across the Hooker River, making it the longest suspension bridge in the country.

Construction started in August last year, and since then workers have faced the challenge of gales and snowfall during construction.

The new 189m long Hooker Valley suspension bridge at Aoraki Mount Cook. Supplied

The man behind the design, bridge architect and engineer, Dan Crocker told Checkpoint that he feels amazed seeing the bridge in its finished form.

"It's been a lot of work getting to this point, but you know, one of the things is when you arrive on site and everything fits and you've got that beautiful scenery, it just looks right."

Bridge engineer Dan Crocker (right) Supplied

As the longest footbridge in Aotearoa, Crocker said it had been no easy feat getting to this point, with the remote site adding an extra layer of challenges.

"Conventionally with a bridge, you might roll up with a crane and concrete trucks. You can't do that in this environment, everything comes in via helicopter."

"You have to work backwards from what you can get to site and working in these challenging environments. It's a very different type of bridge construction in these remote areas"

The bridge will open to the public on 28 July. Supplied / Department of Conservation

Wild weather at the remote site had also presented issues.

"The contractor brings excavators and containers to site, the winds picked up and brought all the gravel with it and it ended up stripping the paint off the excavators and the containers."

"You can only imagine how much of a severe environment that is to work in... it's not much fun, but on the other days when it's beautiful sunshine and you can see the mountains it makes it worth it."

Unlike a traditional suspension bridge, the new structure lacks what gave the 'swing bridge' its name, so those taking on the near 200m journey don't have to worry about losing their footing.

"Some people are comfortable with moving structures and heights, but a lot of people aren't. So what we try and do is make it as stable as possible while still maintaining that lightweight kind of appearance."

"There is a little bit of movement, but it's definitely suppressed compared to what you would normally have."

While the Hooker Valley bridge may be the longest, it is certainly not the first pedestrian bridge Crocker has designed.

"We wake up every morning, jump out of bed ready to design bridges, that's all we do here."

"Generally we focus on cycle bridges, pedestrian bridges, the kind of bridges people want to come and see and want to visit."

The Hooker Valley bridge is the country's longest suspension bridge. Supplied

Crocker said for him, bridges serve as more than a way to get from A to B.

"They connect communities, they connect different areas that people want to visit, but I like to think of them as also placemakers and wayfinders."

"We've got some little bridges here in Cambridge that I've designed - they're wayfinders in Cambridge itself with a little blue pedestrian bridge.. everybody uses it... 'go past the blue bridge and turn left.'"

Crocker said he also loves the way he's seen his bridges instil a sense of community pride, something he's seen in Westport with the Toki Poutangata bridge, inspired by the area's pounamu.

World.title: Universities feel out of favour over 'shambolic' teacher training funding
World.content:
* An earlier version of this story stated students received a bursary of $20,660, but the correct 2026 bursary was $19,930.

Universities are feeling hard-done-by following the release of figures that show government funding for in-school teacher training heavily favoured a newcomer to teacher education that was headed at the time by the chair of the Teaching Council.

The Teachers' Institute was allowed to triple its intake of school-based teacher trainees this year while universities were denied similar growth in what they say was a shambolic and odd process.

Students on one-year School Onsite Training Programme (SOTP) courses were paid $19,930 and were placed in their host schools for three days a week, excluding classroom practicum, while completing a teaching diploma or masters degree.

Figures published by the Education Ministry (MOE) show the government gave more than half the 533 places for this year to non-university providers and most of those to the Teachers' Institute, a charity set up by Auckland schools and led at the time by the then-chair of the Teaching Council David Ferguson.

Information provided by the ministry show some of the organisations did not have Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) funding for those students prompting a late appeal to the commission to approve the money.

Universities say the process for allocating student places for 2026 was overly complex and delayed, which resulted in many failing to fill all of the student places they were allocated.

Overall, 286 of the 533 SOTP places allocated for 2026 went to non-universities and 152 of those to the Teachers' Institute.

The institute was much more successful than most other organisations at filling the student places it was allocated.

The then-chair of the Teaching Council, David Ferguson. RNZ/ Luka Forman

RNZ requested the figures under the Official Information Act (OIA) on 25 February, but was denied in a letter dated 25 May on the basis they would soon be published - which happened this week.

The OIA response said the ministry assessed applications for funding and allocated places for 2026 based on its Teacher Demand and Supply report which showed where teachers were most needed.

Text messages released as part of the OIA response showed Ferguson asked the ministry for tips ahead of a meeting with Tertiary Education Commission chief executive Tim Fowler on 20 November 2025.

The meeting apparently concerned a late request for an increase in the number of tertiary students the commission would subsidise in 2026.

A ministry staff member told Ferguson: "With tim it's really unusual to grow their tec allocation so much, so I think focus on the fact that the business model is aligned with what govt and moe and tec all think is the future.

"He needs you to make a case so he can make a case to his board. He's doing us a big favour and will blame the ministry for not telling them about the sotp allocations. Feel free to let him."

The ministry said the texts referred to a situation where the ministry allocated school-based teacher training places to organisations that did not have Tertiary Education Commission funding for their students.

"The TEC subsequently approved funding for the additional places across the providers who had not received that funding," it said.

The sector had previously alleged favouritism of the Teaching Institute.

The Council of Deans of Education and teacher union the Educational Institute asked earlier this year if the Education Minister Erica Stanford had helped the institute get funding, suggestions the minister and institute denied.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Nick Monro

The ministry told RNZ a potential conflict of interest was identified.

"David Ferguson's appointment to the Teaching Council was included on the SOTP project risk register in August 2025. The conflict was deemed to be a perceived conflict only, as Mr Ferguson's roles on these boards held no bearing or influence on the way that allocation of places to providers were determined. Procurement was not involved in this process," it said.

Asked why the institute's allocation was tripled, but other providers' was not, the ministry did not provide a direct answer.

"As more ITE providers participate in the SOTP programme, the distribution of places may result in some providers receiving fewer places and others receiving more depending on their capacity, host school availability and levels of school and student interest," it said.

A shambolic process

Auckland University's head of School of Education and Social Practice Aaron Wilson said the university started offering an in-school programme for trainee secondary teachers in 2023 - before the Education Ministry began backing the scheme and expanding it.

He said the university developed good relationships with schools and filled all or nearly all of the places it was allocated each year.

But late in 2025 it was told that some of the schools it worked with had been allocated to the Teachers' Institute for 2026, he said.

Wilson said it had never worked before with many of the schools it was partnered with for 2026 contributing to it filling only 40 of its 69 allocated places.

Auckland University's head of School of Education and Social Practice Aaron Wilson. Supplied / University of Auckland

"Last year the ministry initially allocated schools to different providers and we weren't allocated schools that we had long-standing partnerships with and who had actually been with us right from the beginning," he said.

"There was a real change in the process that the Ministry of Education used... a lot of our partner schools were very unhappy and basically it ended up being a scramble at the end of the year trying to establish new relationships that were sort of foisted on us by the ministry."

Wilson said some of the schools the university had worked with in the past were allocated to other providers.

"We did request a review of that decision and there was a bit of a release of some extra places later in the year but it had already caused difficulty for us and the partner schools we had."

Wilson said he did not believe the university was treated fairly.

"I don't think we were treated respectfully, or our partner schools," he said.

"We felt messed around and the schools that we worked with felt messed around by that process."

"It would certainly feel in that process that the Teachers' Institute were in favour and we were out of favour."

The ministry did not confirm whether schools that were formerly assigned to the University of Auckland were assigned to the institute.

"Joint applications from both the ITE providers and schools were required for the 2026 allocations. Schools determined which ITE provider or providers they wanted to work with. Some schools chose to apply with more than one ITE provider," it said.

University of Waikato Pro Vice-Chancellor Education Claire McLachlan told RNZ the process for allocating 2026 places was shambolic and odd.

She said schools had to go through a complicated application process including stating support for government's favoured approach to teaching.

University of Waikato Pro Vice-Chancellor Education, Claire McLachlan. Supplied / University of Waikato

"Last year was shambolic," she said.

"What they did last year was very odd. They went through a process where schools had to explain a whole bunch of complicated things about how they were delivering the science of learning."

McLachlan said Auckland schools that were previously involved with the scheme were furious that some were dropped from it.

"It did feel unusual," she said.

She said she had been told the Teachers' Institute programme was more practically-focused than Waikato's and involved less assessment.

She said some people criticised universities' teacher-training as overly theoretical but that was not true.

"If you only go with practice you wind up with some very, very poor teachers over time because they've got a recipe, they've got a script and that's not going to help them when they're dealing with a diverse group of students," she said.

"I don't accept the criticism that we're overly-theoretical but I would accept the criticism that we probably over-assess."

The Teachers' Insitute said in a statement it received more applications from students this year because it added primary and "foundation programmes" to the courses it offered and increased the number of partner schools it worked with.

It said it had also "developed a strong reputation for training quality teachers in the real-world environment of schools".

Asked why its funded places increased much more than other organisations, it said: "Our funded places increased because we had an increase in the number of confirmed applicants to our teacher training programmes."

Meanwhile, David Ferguson said he had no comment.

A cohort of new teacher trainees are welcomed to The Teachers’ Institute in January 2026. Supplied / The Teachers' Institute

How the SOTP places were allocated

Overall, the 10 organsiations funded to provide SOTP this year filled only 413 or 77 percent of the places they were allocated.

The Teachers' Institute had 48 students in 2025, requested funding for 181 students in 2026, received 152 and filled 143 places.

The University of Waikato filled 52 places in 2025, requested funding for 162 in 2026, received 76 places but only filled 49. It expected to add a further 20 through a mid-year intake.

The University of Auckland also had 52 students in 2025, requested funding for 178 in 2026, received 69 places and managed to fill 40 of them.

Te Rito Maioha Early Childhood New Zealand had 42 students in 2025, asked for 171 for this year, received 90 places and filled 62.

The Open Polytechnic was the only other non-university provider approved for funding this year. It sought 121 places, was granted 44 and succeeded in filling 25.

Massey University sought 109 places, received 40 but filled 54 places after a boost to its initial allocation.

World.title: Police Sergeant Lyn Fleming's husband confronts killer as life sentence handed down
World.content:
Slain Nelson police officer Lyn Fleming's family have told her murderer that while he took her life, he will never be able to erase her legacy.

Hayden Tasker, 33, has been sentenced in the Nelson High Court to life in prison with no parole for 22 years for Fleming's murder.

He was found guilty of murdering Fleming and seriously injuring her colleague, Senior Sergeant Adam Ramsay, after a two-week trial at the Christchurch High Court in May.

The pair were overseeing the New Year's Eve policing operation in Nelson and were on foot patrol in the Buxton Square car park just after 2am on 1 January 2025 when they were hit by a white Honda Odyssey driven by Tasker.

Fleming was thrown around 20 metres in the impact and taken to Nelson Hospital where she was put on life support. Her injuries were described as catastrophic and unsurvivable.

Her son, Aren Olsen, told the court his mother was gone long before he got to hospital.

At her bedside, he said there was no opportunity to say goodbye.

"The truth is that Lyn Fleming was gone long before I made it back to her. Her brain and with it every trace of the person I knew and admired was already shattered and stolen from us by this act of cruel indifference," he said.

Nelson policewoman Lyn Fleming. Supplied / NZ Police

He said if there was any justice, it would come from his mother's enduring legacy of love and aroha for her family and her community, while the name and deeds of the person whose cowardice took her was erased from time and memory.

"I condemn the offender for his actions, but I refuse to allow myself to hate him. He's stolen too much from me and from this family and I deny him the right to take any more," Olsen said.

Fleming's daughter, Rayna Olsen, said her life changed in a matter of seconds when she got a phone call on New Year's Day.

"The images and sounds from the hospital haunt me every single day. I still hear the doctors telling us her injuries were not survivable," she said.

Olsen was pregnant at the time and said Tasker took away Fleming's chance to be a grandmother. As a result, her happiness and joy had been replaced by grief, trauma and sadness.

Lyn Fleming's son Aren Olsen, with his father Bryn Olsen and sister Rayna Olsen. RNZ / Louis Dunham

"Mum made this place feel like home, she made me feel safe. She filled our lives with love and without her, everything was different," she said.

"She was the person I could always rely on for support, guidance and unconditional love. Losing her has devastated every part of my life."

Rayna Olsen said she experienced nightmares, flashbacks, fear and trauma.

"The weight of my loss is suffocating and I am drowning in it," she said.

Fleming's husband, Bryn Olsen, told Tasker that his actions that day were cowardly, as was his choice to defend a charge of murder.

He told Tasker that he did not want to give him another thought after the hearing.

Hayden Tasker at his sentencing. Pool/Stuff/Braden Fastier

"Lyn helped people, you hurt people. Lyn succeeded in life, you failed. Lyn will be remembered, you will be forgotten," he said.

"I just hope the sentence you receive is long enough that by the time you are released you are too old to hurt anyone else.

"You leave no legacy. You are forgotten."

Ramsay told the court he remembered regaining consciousness and realising he had been hit by a car.

He was left with head injuries, a dislocated shoulder, breathing problems and cuts to the bone.

Ramsay said the attack profoundly affected police staff, with some resigning or changing roles after witnessing the violence.

Senior Sergeant Adam Ramsay. Pool/Stuff/Braden Fastier

Addressing Tasker directly in the dock, Ramsay said he hoped Tasker's time in prison felt as empty as the void Fleming's death has left for her family and friends.

The trial

Over two weeks, a Christchurch High Court jury heard from more than 40 witnesses, including members of the public and police officers who were in the central Nelson car park in the early hours of New Year's Day.

Tasker admitted two charges of dangerous driving causing injury and at the beginning of the trial and had earlier plead guilty to charges of driving while disqualified and driving with excess blood alcohol.

The court heard how Tasker drove into the Buxton Square car park in his White Honda Odyssey just after 2am.

What unfolded shortly afterwards was documented by CCTV footage, cellphone videos taken by members of the public and eyewitness accounts.

He drove at a group of police officers and a patrol car near the centre of the car park, forcing members of the public to jump out of the way, before hitting both Ramsay and Fleming.

Lyn Fleming's funeral. RNZ / Anthony Phelps

Ramsay was sent into the air and landed eight metres away near another patrol car, while Fleming was carried with the Odyssey and projected forward, landing around 20 metres from where she was hit.

After hitting the pair, Tasker then looped around the car park and drove back towards the officers, ramming into the back of a white police car, shunting it several metres forward.

The impact knocked over Sergeant Craig Barker who had gone to Ramsay's aid, left Constable Jemma Radcliffe who had been inside the car with a concussion and struck Tasman Cook, who was also helping Ramsay, with enough force it broke her arm.

Tasker was arrested at the scene and breath tested shortly after. He was found to be more than three times over the legal breath alcohol limit.

The jury found he had intended to murder Fleming and injure Ramsay when he hit them with his car, rejecting his claim that he crashed into the officers in a failed attempt to take his own life.

The Crown argued Tasker was motivated by anger towards the police and used his car as a weapon to mow them down.

Tasker's 'irrational and senseless' actions motivated by anger at police - judge

In sentencing, Justice Cameron Mander said the jury's guilty verdicts were inevitable based on the evidence called at trial.

The aggravating features of Tasker's offending were that he intentionally singled out the police officers, that he used his vehicle as a weapon and that while impulsive, there were elements of pre-meditation in the way he manoeuvred his car through Buxton Square.

He said Tasker held a persistent resentment towards police for what he considered to be unfair treatment, which gave insight into his warped motivation and thinking at the time.

"You targeted both officers with the intention of striking them with your vehicle, your actions in doing so were irrational and senseless, but they were by design, motivated by anger at the police."

Mander said Tasker's "unfathomable actions" were "grossly disproportionate" to the source of his grievance.

"Neither of them had any previous involvement with you, nor did you know them. You drove your vehicle at them because they were wearing a blue uniform and a police cap. That illustrates the randomness of them being your victims. They could have been any police officers going about their duties."

Tasker was disqualified from driving, and more than three times the legal breath alcohol limit, when he drove at the officers.

He said a previous conviction for assaulting a person using a vehicle as a weapon showed Tasker's inclination, while sitting behind the wheel of a car, to use it as a means to attack others if angered.

Mander said Tasker hadn't demonstrated genuine remorse or insight, or fully accepted responsibility for his actions.

He said Fleming's death was an irreparable loss that could not be mitigated by any sentence imposed by the court.

"The shattering consequences of Lyn Fleming's murder on her family, who have been left distraught and heartbroken by her sudden and arbitrary killing cannot be adequately captured in my sentencing remarks.

"They have been left entirely bereft. Their loss is permanent. Their pain is enduring."

Justice Mander said Nelson too, mourned a person in Fleming who gave much to her community.

He said attacks against police officers carried severe consequences and would not be tolerated.

"Policemen and women work for all members of society. Each day they undertake difficult, demanding and dangerous work. They stand in harm's way on behalf of others. When a police officer is killed, all of society is affected."

Police pay tribute

Commissioner Richard Chambers said sentencing marked the conclusion of a long and difficult chapter for police who had been profoundly affected.

"Lyn Fleming and Adam Ramsay showed up to work on New Year's Eve, ready to keep people in Nelson safe on what should have been a night of celebration. Instead, Lyn and Adam were targeted by the offender, simply because they were Police officers.

"This cowardly and senseless act has changed many people's lives forever. A life taken in just moments has left behind family, friends and colleagues who are still feeling deep pain at Lyn's loss. We know that every milestone in life without her feels heavy as she should still be with us," Chambers said.

"Lyn gave her community over 38 years' service and was highly respected by her colleagues. I want to acknowledge the incredible strength and dignity shown by Lyn's family. Having to listen to the evidence during the trial and see what happened to Lyn was harrowing. Particularly to Lyn's husband Bryn, and children Aren and Rayna, we are with you. You will always be part of our police family.

"There will not have been a single officer across the country who has not been impacted by what has occurred. The fact it was so random and completely unprovoked shows the danger which is faced by our officers every day."

Chambers said Ramsay faced a long road to recovery and would forever carry "dreadful" memories of that day.

"He has shown immense courage and bravery since this incident, including when he had to relive these moments in court. The fact that he continues to show up to work despite what he has been through, is a testament to his character and commitment to our community."

Area Commander for Nelson Bays Inspector Steve Collins thanked everyone in Nelson and across Aotearoa who sent cards, laid flowers or gave their condolences.

"You gave some comfort at a difficult time as our staff worked to come to terms with the shock of what had happened. Thank you for caring.

"Nelson is a beautiful and safe place to live, work and visit, this incident did not reflect our community and the outpouring of grief and support for Lyn's family, as well as for Adam, shows this."

Police response to verdict

Deputy Commissioner Jill Rogers said Fleming's death had left lasting scars across police, prompting officers to question their careers and safety.

"This was New Year's Eve. This was an event that should have been celebrated but will forever be etched in the memories of so many," she said.

"Adam and Lyn were two leaders who stood up and were doing exactly what we ask of our team. The consequences of what happened on the 1st of January have left irreparable damage."

It was hard to put into words how senseless the attack was, Rogers said.

"We have heard repeatedly today of the devastation ... that this ... has had on so many," she said.

Nelson area commander Inspector Steve Collins said no sentence could ever compensate Fleming's family nor offset the emotional toll on police.

Fleming was a dedicated public servant who cared deeply about her staff and the community, he said.

"Everyone at the Nelson police respected her. She was a role model to both males and females inside and outside the police. She was a modest and capable and deserving of being remembered as a quality human being," Collins said.

"As police we have to move on but she will never be forgotten here. Her hope, her values and her dedication will live on with the staff that work from Nelson Police Station. She will live on in the community, a community I want to thank for the outpouring of support that we received during our very dark days. It was some comfort and some reassurance to know that the New Zealand public, and specifically here the Nelson public, were behind us."

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers said the sentencing had closed a long and painful chapter but nothing could undo the harm caused by her killer's actions.

"This cowardly and senseless act has changed many people's lives forever. A life taken in just moments has left behind family, friends and colleagues who are still feeling deep pain at Lyn's loss," Chambers said.

World.title: Outdoor education subject saved from government overhaul
World.content:
Education Outdoors New Zealand says the government has changed its mind over the future of outdoor education as a secondary school subject.

It said outdoor education had been dropped from a list of subjects that would be developed by industry bodies ahead of the replacement of the NCEA qualification from 2028.

Instead the Education Ministry would develop the subject for study by students in Years 12 and 13.

EONZ chief executive Fiona McDonald said it was celebrating the decision because it would ensure the subject retained broad appeal to secondary students.

"The advantage of a ministry-led subject for outdoor education is it can be a much broader curriculum than just focusing on the skills and knowledge needed for students to go on into the outdoor ed industry," McDonald said.

She said it would lead students to all sorts of further study without necessarily wanting to learn in what she described as "a rather small outdoor industry".

McDonald said shifting the subject to industry-driven would have reduced schools' ability to deliver an outdoor education programme and fewer students would have been interested in the subject.

She said more than 3000 Year 11 students studied outdoor education and EONZ was concerned the government did not plan to offer the subject for that year level.

McDonald said more than 53,000 people signed a petition calling for outdoor education to remain a recognised Ministry-led senior subject.

The Education Ministry confirmed the decision.

"This reflects the significant educational value of the subject beyond any single industry, as well as feedback received through the curriculum refresh process," it said.

World.title: Fiji's former chief prosecutor claims govt conspiracy to remove him
World.content:
Fiji's former chief prosecutor, Christopher Pryde, claims there was a racist, government-led conspiracy to get rid of him.

The New Zealand lawyer, who is in Aotearoa, spoke to Pacific Waves after corruption charges against him in Fiji were dropped this week.

Fiji's Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) threw out three charges in the Suva Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

A statement from FICAC said "the decision was taken because FICAC has been unable to effect service on Mr Pryde in New Zealand, despite attempts to do so."

"The proceedings concerned charges previously filed in relation to nearly $NZ150,000 in payments and reimbursements received during his tenure as Director of Public Prosecutions.Those allegations have not been determined in court," the statement said.

"Under section 49 of the Criminal Procedure, the entry of a nolle prosequi brings the present proceedings to an end but does not prevent subsequent proceedings based on the same facts."

'Bitter taste'

Pryde, aged 60, has always maintained he was innocent and said the allegations against him were contractual matters rather than criminal offences.

He has previously described the charges as bogus, politically-driven and designed to prevent him from returning to Fiji to prosecute an elite group maligned in last year's damning Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of Barbara Malimali as FICAC head.

"I am left with a bitter taste towards the current Fijian government and the Judicial Services Commission (JSC) because I don't think they have played ball with me.

"They made up their mind they wanted to get rid of me and they employed all sorts of tactics in order to do that," Pryde said.

Pryde claimed that the government's tactics were designed to intimidate him, and should serve as a warning to expatriates keen to work in Fiji.

"Unfortunately it is a salutary reminder to other expatriates that might be considering taking up a role in public service in Fiji to be careful." he said.

However he added that the dispute he had with the government and the JSC did not effect the relationship he had with the wider community, after living in Fiji for 18 years.

Alleged witch-hunt

The Sitiveni Rabuka-led coalition government's information director, Samisoni Pareti, declined to respond to questions by RNZ Pacific.

Pryde claims FICAC has accused him of evading diplomats who were sent by Fiji to serve him with legal documents.

"It's ridiculous, they know where I live, they've had every opportunity over the last twelve months to serve me," he said.

Last December, Pryde claimed the Fijian government committed an illegal act on New Zealand soil and sent foreign diplomats to stalk him at home.

"They sent people from the Fijian High Commission in Wellington to my home (in Christchurch) and harangued my neighbours by questioning them as to my whereabouts.

Fiji's coalition government continues to struggle at bringing democratic processes back after 16 years of dictatorship. (Supplied) ABC/Supplied

"They acted in an intimidatory way by staking out my home whilst I was away attending my mother's funeral," he said, adding that it was the subject of a formal and ongoing police complaint in New Zealand.

"The Prime Minister was made aware of this breach of diplomatic convention but chose to ignore it."

"The witch-hunt against me began when the acting Attorney-General, Siriomi Turaga, accused me of wrongdoing after I was seen with the former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum at a reception at the Japanese Embassy in February 2023," he said.

'As long as iTaukei are on top'

Pryde was suspended on full pay for "misbehaviour" two months later and faced a further charge of receiving superannuation payments that had not been approved by the JSC in April 2024.

His superannuation ceased then his salary and all contractual benefits were "unilaterally" cut off by the Fijian government three months later.

"They (the government) want to get rid of me, it's all part of their ethno-national agenda," Pryde told RNZ Pacific in December 2024.

"Vulagi (foreigners) and Indo-Fijians are being replaced by iTaukei (indigenous Fijians).

"Hiring in Fiji is not based on merit, the government doesn't care, as long as iTaukei are at the top and in control." he said.

A tribunal exonerated Pryde on all charges in January 2025 and he was reinstated to the role, but he stayed in Aotearoa for fear he would be arrested on his return.

Several days after the Tribunal's decision, FICAC laid fresh corruption charges on him, including receiving a $NZ100,000 gratuity without the President's approval.

Wrongdoing denied

"I categorically deny any wrongdoing, the dispute was between myself and the JSC, whose chairman, the Chief Justice, Salesi Temo, tried and failed to convince the tribunal hearing that I had done something wrong," Pryde said.

"Issues around the payment of the gratuity were brought up at the tribunal and they were dismissed by the tribunal. So then we have a rehash of things into another format, they failed (with the charges) in the tribunal so they got FICAC to deal with them. That's not acceptable."

Prime Minister Rabuka criticised Pryde last July for failing to turn up to work, seven months after he was reinstated.

President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu then suspended his NZ$185,000 salary and benefits, following a public backlash over his absence.

Pryde said he had been living on his savings over the past year and was "relieved" that the latest corruption charges were dropped.

However he has filed a judicial review of the President's decision to cut his pay in the Suva High Court.

World.title: Brown slams Crows coach for his response to Quaynor booing
World.content:
Former AFL player and LGBTQIA+ advocate Mitch Brown says the culture of footy is ripe for change and more men need to call out bad behaviour after repeated booing of Collingwood's Isaac Quaynor.

A section of the Crows fans at Adelaide Oval for Thursday night's match against Collingwood could be heard booing every time Magpies defender Quaynor got the ball.

Last year, Quaynor had a homophobic slur used against him by Adelaide's Izak Rankine in a game in round 23.

Rankine received a four-match ban after an investigation by the AFL's Integrity Unit.

The ban effectively ended his season as the Crows lost their first two finals while he was suspended.

Matthew Nicks said it was "not ideal how it played out" after some Crows fans repeatedly booed Isaac Quaynor. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

In the aftermath of Thursday's game, Crows coach Matthew Nicks was asked about the incident and the booing.

"The game, it's about entertainment, enjoyment, passion," he replied.

"The game's a passionate game, and sometimes we lose our way in that a little.

"And with the backdrop, and the background leading into this game, it's not ideal the way it played out tonight."

Brown, who last year became the first current or former AFL player to come out as bisexual, told ABC Melbourne on Friday that men needed to "stand up … use our voices and not fear calling things out."

"I look at the best leaders in Australia, and the ones that I admire are the ones that are prepared to put their hand up and say, 'We are part of a problem,'" he said.

"I was really disappointed in the response by Adelaide's coach by not just saying this is completely out of order and [not] seeing the players and coach actually stand up and say we don't want to see this [booing] as part of our game and completely reject that any player should be targeted after they were the victim of abuse.

"When you don't call something out with conviction, silence is deafening.

"And I'm sure Matthew Nicks and coaches … consider themselves strong leaders.

"They say this phrase and we've all heard it: The standards we walk by are the standards we accept."

Crows say behaviour of some fans 'crossed the line'

The Crows released a statement on Friday from club CEO Tim Silvers.

"We … strongly believe there is a line between passionate support and behaviour that falls short of our values and those of the game," he said.

"We want our people to be vocal, engaged and passionate, but to do so respectfully.

"The overwhelming majority of our members and supporters represent the club exceptionally well.

"However, the behaviour of some crossed the line last night. Put simply, it was inappropriate and not good enough.

"Respect for all players, coaches, officials and fellow supporters is paramount, and it is a standard we must all uphold."

Loading Instagram content

The AFL Players Association condemned the actions of the section of fans, saying the game had to be safe for everyone.

"The incessant and targeted booing last night was unacceptable and should never happen," AFLPA CEO James Gallagher said.

"Targeted booing can cause significant harm to the person subjected to it. It also causes harm to others across our football community and signals that the game isn't safe for them.

"Our game must be inclusive and safe for all. Thank you to those who have shown leadership by calling it out."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The AFL also released a statement from CEO Andrew Dillon.

"AFL footy fans are some of the most passionate in world sport, and that passion is one of the things that makes our game so special," he said.

"But the targeted booing last night should not have happened and is not what we want to see in our game.

"We see the best of our fans every single week at matches across the country as they cheer, barrack and support their respective clubs, however, what we saw last night at Adelaide Oval fell well short of that."

World.title: Socceroos star allegedly tests positive for cocaine after speeding
World.content:
Socceroos star Cristian Volpato has allegedly tested positive for cocaine while driving in Sydney.

The 22-year-old was stopped in a BMW Coupe about 1am today, allegedly travelling 109 kilometres an hour on the Anzac Bridge, a 60km/h zone.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test, which allegedly returned a positive result for cocaine.

Mr Volpato was issued with a speeding fine and has had his international driver's licence suspended for six months, meaning he cannot drive in New South Wales.

A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis, with police confirming inquiries were continuing.

Police will allege they stopped Mr Volpato a few hours earlier, about 11pm yesterday, in the same area where he was also speeding.

He was subjected to a roadside alcohol breath test, which returned a negative result.

The ABC has contacted Football Australia for comment.

The 22-year-old professional soccer player made headlines when he switched allegiance from Italy to Australia in the World Cup this year.

Football Australia has a strict drug regulation policy managed through Sport Integrity Australia.

Players and officials who test positive to prohibited substances without a valid therapeutic use exemption can be suspended for up to four years.

That can be reduced to three months if the use was out of competition and not performance-related.

World.title: Swimmer praises Rinehart for bonuses amid warning to not thank billionaire
World.content:
Freestyle king Kyle Chalmers has welcomed potential windfalls for Australia's Commonwealth Games swimmers after Gina Rinehart offered up cash bonuses for medals and world records.

Amid a spate of high-profile athlete withdrawals from Glasgow 2026, Dolphins squad members have been given a significant incentive to take part.

Billionaire Rinehart said she would deliver the same bonuses that were on offer in the pool at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

Individual swimmers will pocket $20,000 for a gold medal, $15,000 for silver and $10,000 for bronze and $30,000 for a world record.

Gina Rinehart and swimming legend Dawn Fraser watch on at the 2024 Australian Swimming Trials. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Relay team members will also be rewarded with $7,500 per person for a world record, $5,000 for a gold medal, $3,750 for silver and $2,500 for bronze.

Australians are well placed to cash in, with Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh skipping the Glasgow Games as she and other rivals focus on the ensuing Pan Pacific championships.

The swimming bonanza comes as many athletes in other sports lament a lack of financial support, despite Commonwealth Games Australia (CGA) providing a $5,000 grant to every member of the Glasgow team.

Glasgow was asleep and the Games weren't open as Australia got its first win Australia's first victory of the Commonwealth Games comes in a surprise extra session as the bowlers start before the opening ceremony.

"I'm super grateful to have the support of CGA to get us here, but to be able to have some medal incentive, it gives us a lot more purpose and reason," sprint star Chalmers said ahead of the opening ceremony.

"Otherwise you get a medal and the uniform ... so [I'm] very grateful to have supporters.

"CGA's made this possible, and the Commonwealth Games internationally being able to put it on, but to have some incentive for all of our hard work is crucial, especially for us older athletes."

The 28-year-old said Australia's swimmers were "very lucky" with the level of support they received compared to some other sports.

But the seven-time Commonwealth Games gold medallist said it remained "very challenging" for many swimmers to juggle arduous training schedules with work and study.

"It's a choice you make and I guess you kind of understand the financial position of the sport," Chalmers said.

"But fingers crossed there can be change for the next generation to kind of motivate them to continue to make the sacrifices and choose our sport, just to keep those talented athletes in there."

Petria Thomas has distanced the Commonwealth Games team from Ms Rinehart's bonuses. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Rinehart's bonus scheme was announced by Swimming Queensland, of which the mining magnate is patron, while Australia's chef de mission Petria Thomas distanced CGA from it.

"That's a separate arrangement and it's not something that Commonwealth Games Australia is involved in whatsoever," former swimmer Thomas said.

"Good luck to the swimmers, I guess. They have someone backing that performance, but that's a separate matter for them."

A statement from Commonwealth Games Australia "commended" Rinehart for her support of the swimmers, while stressing existing sponsors had committed millions of dollars to get the whole 255-strong team across all sports to Glasgow.

"Mrs Rinehart and her companies are not Australian Team partners," a spokesperson said.

A report in the Sydney Morning Herald today said swimmers had been told not to thank Rinehart when talking to the media after swimming.

Shortly before flying to Scotland, a number of swimmers, including Shayna Jack and Sienna Toohey, posted messages on social media thanking the mining magnate for allowing them to "chase [their] dreams".

Loading Instagram content

The bonuses come on top of annual payments Rinehart makes to many of Australia's top-tier swimmers.

Athletes who win multiple medals will receive a payment for every medal they win.

Your guide to every day of the Comm Games in Australian time Here's the full schedule of every day of the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games with all times and days in AEST.

In a statement, Rinehart said the bonuses were a way of Australia showing appreciation.

"There is something very uplifting about seeing an Australian athlete stand on the podium while our flag is raised," Rinehart said.

Meanwhile, Katarina Johnson-Thompson heads a list of nine members of the England athletics squad that pulled out of the Games on the morning of the opening ceremony.

Four more Olympic medallists – Dina Asher-Smith, Daryll Neita, Matthew Hudson-Smith and Amber Anning – are also out.

Like Keely Hodgkinson, the Olympic 800 metres champion who did not pursue selection, the injured and "gutted" Johnson-Thompson indicated she would switch her focus to the European championships in Birmingham next month.

World.title: Sam Kerr says A-League must find way to bring Matildas back, pay more
World.content:
A lot has been written and said about Sam Kerr over the years, but likening her to a Marvel superhero feels like a new comparison.

"I was really excited when I saw her coming on because I just had this Marvel moment where I was like, 'You have the Hulk," her teammate Midge Purce said after Kerr's influential cameo off the bench in her second game for her new club, which saw it come from 0-2 down to win 3-2.

"Like you thought this was everything and no, we're bringing on the Hulk."

A DC Comics-inspired reference might have been more apt considering she is now playing for Gotham FC, but whether she is Hulk, Batman, or any other fictional crime fighter, Kerr is already back lighting up the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL).

And she hasn't even scored yet.

Kerr made her Gotham FC debut last week. She used to play for the team under its previous banner, Sky Blue FC. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

The Matildas captain opted to resume her career in the USA's top domestic league, after a hugely successful six and a half years with Chelsea in England's Women's Super League (WSL).

"I didn't really see myself starting fresh at a new European club. Coming back to the US has always been something that I wanted to do," Kerr told ABC Sport.

"Being close to [wife Kristie Mewis'] family and just coming back and hopefully winning some trophies.

"I felt like I'd achieved almost everything that I wanted to with Chelsea. So it was just time for change."

A-League Women needs more investment

When it became clear that Kerr was leaving Chelsea, there were some optimists hoping she might return home to Perth Glory in the A-League Women (ALW).

But that is incredibly unlikely while the league remains in its current semi-professional state.

Loading Instagram content

"We need to find a way to get all the best players back," Kerr said, urging greater investment in the Australian women's domestic game.

"If it paid enough and it was a top league, a lot of us Matildas would go back, but to better ourselves for the national team, we have to go overseas.

"I think the A-League was thriving, or the W-League back then was thriving when the national team players and players from the NWSL, players from England were coming over, and whether it was a guest stint or playing, you had the best players in the league, week in, week out, training with our future generation.

"I think the A-League's probably more similar to the NWSL. It's more transitional, probably on the same level as the NWSL off the pitch with things like that.

"But I think the A-League probably needs a little bit more investment, a little bit more time."

Kerr said most Matildas players have to go overseas to further their careers. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Kerr's thoughts reflect broader concerns from players, who have repeatedly spoken out about pay in the ALW, which is the lowest amongst Australia's major women's domestic competitions.

It was not so long ago that the NWSL and ALW, or W-League as it was known, were seen as two of the leading leagues in the world, as players split their time between both.

Now Kerr and goalkeeper Mackenzie Arnold are the only regular Matildas playing in the USA; a handful of others are based in Australia, with most opting to play in Europe.

American league growing

While the ALW has fallen well down the pecking order, the NWSL is now jostling for top billing alongside the WSL.

The NWSL was founded in 2013 with eight teams and now has 16 and has experienced significant commercial growth, exemplified when USA forward Trinity Rodman signed a three-year deal with Washington Spirit reportedly worth $2.86 million a year, making her one of the highest paid female footballers in the world.

Loading...

Gotham is the reigning NWSL champion, and in a huge next chapter, in 2028 will move from its base in New Jersey to a new purpose-built football stadium in Queens, shared alongside Major League Soccer's New York City FC.

Kerr's debut came off the bench in the team's win over Washington last week, which was played at the home of the New York Mets in front of more than 42,000 fans, a record for a women's sport event in New York City.

The home of Major League Baseball's New York Mets hosted Gotham FC's historic game, where Kerr made her club debut. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

A few days later, her second game was a much more low-key affair, playing at a field enveloped by an athletics track, in front of several thousand fans who braved a 2 and a half hour weather delay.

For Kerr, 32, who had played for Gotham FC under its previous iteration as Sky Blue FC, the contrast in her first two games is emblematic of where the league is at.

"It's obviously changed a bit, but a lot has stayed the same too," she said.

"The fans and the stadiums that we're playing in now are what I think we should be playing in.

"And there's always been a lot of fun over here and a lot of excitement about the game, but in so many ways it still feels like the same league."

Kerr said the different styles of football in the NWSL and WSL make them difficult to compare.

Kerr has spent extended periods playing in the ALW, NWSL, and WSL. (Getty Images: Leila Coker/WSL)

"I think everyone's fighting for the top spot in the league, even in men's football, but I don't think it's worth putting my two cents in.

"I love both leagues, but yes, such different games in both countries."

Kerr's teammate, Ireland international Denise O'Sullivan, is another new acquisition for Gotham FC.

"I think it's the best league in the world; we've world-class players in every single team in this league," she said.

"And I think really the best thing about this league is the competitiveness from top to bottom. I don't think you can go into any game not right in it."

Kerr fandom high

Kerr's return is a major talking point for the NWSL and Gotham FC fans.

Amongst the crowd at her second game, there are already several fans sporting newly minted Kerr number 20 jerseys.

The Matildas captain is well known in the global women's football fanbase. (Getty Images: FIFA/Hassan Omar Wamwayi)

"Ecstatic! She's a blue; I'm a Chelsea fan, Gotham fan, so that collaboration, it just works together, I love it," Will from Jersey City said.

Teresa from Brooklyn said she was happy to see Kerr back with the New York-New Jersey-based club.

"Sam has been gone from the league for six and a half years, and we still see her name at the top of the NWSL scoring record. So if any NWSL fan doesn't know her, that's on them," she said.

There's even an eight-year-old girl named, what else but Matilda, or Tilly, who is there with her parents, having just moved to New York from Sydney.

"We love Sam Kerr and we're so excited that this is her team now, our home team is Sam Kerr's new team, super excited," her mum Kiki said.

Kerr is Australia's all-time leading goalscorer. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Not many Australians playing abroad attract this level of fandom, but even as she enters the latter stages of her career, Kerr still has the cachet amongst women's football fans here.

And she will be hoping her form can continue as she eyes off leading the Matildas to next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil.

World.title: Modra's medical records allegedly inappropriately accessed by SA Health staff
World.content:
Three South Australian health staff are being investigated for alleged inappropriate access to the private medical records of AFL star Tony Modra, who suffered serious injuries in a truck crash last month.

SA Health said another five employees were also being "assessed" to determine whether their access to the records "was always appropriate".

While the health department has apologised to Modra's family "for any distress caused", Acting Health Minister Chris Picton described the matter as "concerning".

"Where we do identify somebody who has done the wrong thing, we need to make sure that action is taken," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"People have lost their jobs for this before."

A close-up of the windscreen on the truck Modra was driving at the time of the crash. (Supplied: 9News Adelaide)

Modra underwent facial surgery and was in hospital for days after the crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, in June.

On Instagram, earlier this week the Crows legend posted an update of his progress, saying he was now able to get "out and about", and shared photos of himself in intensive care and recovering with his family.

The Modra family said they do not wish to comment at this time.

The alleged SA Health breach is not the first time that concerns have been raised about hospital staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving high-profile individuals.

A photo of Modra with family a month after the crash. (Instagram: tonymodraofficial)

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after being caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh, who was charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed an SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

Mr Picton was asked about how the alleged breach relating to Modra's records had come to the attention of authorities, and replied that he could not "exactly give you all the details, but I'm happy to check".

Modra shared a photo on Instagram of him in intensive care. (Instagram: tonymodraofficial)

"Because of the way we've got tracking of the system now, we can see every time someone's logged in, every case that people have looked at, and that's why we're able to know and able to investigate these things," he said.

" The very, very small percentage of people who would seek to do such a thing — they can be caught. "

In a statement, SA Health said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

"As a result of a standard audit, three staff are currently under investigation for potential inappropriate access of a SAHLN patient's record. Another five employees are being assessed to ensure their access was always appropriate," the statement said.

"Any staff member who has accessed information inappropriately may be subject to disciplinary processes, which may include termination of their employment.

"Our sincerest apologies go to the family for any distress caused."

SA Health Minister Chris Picton says the majority of staff do the right thing. (ABC News)

Opposition spokesperson Ben Hood said the latest revelation strengthened the case for an inquiry into patient record privacy breaches.

"It's deeply concerning that this again has happened in SA Health. It's a case of the 'standard you walk past is the standard you accept'," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"There is obviously an issue of culture in the department and the government with regards to this, and we think there needs to be an inquiry into it."

The truck Modra was driving at the time of the crash in June. (Supplied: 9News Adelaide)

Premier Peter Malinauskas said the alleged breach was a "disappointing development" but that the "overall majority" of the SA Health workforce, which he said numbered 50,000, did the right thing.

"It's unfortunate that a few individuals here have gone beyond their remit," he said.

"We've seen this happen before with other instances of high-profile incidents and people get caught — and they get caught because we have the systems in place to be able to detect this type of activity."

SASMOA chief industrial officer Bernadette Mulholland says the public needs to have confidence in the integrity of the system. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

South Australian Salaried Medical Officers Association chief industrial officer Bernadette Mulholland said such cases eroded trust in the system.

"It does create some significant concern when we hear these sorts of things may be happening," she said.

"It's really important that these records are to remain confidential, and the only people who should be looking at those records are people providing clinical care or it's necessary for the patient care.

"We want to have confidence in our health system."

World.title: Norway set to file complaint over Trump's push to overturn red card
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's role in clearing Folarin Balogun from a mandatory one-game ban at the World Cup is set to provoke a formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators.

The Norway soccer federation said its board of directors will consider filing the complaint at its next meeting, likely on August 6.

"We need our leader in FIFA to say that this was an error," Norwegian federation president Lise Klaveness told The Times in an interview.

After Trump called FIFA president Gianni Infantino, a one-game ban for Balogun's red-card tackle against Bosnia-Herzegovina was deferred so he could play against Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake.

Belgium beat the US 4-1 after a chaotic 36 hours at the World Cup. The Belgium players were seemingly fired up by one of the greatest controversies in tournament history.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (left) with Crown Prince Haakon of Norway and Football Association of Norway president Lise Klaveness. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Trump called the referee's red card for Balogun after video review a "horrible" call and took credit for getting FIFA to review what should routinely have been a one-game ban.

"We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process," Klaveness said of the FIFA ruling that was unprecedented in the past 60 years at World Cups.

"When you bend a rule like this, you're on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk," said the former Women's World Cup player for Norway, who is an elected member of European soccer body UEFA's executive committee.

Klaveness is a lawyer and judge who has positioned the Norwegian federation as a conscience in world soccer since her election in 2022.

"It is a worry for the game when you compromise fundamental rules of the game," she said about not enforcing Balogun's ban.

Norway previously joined a London-based NGO's complaint to the FIFA ethics committee alleging Infantino breached a statutory duty of political neutrality, including by creating a peace prize to award to Trump at the World Cup draw in December.

EU politicians launch bid to investigate FIFA boss A group of European politicians launches a bid to begin an investigation into how and why a red card for an American football star was overturned at the World Cup.

The close personal and political ties between Trump and Infantino include the US president believing the soccer official could be a good pick as next secretary general of the United Nations, the New York Post reported this week.

The human rights NGO, FairSquare, also has filed an ethics complaint about the Balogun incident to the International Olympic Committee, where Infantino is an elected member, about breaching its rules on political neutrality.

FIFA and the IOC rarely acknowledge or provide updates on potential cases before their ethics bodies.

The independence of FIFA's process to handle complaints alleging unethical conduct has been questioned since the lead investigator and judge both were replaced in 2017, in the second year of Infantino's presidency.

FIFA has yet to publish documents explaining how its disciplinary judges reached verdicts about Balogun or other World Cup players.
